div.head: McDOUCALUS Pateo SELF-RAISING FLOUR AME:ED, FASHIONS OF TO-DA N% WOMEN'S CHAT,
div.p: McDOUCALUS Pateo SELF-RAISING FLOUR AME:ED, FASHIONS OF TO-DA N% WOMEN'S CHAT,

Among the very charming adjuncts of a fashionable woman's toilette are dainty shoulder scarves and fluffy feather boas which, to be worn correctly, are carelessly draped round the shoulders. At all the smartest social functions these pretty out- door wraps are much izt evidence, and it is only their expensiveness which will debar them from becoming common as they are ex- ceedingly and generally becoming. The shoulder scarves, however, are much less costly than the feather stoles and are almost as pretty. Some of the newest are of soft chine ribbon or -gauze, some twenty-five to thirty inches wide draped round the shoulders and gathered into an ornamental clasp or buckle in front, while the ends are left to fall loose in front and are finished by fringe or lace. Others again are shaped something like a cape in .'front and are made of embroidered crepe de chine edged with silk fringe. Old lace scarves which are priceless heirlooms hitherto useless may also be used for the same

Children's parties have become quite fashionable. This was not the case before the one given by the King and Queen at Buckingham Palace,but since then,several of the house,s and gardens of the great and wealthy,have been gay with the patter of little feet and childish voices. It is scarcely likely that the stately butler, or the gorgeous footman, can approve of these juvenile entertainments as it has not hitherto been the custom , for the great mansions to be invaded by hosts of little folks, but since it has become fashionable to give a . children's party they have perforce had to put up with it, Not all however are intended to benefit ona,y the chil- dren of the wealthy, as the fete given by Lady Ancaster ; at the Batanic Gardens, Regents Park, has been organised chiefly for the entertainment of the children of the poor. It is sometimes a little embarrassing to receive credit for acts which one never contemplated, even though the acts are such as a great many peopledesired to see per- formed. Some such reflection as this must have entered the mind of the King, who, since his accession has been credited with pee'sonal intervention on behalf of a good many causes. It may be that in some cases the reports which have been published in reference to his Majesty's action are not without foundation, but it is certain that if the market for such paragraphs continues to grow, there will be no backwardness in supplying them on the , ?art of those enterprising writers who make so many contributions, more or less dependable to the columns of the London Press. The opportunities which offer themselves in this direction are the more abundant on account of a rule from which the Royal family very rarely depart, that erroneous statements which appear in the public press are not to be corrected. This rule has many disadvantages, but perhaps the advantages outweigh them, because if there were no such understanding, when speculative announceanents were riot contradicted it would at once be assumed that they were accurate. France has been quick to do honour to Madame Curie, to whom belongs, with her husband, Professor P. Curie, the distinction of having discovered radium. Not since Rontgen startled the world by his discovery of the X rays, has science rendered up such wonderful secrets, as Madame Curie has 'discovered in the almost ethereal properties of radium, and the new theories it suggests with regard to our universe. Madame Curie, whose native country is Poland, began her researches into the rare elements some six or seven years ago, before the discovery of the Rontgen rays was made known. The wonders of radium are not easily grasped by ordinary people, and consequently popular interest has not been greatly excited over their discovery, but nevertheless Madame Curie will rank as second to none amongst the 'great scientific discoverers of this, or any other age. The little hand of clerics has once more succeedSd in --,preventing the passage of the perennial Deceased Wife's Sister Bill. Public opinion as represented in Parliament, has repeatedly declared itself, in favour of altering the civil law so as to perm t a man to marry the sister of a former wife, yet year after year the tortuous andeunbusiness-like methods of the Legislature permit the will of the majority to be defied. This state of things inflicts a great injustice upon many women in the British Colonies, and it is one that exists alone in this country throughout the civilised world. The country just now, though looking at its best, has few attractions for those people who suffer from that distressing complaint "hay fever." Most authorities agree that, it is caused by the pollem of flowering grasses, but there are many town residents living far removed from hay fields, who habitually fall victims to the fever. Some indeed have even gone so far as to declare that an attack of hay fever has been induced by the mere sight of a picture of haymaking. To some minds this would seem to be an utter impossibility, but it is certain that many people are extremely susceptible to the ailment, and though many remedies may be tried it is rarely that one can be found that is effective. Opinions differ as to whether a sun hat is of any use to a horse, but fashion has certainly moved in a sensible and humanitarian direction, in permitting coachmen and footmen to wear summer headgear and livery, during the hot broiling days. Not so long ago, the tall Silk hat, and livery of superfine clothovere the only possible wear for the servants of a smart equipage, but recent years have seen various relaxations of this cast-iron rule. Some people thought that the change, and also the provision of straw hats for horses and dogs; woUld prove but a mere passing eccentricity but we seem at last to have learned that it is a duty, in very hot weather, as in very cold, to extend help, and show.con- sideration for others. - _ - -

Court festivities have been frequent of late, and it is often amusing to note the varied descriptions in the different papers of the toilettes worn by the Royal ladies. One will put her Majesty into white, another insists upon pale mauve orheliotrope, whileanother fixes upon grey. Then the descriptions of the jewels worn would bewilder anyone searching after accuracy. When her Majesty wears colours these are almost invariably res- tricted to mauve, grey, and heliotrope, though lately she has appeared, on severval occasions, in pale biscuit tones, which become her so well. River hats are prettier than ever, the most charming perhaps being the capeline of drawn lace, the lace droop- ing here and there over the brim, and the whole wreathed with roses. The Breton hat is another favour- ite form of headgear for river wear, and it Will be much in evidence at the seaside and in the,country,this month and next. Built of coloured linen, it matches the gown with which it is worn, and the brim bound with a darker shade, is stitched with many rows ,of silk. Such a hat may have a ruching, or twist of soft iibbon round the crown, ending in a large knot at the side, or it may be left severely alone, when with a neat holland ()I- nnen gown, it perhaps looks its best and is most useful. An excellent way of blending skirt and blouse to- gether—a very necessary procedure just now—is to have pinafore straps of the same fabric as the kirt cut in one with the shaped waist belt, these straps•crossing the shoulders where they widen out into small capes. Dainty brooches, or buttons, fasten the straps here and there and keep them in position. To the home worker, such an idea opens up wide possibilities, as infinite variety can be secured by means of blouses worn beneath the straps, yet always these blend the whole into one complete costume.

div.head: PRETTY EVENM4G TCSItETTE.
div.p: A PRETTY EVENM4G TCSItETTE.

purpose. The feather boas are most popular in white, and perhaps the prettiest are of marabout, but these .are also the most perish- able. Others again are of coque's feathers and are most becoming, while ostrich feathers lightly curled always look well and do not suffer from a visit to the cleaners, but look as good as new. All these airy nothings are more ornamental than useful but give a pretty look to a toilette. The most 'fashionable shape •of boa is depicted in my first illustration. It is wide and flat and finished by tails of the marabout feathers in very much the same manner as our furs vil.n.e last winter. A wrap of this description can not only be worn in the afternoon with a dressy frock, but is suited for theatre or restaumnt. _

The pretty evening toilette depicted is made of fine lace and trimmed with ,roses of different tones of pink and cream. ,Lace is everywhere popular for evening wear, and is -either of the very fine or very coarse description. 'Some of the smartest evening toilettes for young girls are made with floral sashes, these consisting ,of a deep waistband of silk or folded chiffon from which Collif two

div.head: -THE FASHIONABLE BOA'
div.p: -THE FASHIONABLE BOA'

long ends made of a lattice work of rose ,-r-,talks and rose buds caught at the . points with tiny roses. The effect is very charming, bit: the wearer -of this dainty novelty must never forget its presence as to sit on it would work instant destruction to its fragile loveliness! Other sashes are of very wide ribbon on which are hand-painted clusters and wreaths of flowers. An opportunity is therefore given by the girl of artistic tastes to employ her leisure hours in painting original designs on the riblxin and so giving her gown a cachet all its own at the expense of a little trouble and time. It is 'noticeable that sashes this season are made without any loops or bows at the back, the two long ends coming simply from below the back of the high swathed waistband. There are many and charming specimens of headgear just now of p cturesque or plaih description. Of -the latter the so - called "cornet de plaisir " toquet is perhaps the most admirable with its up-rolled brim tied over the crown and the round flat shape which has a wide round brim slightly up-turned and a low bee-hive crown. iThis shape which is decidedly French-looking is worn tilted well forward over a high coiffure with for trim- ming a stiff wreath saf foliage r- flowers, or a

div.head: SMART HAT.
div.p: A SMART HAT.

wreath of ribbon loops arr#nged round the crown, while flowers are massed at the back where the hat is turned up sharply. There is something very chic about this kind of hat which is particularly suited to a round face. Leghorn and Tuscan straws are amongst the most fashionable, while coarse straws are not nearly so much in evidence.. The low dressed coiffure is not suited to the present day hat, and has therefore been abandoned by the most fashionable women.

The accompanying illustration gives a good idea of what the back view of hat and hair should be of a really smart woman. The hair, whether worn high dr low, is rather full at the sides and nape of the neck, and pretty jewel- studded combs and clasps are worn in the evening with charming results. For day time imitation turquoises or amber are introduced into the tortoise-shell. Earrings are also still worn, and the introduction of the screW ear- ring has obviated the necessity of piercing the ears, a somewhat barbarous custom which has up to recently been considered necessary. The fashion is growing of wearing coloured veils to match the colour of the hat. In navy blue, brown, or even green the mode may be con- sidered successful, but it is not always a fashion to be adopted as there are some com- plexions which do not look nice in these circumstances. Nothing really looks so nice or is so becoming as a fine black veil or one with a fine white ground and black spots. Of course, there are veils with lattice work lines in black on a white ground or vice versa, but these are not really very becoming, but only obtain a vogue because of their novelty. In France the fashion of wearing a long lace veil hanging straight from the hat almost to the waist has been revived, but it is too un- English to obtain popularity on this side a att Channel,

div.head: LYMM CONTEST.
div.p: LYMM CONTEST.

The first walking contest arranged in the village took place on Saturday, when 13 started from the Crown Inn, Booth's Hill, to walk to the Cat and Lion, Stretton, and back, a distance of about 12 miles. There was a goodly crowd to watch the start and the finish created consider- able interest. Private Harold Clare, of the Lymtn Voltmteers, who went to the front during the late war under Lieutenant Ridgway,was the first in (Ihr. 43min.), and his win was a very popular one. The second was George Shaw (11r. 47nin.), and the third William Leather (Ihr. 49min.). Medals were given as prizes.
Up to Wednesday 142 dead bodies and 69 injured per- sons have been extricated from the wreckage of the train at Asencio, North Spain. It is believed that there are 50 corpses yet to be brought out.

div.head: BY HARRIS BURLAND. AUTHOR OF ibACOBRAIETC.
div.p: BY HARRIS BURLAND. AUTHOR OF ibACOBRAIETC.
CHAPTER IV.—Contzflued.

Mavaziwy stood for a few minutes by the terrace, trying to calm the fury of her mind and collect her thoughts. She was still breathing hard from the struggle, and two red rings round her wrists bore witness to her silame. She turned towards the house, walking round the shrubbery to aside entrance where she hoped to slip in unobserved, and go straight to her own room. It was no time to go through the farce of being a polite hostess. The ready excuse of a headache would do for John Walroyd. His brother needed nn excuse at all. As she passed into the drive she heard the sound of footsteps coming up the hill. She shrank out of the moonlight behind a laurustinus. She had to cross the drive Ito Teach her destination, •and did not wish 'to meet anyone. She thought it was probably Cyrus Walroyd who might have taken a short walk to master his agitation before he entered 'the house.

Then the tall figure of a man strode ,out of the shadow of the avenue into an open patch of light and stood still with the moon stream ing full on his face. Mavanwy drew 'in breath sharply, and bit her lips to restrain cry._ For it was the face and form Of Emr

Tredegar. He was str.ring at a window in lihe house, llavanw's ,own bedroom window. It was in darkness out in gazed at it as though it held all the light of the universe. Mavanwy looked at him in horror. His face was drawn and white, and there was something unearthly in the I.ook of his eyes. His hair was wild and unkempt. She knew that he 'had come for her, that her dead lover had come from the sea to call her, to speak to her, to take her away with him. She had waited for this hour and now he had come. Her overwrought ixain fancied that he had come up the silver vithway from the west and together they ltould tread the same pathway back to whence he came. She stepped forward with open Oitms, and crying out his name, sank heavily ‘Lo,the ground. When she Came to her senses she found herself in a pair of strong arms and warm 'tassionate kisses were being showered upon her eyes and cheeks, and lips and hands. She smiled faintly and closed her hands. If .this were death, it was good to die. " Mavanwy, Mavanwy," he cried, "what is the matter, darling ? Don't you know me? I am here, safe and well, your lover Emrys. I landed two hours ago. The ship is still in the bay. Mavanwy, my dearest one, speak to me, look at me, after all these months." And again he kissed her and still again. She opened her eyes and looked at him. Then she threw her arms round his neck and knew the glorious truth. Emrys Tredegar was alive.

estimating the truth of the story. When Tredegar had finished, he drew from us pocket the half disc of yellow metal. He told them he had picked it up on the shore He handed it to Mr. Morgan. The latter examined it carefully, and with evident interest. "This is very extraordinary," he said, after he had scrutinised the lettering. "It is an old Welsh thing. I cannot translata it for you, but I c.-:.n give you a letter of introduction to a man who is an expert in such matters. I should say it had something to do with bards or priests. There is a sym- bol on it which I have seen before somewhere —a circle and a triangle. Let me see, where was it? Ah, I remember now I It was on the gold ring you gave me last Christmas, Cyrus. That is very curious." Cyrus Walroyd leaned forward and laughed. "It is curious," he said. "I remember the ring. I bought it in London. It was guaranteed to be early Welsh; but then we Americans generally get taken in." Mr. Morgan crossed the room to the cabinet, and the two Walroyds exchanged swift glances when his back was turned. He fOund the ring, and showed it to Emrys. It was a plain circlet of dull gold, and the mark was certainly there, faint and small, on the inner surface. "This is very extraordinary 1" Tredegar said. "I cannot understand how such a i ring could have any connection with a half disc found on a lonely Pacific island." "You spoke of a ship," John Walroyd said —" an old Spanish galloon. It is possibly a piece of captured treasure. It might have belonged to some Welsh or English gentle- man taken on the high seas. May I look at it for a moment ?" Tredegar handed him the disc, and the latter examined it carefully, and passed it to his brother. Cyrus Walroyd weighed it thoughtfully in his hand. "It is certainly gold," he said, "and doubt- less of great antiquity. It is a pity that half of it is missing. I am collecting Welsh antiquities. You need not smile, John P. Walroyd. I am one of those Americans who like to interest themselves in the old things of the country they live in. You , would not care to -sell it, I suppose, Mr. : Tredegar ? " " I don't think so:" Tredegar ianswered. , "It means more to me than anyone else." 1 : "Of course—of course." Cyrus exclaimed; ' "it does mean more .to you than to anyone else. Yet it will .not recall very pleasant ' memories." "The remembrance of past misery is often happiness," Mavanwy said with a smile. "Just as the recollection of past pleasure is often pain." Cyrus Walroyd •frowned ever so slightly and handed the disc 'back to Tredegar, who placed it in his pocket. For a few seconds there was silence. Then Tredegar rose from his chair to go. 'lt was after twelve o'clock and he had a long walk before him. "You will go by the road, I suppose," said Mr. Morgan, rising and holding out the box of cigars to his visitor. "No, by the path across the bog," replied i Tredegar, taking a cigar and biting off the end. "It is quite light and I know the way well." ' The two Walroyds rose simultaneously. "We may as well walk with you, Mr. Trede- gar," they said. "We told 'the coachman not to call for us. We shall go most of the way together. I suppose you are staying in the village." "Yes, at the Tredegar Arms. It's stuffy and uncomfortable, but one can't choose in a place like Garth." "Good-night, Mavanwy." And he held out his hand. She took it, and he saw a sudden ~look of anxiety cross her face. "Good-night," she said glancing at the ; others. She wanted to speak for a moment with him alone. But she did not see how it could be managed, or how to let Tredegar . know that she wished it. Neither her father nor Cyrus Walroyd were likely to give her the chance. But .her woman's quick wit con- ceived an idea. It was only a possibility. But she snatched at it. 1 They all went out into the hall together, 1 while the Walroyds put on their coats. Tredegar had nothing but the clothes he stood up in. The hall was a large square one with two pillars supporting the ceiling. Three great windows in a line opened out on . to the lawn. The moonlight was shining . brightly outside, but most of the hall was in darkness, save kr the faint light from the candle which Mavanwy had carried out from the drawing-room. Suddenly Mavanwy gave a little cry, and catching Tredegar by the arm dropped the candle and pointed to one of the windows. All the men turned and looked in the direction in which she was pointing. There was nothing to be seen. "What is it, Mavanwy," her father said sharply. "A man! " she replied. "I saw his face at the window:" The two Walroyds and Mr. • Morgan rushed to the door, and made their way quickly round to the lawn. Tredegar would have followed, but he was held back by Mavanwy's touch on the arm. He laughed. He saw her little ruse and loved her for it. He took her in his arms and kissed her. She freed herself from his passionate embrace. "Be careful to-night," she whispered hurriedly. "Some of the planks across the • dykes are narrow, and the dykes are deep. Cyrus Walroyd is no friend of yours. He has no scruples." "I have done him no wrong," 10 answered. "He is no friend of yours," she repeated. "Please be careful for my sake." "Why should he harm me ? " "I can't tell you, Emrys," she answered. "Perhaps you can guess. But be careful." Tredegar laughed. " I think I am a match for the two of them," he said. Three figures passed the window and were silhouetted igainst the moonlight. Tredegar lit a match and groped for the candle on the floor. He re-lit it just as the others entered the hall door. They all three glanced at the lovers. 1 1 "A pretty trick, Mavanwy," said Mr. Morgan with a sneer. " Quite a stage trick. I am sorry you did not come with us, Mr. Tredegar." "I thought Mavanwy might be afraid of being left alone, Mr. Morgan." "Most thoughtful of you, I am sure." Tredegar did not reply. His eyes were fixed on the window. The other three men had their backs to it. Then Mavanwy screamed, and again pointed. But this time it was in earnest. "Beautiful," said Mr. Morgan. 2' You are doing it much better this time, Mavanwy." "You fool ! " exclaimed Tredegar, taking a step forward; "look behind you." They all looked, and black against the moonlight they saw the gigantic head and shoulders of a man, and a great pair of hands grasping the window sill. The flickering candle threw so feeble a light AgrOss the wide hall that none of them could distinguish the features. But the whole outline seemed dim and shaggy, like the outline of a beast. Tredegar sprang forward, and the head and shoulders disappeared. Two seconds later he was out of the window, followed by the others. They saw something moving swiftly down ,the shadows of the shrubbery. Then it slid over the wall and they heard a crash among the trees. They all rushed to the spot, but saw nothing. They could, however, hear it moving through the wood. Tredegar was for following up the chase, but the others refused, and he could not very well go by himself. . They all returned to the drive. There the Walroyds and Tredegar said good-night, and

div.head: CHAPTER V. THE FACE AT THE WINDOW.
div.p: CHAPTER V. THE FACE AT THE WINDOW.

'Flys minutes afterwards they entered the house together. Cyrus Walroyd had already concocted an excuse for Mavanwy, telling the others that she had felt unwell and had gone to bed. Mr. Morgan understood, but he could not read from the American's face what had been the result of their interview. If a thunderbolt had fallen from heaven .it could not have caused more consternation than the appearance of the two lovers at the door of the smoking-room. All three men rose to their feet and looked at the form of Tredegar as though it had been some gigantic apparition looming through the blue wreaths of smoke from their cigars. Mavanwy was ,the first to speak. " Emrys, father," she said, nervously. "Don't you know him? He has come back —he is not dead; he landed to-night in the bay—Captain Edward Williams' boat. I met him at the door."

She stopped, and Emrys moved across the room with extended hand. The three men gave him a cordial greeting. They could scarcely do less with any show of decency. But one or two keen glances passed between Cyrus and Mr. Morgan. Mavanwy noticed them, and her cheeks burned with shame; but Emrys, rejoicing in his return to life and the woman he loved, saw nothing but a kindly circle of men extending him a hearty welcome. Mr. Morgan offered him the most comfortable chair, selected a cigar from his own special box, poured him out a whisky-and-soda, and the whole party drew round the fire, in a genial ring of friendship. And there, in the firelight, Tredegar told of his adventures, of the ship- wredlc, of the horrors of the island, of his solitary life, and how nine months after he had first landed a small ship had appeared off ,the coast. Her sails were torn and some of her spars broken. She had been driven out of her course by a great storm. Then Tredegar told how he had raised a signal on the cliffs—a shirt tied to one of the oars— and how no one had answered. Then how at night he had lit a great fire, and had falYen on his knees and prayed; and in less than an holies time he had heard the splash of oars and the shouts of men's voices. He had then gone down to the shore and shouted out warnings, telling them to wait till daybreak, and then row round the coast to the other !ravine. Then he had heard the oars die away in the distance, and he had spent his last nigh Von the island in making his way round to the place where they had made their first encampment. At the break of day he lit another .fire of damp wood at the entrance of the gorge, and a pillar of smoke had guided his rescuers to the place. When he had .been taken on board the vessel, he found to his surprise that the captain hailed from Garth, and it had seemed to him as though he had stepped straight from .the horrors of the island on to the shores ,of Cardiganshire. The captain, however, had not visited his native village for over two years, and Tre- degar had to give rather than receive news. The ship was bound for Liverpool, and Cap- tain Williams had decided to put into Car- digan Bay, and land for a few hours to see his wife and children. And this is how he, Tre- degar, had come without warning by tele- gram or letter. This was the first place they had touched at since they left the island. All this he told in the firelight ; but one thing he did not tell. He said nothing of the strange monster on the island, nor of how his companions had died. Somehow or other he felt that he could not speak of these terrible things in the presence of Mavanwy. So he was silent on this point. He led his hearers to suppose that some of his companions had been killed by wild beasts, and that some had died of starvation.

While he was telling his story, Mavanwy's eyes were filled with tears. He told it in simple words, with no attempt at exaggerat- ing its horrors or painting his own misery with fine language. But it was sufficiently pathetic in itself. One of his hands was in the shadow by her side, and she touched it gently as he told of the awful solitude of the past nine months. Her touch told him that he had never been alone, and that her heart and thoughts had been always with him. Mr. Morgan listened with keen interest, and his heart was softened towards Tredegar. It was a pity, he said to himself, that the fellow was poor, for he was a fine specimen of a man. He then formed some vague idea in his mind of the young man making his fortune by lecturing on his expei,iences. He had heard of such things being done. The face of Cyrus Wairoyd was in the shadow, and his brother's features were set like a mask. Only the keen eyes showed the interest that he took in the narrative. A close observer might have noticed that they followed every expression of the speaker's features. as though the mind was drinking in every word, weighing the evidence. and

div.head: ExammerPaturday, July 4, 1903.

set out towards Garth. Tredegar remem- bered Mavanwy's warning, and kept all his senses on the alert. It seemed ridiculous to suppose that Cyrus Walroyd meant him any harm. In any case, it was very unlikely that he would do anything on their walk back to Garth. As a matter of fa.ct, he found the two brothers most charming and entertaining companions, and before they were half way across the bog he was ashamed of himself for having harboured any suspicion against them. Cyrus made himself particularly agreeable, and just as they were nearing the place when they would have to part company he gave Emrys a cordial invitation to spend a few days at Plas Tredegar. "As you remarked," he said, "the inn is stuffy and uncomfortable. There are one or two things in connection with the house that I should like to talk over with , you, and I would rather you saw to them personally. Besides, you would perhaps like to have a look at your own home, and see we are not damaging it in any way. I daresay we can fix you up in your old bedroom if you tell IN which it is."

Tredegar gladly accepted the offer and arranged to move in on the following day. He could not get Mavanwy's warning out of his mind. But he did not look forward to the inn with pleasure. Besides, as VValroyd had suggested, he did wish to sleep a night in his old home. From mere sentimental reasons he realised the degradation of the owner of the finest house within twenty miles being an outcast at a small inn. Yet if he had Lou BA es "maid rather have slept on the be." -1 LlSstiel have accepted this insolent hospita!, Walroyd had shrewdly guessed that MaN It- . •

_ had told him nothing. _ They parted where a narrow bridge crossed the little tributary of the Llyn, and in less than a quarter of an hour Tredegar was in his tiny bedroom at the Tredegar Arms. He had much to think of before he went to sleep. It seemed as though his cup of joy was full to overflowing, for had he not once more held Mavanwy in his arms, and all his poverty, and all his past suffering faded away to nothing, in the light of this great happiness. But as he slept the shadow of a great fear came over his dreams. The past horrors of the island rose before him, and a wild face with tawny hair haunted him through all the night.

THE
CHAPTER VI.
WHAT HAPPENED AT THE PLAS TREDEGAR.

IN the morning Tredegar walked over to Llanfihangel, a small town some six miles off, and purchased a complete outfit. He had never realised before how much it cost to equip a man with even theloare necessities of a wardrobe, when one has lost everything. It was fortunate that he was not expected to pay cash for anything. The tradespeople welcomed him with open arms, and he could have bought the contents of every shop if he had wished to do so. He returned with is many brown paper parcels as he could carry and sent them up to the Plas Tredegar. But there was one thing he could not purchase, and that was a suit of clothes. None of the ready-made articles would fit his gigantic form, and he was glad that there was no excuse for buying them. The old blue serge manufactured on board ship by a sailor, would have to serve him for both morning and evening wear. He left the inn at five o'clock and walked up the cliffs to his old home. The Plas Tredegar stood some 300 feet above the level of the sea on a hill facing the North West. It lay about a quarter of a mile inland and the grounds ran down to the edge of the cliff itself. The house was one of the oldest and most important in the county. It was said that a Tredegar had lived there in the tenth century, when the building had consisted of no more than a round low tower of rough and uncemented stone. Part of the tower still remained. It stood alone almiliost on the edge of the cliff. The house itself Was irregular in shape, and comprised almost every style of architecture from the thirteenth to the eighteenth centuries. It was not large compared to some of the great historic houses of England, but no Tredegar would have ex- changed it for Raby, or Alnwick, or Arundel. It had been to them the ever-living symbol of their race ; every wing of it marked some epoch in their history. The Normans, nay even the Saxons before them, were but in- vaders in the eyes of the Tredegars. They ;laimed to be Britons, and their curiously levised pedigree, which was painted on the )ak panels of the hall, showed a descent which ran back through history to the farthest realms of myth and fable. The grounds, like those of many houses along the coast, were thickly wooded, so as to afford some protection from the westerly gales, and the house itself was scarcely visible from the sea. The old builders had small sympathy with extensive views. The beauties of sunset and storm meant nothing to them. They only sought protection—a roof to keep off the rain, deep woods to keep off the wind, and thick walls to keep out their enemies. It was with mingled feelings of pride and shame that Emrys Tredegar returned to the home of his forefathers. Every inch of the house and grounds had been familiar to him from his boyhood. His face flushed as he walked up the drive and caught the faint glimpse of the sunlight on the old grey walls, and the mullioned windows, and the great porch and doorway, built by Inigo Jones in the seventeenth century. It was difficult to accept strangers' hospitality in such a place. Yet he thanked God that it was not yet lost to him, and though the rent he received was barely sufficient to pay the interest on the numerous mortgages executed by his uncle and grandfather, there was still a hope that he might be able to live in it again. Yet it was hard to think that no Tredegar lived within, its walls. As far as Emrys could re- member, he was the first of all his race to hire out his home to strangers. The Walroyds, however, received him with such cordiality and did so much to put him at his ease in a rather embarrassing posilion, that these melancholy thoughts were soon banished from his mind. They set apart a !mite of rooms for his use, consisting of a bed- !room, sitting room, and bath room, told off a man servant to act as his valet, and did their utmost to make him feel that he was the host and owner of the house, and that they were only the guests. Noticinc, his costume, they neither of them dressed for dinner, and even went so kr as to select rather old clothes for the occasion.

After dinner they adjourned to the smoking room and chatted on general subiccts. About 9.30 a man from the village inn brought up a letter for Tredegar. He glanced at the writing, and saw that it was from Mavanwy. He placed it in his pocket. He did not care to read it before the two Wal- royds. At eleven o'clock John Walroyd went to bed. Then Cyrus suggested that they should go to Tredegar's own sittiAg room and discuss business. He told the foctman to take across the cigars, whisky, and glasses. Then the two men went into the room and settled themselves down in two comfortable chairs. This room was one of the oldest in the house, and had formed part of the original dwelling built by Mabon Tredegar in the twelfth century. The walls and floors were of stone, and the single large window with its semi-circular arch had been constructed before the time of mullions and transoms, The lower half of it had been filled in with a large sheet of plate glass framed in iron which opened outwards on hinges. Opposite to the entrance of the apartment there was another door set in a deep stone archway. This opened into the bedroom. Beyond the latter was a third room, originally nothing but a small stone cell. This had been converted into a bath room. All the rooms were on the ground floor. From his earliest boyhood Tredegar had always taken a fancy to these rooms. He had conjured up all sorts of legends about them. Their very discomfort, and their grim cold- ness had spoken to his boyish fancy of warlike people and troublous times. It was here that he had conjured up visions of Cadwallader,. and Taliesin, and had held the place single handed against a hundred English knights. In those days the sitting room had been his bedroom, and the other two apartments had

been filled with lumber. As he looked at them now, he could not help feeling jealous of the changes that wealth had accomplished. The stone floors were covered with thick Turkey carpets, and the bare walls hung with velvet tapestries. The electric light glowed from a dozen shaded globes. Handsome pieces of old oak furniture were scattered about the room, and rare pieces of china ornamented every shelf and table. The bedroom had been furnished by Maple in the Louis XV. style, and the bathroom had been transformed into a little paradise of white tiles and smooth marble, and nickel plated fittings. All this had been done in a year by the power of an unlimited banking account. The Walroyds had taken the place for fourteen years, and had spared no expense in making it a luxurious home.

The two men lit their cigars and for a few moments neither of them spoke. Tredegar's th ughts had run back through the past years to his boyhood, and Walroyd seemed to be turning over some knotty problem in his mind. At last the latter broke the,rsilence.

"I have a proposition to make to you, Mr, Tredegar," he said. "It will of course require consideration on your part, for it is on a matter of considerable importance. I only hope you will not be offended it I speak a little plainly. At any rate you may be sure that I mean no offence." "I shall take no offence if none is meant, Mr. Walroyd," he replied. "The rent I pay for this house is as much as I can afford," Walroyd con,tinued. "It is, in fact, more than you could get from anyone else. But I think I am right in saying that this sum, together with the rents you get from the farms, cottages, etc., is barely sufficient to pay the interest on the mortgages." "If you wish to know," Tregedar an- swered coldly, " I will tell you that I get at present about Lzoo a year from the estate. Six years ago it was about 800. The farms and houses are all let, and the decrease is not due to loss of tenants, but to general agricultural depression. If one farmer was to go, I should have nothing. This, however, can scarcely interest you." "It interests me greatly," answered Wal- royd. "I do not ask out of idle curiosity. I am prepared to make you an offer for the house and estate, which will pay off the mortgages and leave you a clear sum of 50,000. You will have a decent income for life."

"It is impossible to consider it," Tredegar answered, abruptly. "You will, moreover," continued Walroyd, "be freed from the possibility of • absolute ruin. The mortgagees cannot be very com- fortable about their security. A margin of E,200 a year is not much when the interest amounts to nearly 8,000 a year. If they foreclose and there is a forced sale, they will probably not get their money back, and you will get nothing." "It is impossible to sell the Tredegar estate," Tredegar replied; and then as he moved slightly in his chair something crackled in his pocket. It was Mavanwy's letter. He took a long drink of whisky-and-soda, and took up a cigarette with trembling fingers. He must think! He must think! 'Mavanwy ! With this money they could be married! He rose to his feet and, turning his face away from Walroyd, who was watching him narrowly, pretended to search on the mantel piece for a match-box. He could not think clearly. It was impossible to decide. On the one hand, happiness; on the other, the duty he owed to his an- cestors—the pride of race which bade him hold on to the estate to the last. It was im- possible to decide till the matter had been thrashed out in his mind. He turned to Wal- royd with a smile. "It is a big matter," he said. " I will think it over. Let us talk of something else." And sitting down in his chair, he drained his glass and puffed at his cigarette till he was almost hidden in the blue smoke. The conversation turned on general topics, qnd neither man mentioned the thing that was uppermost in their minds. At twelve o'clock Cyrus Walroyd poured Tredegar out another whisky-and-soda, .said "good -night," and went off to bed. Tredegar heard him walk along the passage, and then heard his footsteps die away up a flight of stone stairs. Directly Tredegar was alone he drew Mavanwy's letter from his pocket, and opened it with the eager expectancy of a lover. But after he had read half a dozen lines, he rose to his feet with an oath, and striding across the floor, laid his hand on the handle of the door. Then he appeared to think better of his intentions, and returning to the fireplace, finished the letter. It was short, and ran as follows: "DEAREST,--I have just heard that you have accepted the Walroyds' invitation to stay at the Plas Tredegar. I hinted some- thing to you last night, but now I must speak out. If Cyrus W alroyd had been a man of honour, he would not have asked you to be his guest. As a man of honour yourself, you cannot accept him as a host. Cyrus Walroyd asked me to marry him last night. I refused, and he insulted me. My father wishes me to marry him. He is your worst enemy. If this is too late to stop you from going to his house, leave it as soon as you can. With fondest love, my darling Emrys. I thank God every hour that you have been brought back to me..

"From your loving and devoted " MAVANWY." Tredegar's face flushed scarlet, and his huge frame trembled with emotion. Once again he clenched his great fists and strode towards the door. He would haul this cad from his room and beat the life out of him! The insolence of the beast ! To receive with open arms the rival he had tried to displace And on the very night of his attempt ! "He insulted her !" he repeated. "He insulted her !" By all that is holy he shall pay for it. But not yet !" (Tc It rontinued.)

ALMOST INCREDIBLE!

(To THE EDITOR OF THE WARRINGTON EXAMINER.) DEAR SIR, As very many readers will doubtless be like myself, firm believers in that handy and effective household remedy, Chas. Forde's bile beans, I should like to report an interesting experience I recently had. I was per- mitted to look through the foreign letters received at the bile bean company's central depot, Leeds, and the experience was what might be described as an "eye- opener." I cannot, of course, bear in mind all the places I saw written at the heads of the letters, but I do remem- ber seeing actual orders from Constantinople; Smyrna; Accra, Gold Coast, Western Africa; Mani- toba • Jamacia ; The Straits Settlements; Secundera- bad,Adia •' Irkutsk, Siberia; Venice . Shiraz, Persia; Egypt ; Barbadoes; Hamburg ; Nice ; Salonica, ; Lausanne; Malta; Toronto ; Bloemfontein; Paris ; and Antwerp. This is a most interesting list, especially if one call§to mind the various races to which the bile beans would be sent, and the various conditions under which those orders I saw had been despatched. I should like to know if any other household remedy has ever achieved so great a fame in so short a time. My own opinion is, that no other has so well deserved success. Your truly, "Householder."

[lt is almost incredible, that a household medicine should, in two or three years, build up such a reputation that it is to be found in the homes of England,the tents of Kaffir, the houses of Turks, the hovels of Siberian peasants, and indeed in every corner of the globe. Such, however, as "Householder" writes, has been the case with the vegetable remedy, Chas. Forde's bile beans. Discovered first in Australia, it was introduced into England only two or three years ago, and from the first was appreciated by the British public. Its very newness was one of its strongest points. While most existing remedies were altogether out of date, here was a nrepara- tion new from the halls of modern science. While most of the old remedies depended for what curative proper- ties they possessed upon the presence of iron, bismuth mercury. or some poisonous minerals, here was a remedy vegetable from coattng to kernel. No wonder,therefore, that it enjoys a world-wide and rapidly growing sale.]

div.head: OVERLOOKER'S SHOCKING DEATH.
div.p: OVERLOOKER'S SHOCKING DEATH.

A jacquard overlooker named Robert Hogg (23), of Balaclava-street, Blackburn, who was employed at the Ward-street Mill Company's mill, met with a shocking death on Wednesday afternoon. He was engaged in repairing some jacquards when his loose coat became entangled in the shafting. He was whirled round and was dead when released, a leg -and an arm having been wrenched from the body.

div.p: WEEK.
,ESTCOURT.
SIR RDVVARD LAWSON, BARTI

MR. MICHAEL BIDDU THE NEW PEERS.— _,We give to-day portraits of the four new peers—Sir Edward Lawson, Mr. Watson-Arm- strong, Mr. Michael Biddulph, and Mr. G. T. 1 Sotheron-Estcourt. Sir Edward Lawson is the son of the late Mr. J. M. Levy, J.P., one of the founders of the cheap press, and was born in 1833. He was educated at University Col- lege School. He is J.P. and D.L. for Bucks, , and a Lieutenant for the City of London. He f was prominently connected with the repeal of the paper duties, and during the long period •of his direction of the Daily Telegraph was 'responsible for the organisation and success of funds in relief of the cotton famine in Lancashire, in 1860-65, and of the poor of Paris after the Siege of 1870-71. In conjunc- tion with the proprietors of the New York Herald he organised Sir Henry Stanley's great journey across Africa, 1874-7, whereby the Congo was discovered. Mr. William Henry Armstrong Fitzpatrick Watson-Armstrong, of Cragside, is the heir of the late Lord Arm- strong, founder of the great engineering works at Elswick. He was born in May, 1863. Mr. Mithael Biddulph, of Ledbury, is a Deputy- Lieutenant of the County of Hereford, which he represented in Parliament first as a Liberal, and later (the Southern and Ross Divisions) as a Liberal Unionist, from 1865 to his retirement in 1900. Mr. Biddulph is in his seventieth year, and is a partner of the well-known banking firm of Cocks, Biddulph & Co., and a director of the Economic Life Assurance Company. Mr. George Thomas John Sotheron-Estcourt, of Estcourt, Tetbury, Gloucestershire, and of Darrington Hall, Pon- tefract, belongs to an old family which has long enjoyed a considerable amount of influ- ence in the counties of Gloucester and Wilts. In the church of Shipton Moigne, which was rebuilt by the Estcourts, is an altar-tomb, which has under a canopy a figure of Sir Thomas Estcourt, who died at Cirencester in 1624, from the plague.

div.head: CMPTED FRENCH ACTRESS.
div.p: A CMPTED FRENCH ACTRESS.

Rejane is the latest of the French Anvasion, and she has succeeded Madame Jeanne Gran- ier at the Garrick. Like Sarah Bernhardt, she is becoming an annual visitor, and she is very popular in London. She herself has lately expressed her warm appreciation of the English audien- ces, and it is a feeling that is obviously reci- procated.Rejane has brought over w.th her the whole of the company from the Vaudeville Theatre, Paris, so she has an able backing-up, which shows her off to the best advantage. She has been play- ing "La Demi- monde" with conspicuous success, but she has varied her programme MADAME REJANE4 almost nightly.

Amongst -other pieces which she has brought over with her are "La Passerolle," the original of "The Marriage of Kitty," '‘ Sapho," "Ma Cousirie," " Divorcons," the original of "The Queen's Proctor," and others. Unfortunately her season is all too short, and closes at the end .of next week. Madame Bernhardt closes this -week; and Madame Granter and Madame Jane Hading have already gone. So in' a few days more the French invasion will be over—but only, it is to be hoped, till next season.

div.head: TEAM FOR AUSTRALIA.
div.p: THE TEAM FOR AUSTRALIA.

An English eleven rfor Australia is always a subject of interest to cricketers throughout the world, and the announcement that the M.C.C. have decided to send one out under their own direct auspices is a new departure which will meet with universal approval. It has long been felt that the M.C.C. were the right people to undertake these tours, ?,,.d that theyhadno right to he left, more or less, to private enterprise. I f for no other reason, the lat- ter *ate of affairs was un- satisfactory, as questions were always being raised as to how far these teams could be con- sidered as repre- sentative of English cricket 'P. F. WARNER, CAPTAIN, as a whole. The

• M.C.C., so to speak, lends a ball- mark to the tour which it would other*ise have lacked. Of course, whether, under the auspices of the M.C.C. or private auspices, it is always a matter of difficulty to secure a thoroughly representative team, as so many leading cricketers are tied to this country for the winter. Yorkshire, for instance, has always held aloof as a county, but it is thought that the fact of the M.C.C. being at the back of the new team may influence them to adopt a different attitude. In fact, the M.C.C. will more easily be able to get hold of the best professionals, where private enterprise failed, though it often managed to secure amateurs who would other- wise have been unwilling, from personal reasons. So far, only one member of the M.C.O eleven is a certainty, and he is Mr. P. F. Warner, who is to captain the team. div.head: ONLY OPEN-AIR THEATRE.
div.p: THE ONLY OPEN-AIR THEATRE.

Port Sunlight, distinguished to the point of wonderment in the commercial world, is now unique in the sphere of drama. It possesses the only open air theatre in England at present, hut there is no doubt that it is the pioneer of trany of a similar nature. Sunlight Theatre, to give the novelty a doubly appropriate name, will be both idyllic and homely. Ladies will be allowed to take their knitting or any other finger-work they choose, and every facility Nvill be afforded patrons of being absolutely at their ease. Tables are to be provided, and garden seats will be plentiful. Three th9usand people will be able to take their seats, and the charge will be 2d. and 4d. In addition to theatrical performances, public meetings, band and other contests, athletic displays, and gatherings of all sorts will be held at the theatre throughout at least four months of the year. It is situated in a picturesque dell, the wooded green slopes of which shield the entire auditorium from the violent blasts that sometimes sweep up from the river—a charm- ing and fragrant and peaceful spot: The stage is soft. wide by 35ft: deep, with dressing

THE OPEN-AIR THEATRE AT PORT SUNLIGHT: rooms and green room on one side, and rooms for a band, stores, carpenters, and scene- painters on the other. Large doors for the admission bf scenery occupy the back of the stage, which is framed towards the front by a terra-cotta proscenium arch, aft. wide and 2oft,/ high, fitted with a revolving steel curtain. The orchestra enclosure, with a terra-cotta balustrade, stands immediately in front. Ruabon red bricks have been used in the construction of the building, which is in the classic style, with proscenium cornices, ' columns, arches, niches, and other dressings of salmon-tinted terra-cottaA richly moulded and modelled. The space en- closed in the great pediment is filled with an ex- quisite bas-relief. The subject is "Aurora," the tesign being adapted from Guido Reni's famous fresco in Rome. The auditorium is about i 58ft: long by 95ft. wide. It rises gradually, and there are broad-stepped galleries all round. Provision las been made for the variableness of the British climate. The curtain may lise in bright sunshine, but before the first act is closed the rain may be falling. A slender steel framework has been built over the auditorium, across which, if necessary, a sliding canvas roof can be stretched in a few minutes, and the open air auditorium converted into a marquee.

div.head: CASE OF DAN LENO.
div.p: THE CASE OF DAN LENO.

London is very distressed at the illness of its favourite comedian, Mr. Dan Leno, who broke down again on Whit Monday, and has since been in a private hospital at Peckhami -it will be remembered that about a year ago he broke down in a similar fashion from the st-rain of over-
work, but then

he picked up , ---,...-_-. unexpectedly quickly, and was not only able to , play in the pan- - tomime atDrury Lane, but was .51 also able to fulfil k some earlier en- gagements at -- , the music halls. `--- This year, how- ever, he has again overtaxed his strength, 11..-", mental and phy- sical, -- , breakdown is said to be far more severe. In-
deed, since be
MR. DAN LENOI
resumed work
after
his last

breakdown he did not take a single night off till he again gave way on Whit Monday. His physical health has improved considerably since he went into hospital, but his over- strained mind is not picking up as quickly this year, and it is feared that he may not be fit to appear in the Drury Lane pantomime, as he usually does. Always a most liberal and generous man, his mental trouble has taken the form of giving away large sums of money; but , he is quite quiet and con- tented, and spends a large part of his time .in drawing caricatures, at which he is remark- ably clever. Mr. Dan Leno has a whole host of friends and admirers, and the greatest sym- pathy has been evinced during his illness. It is hoped that a long rest and a sea voyage will restore him to himself; but he will in the future have to be more careful of his health., Mr. Arthut Collins is placed in a serious dilemma by the unlikelihood of Mr. Leno being able to appear at Drury Lane, as he was naturally counting on him as his chief attrac- tion.• If it is finally found that he is not fit to appear, his place will probably be filled, if theatrical gossip is to be believed, by Mr. Huntley Wright or Mr. George Robey—more probably the latter, as Mr. Huntley Wright is under contract to Mr. George Edwardes for two years more. Mr. George Robey has an immense following; but he, too, is booked, and is due to appear in the Glasgow panto- mime. It is thought, however, that an ar- rangement may be arrived at between MU Collins and the Glasgow managements

he .examiner, Saturday, July 4, 1903. WARRINGTON'S WATER SUPPLY. A BIG SCHEME SUCCESSFULLY LAUNCHED. Official Opening of the Extensions. Interesting Proceedings

11 The members of the Warrington Corporation were given an opportunity on Tues.-lay of inspecting the extensions of the waterworks which have:leen made within recent years at a cost of £133,003. A large number responded to the invitations of the Mayor, but the non-trading members were conspicuous by their absence. Briefly stated, the extensions may be said to easily divide themselves into three portions. An entirely now pumping station has been established at Delph-lane ; a new reservoir with a capacity of 41 million gallons has been constructed at Winwick; and on the Cheshire side of the town, a new service reser- voir has been constructed at Hill Warren and exten- sions made at the Appleton reservoir. The works for the domestic supply comprise a new pumping station at Delph-lane, about 11 miles east of Winwick, with a pump-welll2ft. 6in. in diameter and 160 ft. deep, at the bottom of which an adit Oft. high by 4ft. wide is driven in a north-easterly direction for a distance of about 1200 yards, there being three working shafts in addition to the pump-well. The water is lifted by means of a triple expansion vertical receiver engine actuating two deep-well pumps, and thence the water is delivered by means of two force pumps through 11 miles of main to the Winwick reservoirs. At Winwick the service reservoir accommodation has been increased by a new reservoir 215 ft by 190 ft and 20ft. depth of water, with a capacity of 4i million gallons. It is entirely of concrete, the roof being formed of concrete arches supported on eleven cross- walls. A pair of pumps have been fixed in a new engine house close to the reservoirs, and the engines deliver into the new high-level service reservoir at Hill Warren. This reservoir is circular in plan and has a capaoity of 11 million gallons. Turning now to the works for the supply of trade water, several improvements have been made to the existing filters and a new covered clear water tank has been constructed of a capacity of 700,000 gallons. An approach road has been formed, the stream whioh formerly meandered through the site has been culverted and a new waterman's house, with committee room has been built.

them in starting the first engine, lie hoped its record would be a great and glorious one ; and that it would pump water for the inhabitants for any purpose they wished for many years. He proceeded to refer to the time when the water supply was nearly exhausted last year and when his firm were called upon to erect tem- porary pumps. The works had not been extended a minute too soon, and the money which had been spent had not been spent a minute before it was required. The inhabitants of Warrington had now a large volume of water at their disposal. He expressed the opinion that the Council, Water Committee, or engineer would be very bold to attempt to run the water supply from the new works another summer without duplicate machinery.

Alderman SUTTON observed that the work which had been done had been of a formidable character, and it had given great anxiety and trouble to the officials. Hie thought, therefore, that they should not separate with- out proposing the health of the Chairman of the Water Committee, the Deputy Chairman, and the Engineer,Mr. Deas, whohad devoted much time and labour in carry- ing out such an important work as that which had been brought to such a successful conclusion. (Applause.) Alderman FRA.NCOMB and Councillor JOHN EVANS briefly replied, Councillor John Evans remarking that what he had done had been a matter of duty. While Alderman Francomb was ill a great deal of work neces- sarily fell upon the shoulders of the engineer and on his own shoulders, but it was a great satisfaction to know that the Council were satisfied. (Applause.) Dr. SMITH (West Kirby) thanked the Water Commit- tee and Mr.Deas for the kind invitation which had been extended to him to be present on that interesting occa- sion. Mr. Deas was quite equal to the work which was entrusted to him—quite capable, indeed, of any work which might be placed in his hands. (Hear, hear.) The visitors then proceeded to the Winwick works, where considerable alterations have been made. It was noticed that a stream of clear water was being pumped into the new reservoir from the station at Delph-lane and a sample was taken of it. The engines which pump the water to the high level reservoir at Hill Warren a distance of six miles, were seen at work. Much interest was taken in a Venturi meter which records the height of the water in the reservoirs and indicates the daily consumption of water. The party afterwards returned to the Town Hall where tea and coffee and light refreshments were served. Appleton waterworks were next visited. A beautiful bouquet was presented to Miss Frapoomb by Mr. Deas, after which a start was made for town, which was safely reached shortly after seven o'clock. The members of the Council were greatly pleased with their visit and gained a great deal of useful informa- tion respec ting the water works undertaking.

div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Poole—Bramhall.

A marriage which aroused considerable local interest was solemnized at the Independent Methodist Church, Friar's-green, at noon on Tuesday,the contracting parties being Mr. Biddulph Poole,a well-known baritone singer, and a member of the Parish Church choir, and Miss Amelia Bramhall, youngest daughter of Mr. William. Bramhall, of Manchester-road. The service was con- ducted by Councillor Barton. The bride, who for several years has beena teacher lathe Sunday school connected with the Independent Methodist Church, was given away by her father. She was attired in a beautiful dross of ivory linen de soie trimmed with chiffon and orange blossom, while a Brussels net veil surmounted a wreath of orange blossom. She carried a shower bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley the gift of the bride- groom. There were two bridesmaids—Miss Gertie Poole of Wolverhamhton, sister of the bridegroom, and Miss Lily Barton, cousin of the bride. They wore dresses of white figured muslin over pale Roman satin, and wreaths of forget-me-riots and ivy leaves. Their bouquets were composed of sweet peas. Mr. George Mercer, of Manchester, was the best man, and Mr. J. G. Critchley, organist, played Mendelssohn's "Wedding March "as the party left the church for the residence of the bride's parents, where a recep- tion was held. Mr. and Mrs. Poole departed for Morecambe where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling costume consisted of a dress of reside crepe de chine trimmed with black medallions, lace stole, and white silk front threaded with green silk. She wore a black picture hat. The following presents have been received :—Mr. and Mrs. Bramhall,mahogany over- mantel; Mr. and Mrs. Poole, copper and black suite of fire-irons ; Mr. 9nd Mrs.W. W. Whittle, black skin rug; Mr. and Mrs. Birch, set of carvers, knives, prongs, U.; Mr. Thomas Bramhall, dining tabllA,4 Mrs. Molyneux, kitchen table and clock; Mr. and Mrs. William Poole, family Bible; Miss Poole, photo frames; Miss Lily Barton, pair of embossed plaques; , Mr. Frank Poole, photo frame and cigarette stand; Councillor and Mrs. and Miss Barton, copper jardiniere flower stand; Mr. and Mrs. Newey (Wolverhampton), silver and cut glass jug and jam dish; Mr. Bert Newey, silver butter dish; Mr. W. The cost of these works with extensions of mains to the outlying districts of dulcheth, Kenyon, Burtonwood, Daresbury, Thelwall, &c, is about £135,000. The work has been successfully completed under the direction of Mr. Dees, A.M.1.C.E., water engineer. Shortly after two o'clock on Tuesday afternoon,a large partyleft the Town Hall on a tour of inspection. The Mayor (Mr. J. C. Parr) was unVertaftately unable to be pre- sent, and the opening ceremony was performed in his absence by Mr. Alderman Francomb (chairman of the WaterCommittee).The following letter was recived from the Mayor :—"Grappenhall Heyes,Warrington,June 17th, 1903. Dear Alderman Francomb,—l am sorry I shall not be able to be present at the inspection and opening of the new water works on the 30th. I had made arrangements for that day before I had any intimation of your proposed inauguration, and I cannot now undo them. lam sure the inspection and subsequent opening will be most interesting, and I hope you will have a fine day for the purpose.—Yours faithfully, J. CHARLTON PARR, Mayor." Conveyances were provided for the convenience of the deputation. Alderman Prancomb, Mrs. Francomb, Miss Francomb and Mr. Dais occupied a landau, and the following members of the Corporation, officials, and other gentlemen followed ma brake and char-a-bane:— Aldermen Hutchinson, Smethurst, Sutton and Bennett; Councillors Pierpoint, John Evans, Rogers, James Evans, Brophy, Peacock, Davies' Sampson, Ellison, Duncan, and William Roberts; the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Wilson), Mr. T. Longdin (borough surveyor). Mr. A. M. Ker (deputy borough surveyor), Mr. Frank Turner (superintendent of the fire brigade), Mr. W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), Mr. George Mitchell (chief assistant engineer in the water department), and Mr. Fletcher (clerk of the works for the extensions at the Appleton water works), Mr. Hendry Smith, of London, of the firm of Messrs. James Simpson and Co. (who constructed the engines), Mr. Bailee McNicholl, of Perth (father-in law to Mr. Dees); Dr. Smith (chairman of the West Kirby Witter Company), and Messrs. Alfred Jolley and Wesley Dallow (representing Mr. C. W. Davenport, builder and contractor.). The first place to be visited was the new pumping station at Delph-lane. The chimney shaft can be seen a great distance away. It is circular in bore and towers to a height of 160 ft. The engine house is approached through a stone gateway and the buildings themselves are constructed on the most modern lines. The engine house has been built large enough to allow of a duplicate set of engines to be laid down at any future time with- out involving building extensions. The interior is of white glazed bricks and the exterior is of red brick with stone facings. In declaring the station open, Alderman FRANCOMB made a, few observations. In the year 1830, he said, the Warrington Corporation purchased from the Old Water- works Company the water undertaking for the sum of £278,000. At the time of the purchase he (Alderman Francomb) had the honour of being Mayor of Warring- ton, and on July 7th,1891, he was unanimously appointed the first chairman of the new Water Committee. (Hear, hear). They at once set to work to lay down larger mains for the use of, their steam fire engine3,and also for giving a better supply of water for domestic purposes. In 1898 the demand for water was so great that additional sup- plies were necessary, and the Corporation instructed Mr. Dens, thele water engineer, to prepare plans, and Mr. James Mansergh., the eminent water engineer, was called in to assist the Corporation in getting their Bill through Parliament. Powers were obtained in 1899, and in the autumn of that year the various works were commenced, and had now been completed from the plans of Mr. Deas, and under his superintend- ence. At Delph-lane they had sunk a well 12ft. 6in. in diameter and 160 ft. deep, and at the bottom they had driven an adit 1,200 yards long, 6ft. high, and 4ft. wide. In addition to this they had three working shafts—one at each 400 yards along the adit. This contract had been entrusted to Mr. George Lawson, of Rutherglen, and the price was £24,000. The whole of the buildings had been erected by Mr. C. W. Davenport, of' Stockton Heath, for the sum of £8,271, and he thought it reflected the greatest credit upon his ability as a builder. (Applause.) The whole of the water from the various shafts and adits was brought by gravitation to Delph-lane, and was then forced by very powerful pumps through a 20in. pipe to the new reser- voir at Winwick, a distance of 1 miles. The whole of the machinery at Delph-lane had been supplied by Messrs. J. Simpson and Co., of London, and, after they had had an opportunity of inspecting the powerful engine and pumps, he thought they would agree with him that the work reflected the greatest possible credit upon Messrs, Simpson and Co., and that they could pride themselves upon having one of the best equipped pumping plants in the kingdom. (Hear, hear.) The contract price for this machinery was £11,175. At present they were pumping 600,000 gallons of water per day, and as soon as the shafts were coupled up they expected to get 11 million gallons per day. At Winwick they had constructed a new service reservoir, which wouldhold 4i million gallons of water. The con- tract for this .work was let to Mr. Geo. Bell, of Man- chester, and Messrs. G. M. Callender and Co., for the sum of £22,000 and they had every reason to believe that the work had been well carried out. Anew engine house had been built by Messrs. R. Collin and Son, of Warrington, and they had given the Water Committee every satisfaction by the excellent manner in which they had carried out their contract. The engines had been supplied by Messrs. J. Simpson and Co., and delivered the water through a 10in. and 81n. rising main to the ne high level service reservoir at Hill Warren, a dis- tance of six miles. From this reservoir they could supply by gravitation the whole of the property at, Stockton Heath, Daresburyand Moore. The Hill Warren reservoir was constructed ,by Mr. C. W. Davenport at a contract price of £6,748. At Appleton a great many additions and alterations had been made, and Messrs. Bennie and Thompson had successfully carried out this work for the sum of £8,867. div.head: Mottram —Johnson.
div.p: Mottram —Johnson.

At St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath, on Tuesday afternoon the marriage was solemnized of Miss Julia Johnson. daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Johnson, 123, London road, and Mr. Alfred Mottram, son of the late Mr. John Mottram and stepson of Mr. Studer, Helvetia, Grappenhap road. The Rev. C: A. M. Evans, curate, officiated. The bride who was given away by her father was charmingly attired in a white silk dress with hat to match, and carried a lovely bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley, the gift of the bridegroom The bridesmaids were Miss Mottntm sister of the bride groom) and the Misses Bertha and Frances Johnson (sister of the bride.) They wore pretty grey and blue dresses and black picture hats, and their bouquets were composed of sweet peas. Mr. Frank Plumpton dis- charged the duties of best man and Mr. Hodson, of Liverpool, acted as groomsman. Mr. F. Rose presided at the organ and played appropriate selections. A ' reception was afterwards held at the house of the bride's father and during the day the newly-married couple left for Llandudno where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride wore a grey travelling costume with toque to match. div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

It was quite possible to play cricket on Saturday afternoon but the weather conditions were such as to render an indulgence in the pastime far from pleasant. There was an abundance of rain but still it did not fall heav,ly enough to necessitate the total abandon- ment of matches. Warrington first eleven journeyed to Bolton and owing to the stoppages through the rain, the match resulted in a draw. Warrington having aniassed 115 for the loss of six wickets declared their innings; and when stumps were drawn the Bolton aggregate stood at 46 for the loss of one wicket. Such a result was unsatisfactory to both sides as neither could lay claim to the advantage.

Alfred Thewlis, the old professional, again gave Warrington the benefit of his services and compiled the respectable figure of 26. P. B. Hawtin was also to the fore with a contribution of 26, and J. W. Bibby, the popular captain, knocked up 23. B. Silcock was. the only other batsman to attain double figures and he was responsible for 18.
Bolton's most successful batsman was P. Staton who placed 25 (not out)to his credit. Atkinson scored 18 (not out). To-day Warrington will meet Cheadle Hulme at Arpley.

Warrington second had the 1335 t of an encounter with Bolton second contingent. The respective totals were 139 and 87 leaving the substantial margin of 52 in favour of the home eleven. The top scorer for the winner was W. Richardson (34), and other useful con- tributors were G-. Newbourne (31), W. Bennett (21 not out), E. Pierpoint (15) and A. Duckworth (15). A noteworthy feature was the fine stand by G-. Newboume. and W. Bennett for the last wicket, their innings being productive of 52. The visitors did not make much headway against the deliveries of D. Pliw3ton and W. Bennett, and the fielding of the home team was very smart. Plinston captured 5 wickets for 30 runs.

Sankey Wire Mills met Hough Green and a draw was the result of the game. Clarke (15), J. Evans (13),and H.Cook(ll)batted in capital style for the Wire Mills and N. Cook bowled splendidly, accounting for 7 wickets at a cost of 18 runs. Martindale (19) was the highest scorer for the opposing side.

Warrington Grammar School received an unmerci ful drubbing at the hands of Hulme Grammar School. Their innings realized only 37, whereas Hulme com- piled 112. Burgess (12) was the only Warrington batsman to reach double figures. Ford (37) batted in fine style for the winners.
Latchford Baptists defeated Moss Side Baptists by a margin of 25. No strikinefeature was presented by the innings of either team, Fletcher (14) being the most successful batsman.

Warrington Co-operative had very little difficulty in accounting for Penke riends' school on Tuesday the majority in their liq reaching 40. Mann batted in grand form for the winners hi s innings being productive of 44.

div.head: cycling.
div.p: cycling.

A cycling accident occurred on the Manchester, road on Saturday afternoon. Mr. W. Jackson, 127- Bridge-street, was cycling in the direction of Woolston when another cyclist ran into the back wheel of his machine and caused him to fall. A brougham was passing at the time, and Mr. Jackson was trampled upon by the horse. He proceeded home much shaken, and was attended by Dr. Braide.

For the last three or four years "Ladies' day" in connection with the Warrington Cycling Club has been marred by wet weather. Unfortunately the event this year proved no exception to the rule in that res- pect rain falling frequently on Saturday. Only a dozen members, including two ladies turned out, the destina- tion being Lower Peover. Notwithstanding the weather the wheelers were able to spend a fairly pleasant time. On Tuesday evening twenty members had a spin to Little Leigh.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

To some members of the Warrington Anglers' Asso- ciation, special attention is drawn to the latter por- tion of Rule 6 of the Society' which intimates that all subscriptions should be paid before June 30th, or they are liable to forfeiture of all privileges and to have their cards cancelled as per Rule 22. The Juvenile Branch of the Association now numbers 30 member s and there are also 11 lady members of the Society. The contest in aid of the Benevolent Fund will be de- cided at "London Bridge," Stockton Heath on Satur- day afternoon next. The draw will be undertaken at 3 p.m.

At the monthly meeting of the Jolly Anglers Society held at the Bowling Green Hotel, Bank Quay, on Monday last, the prizes won in the eel and flounder competitions, which had been conducted during the close season for other fish, were distributed. Winners, Eel Competition: Ist S. Stewart, 2nd and 3rd E. Grimshaw. Flounder Competition: Ist J. Alleock, 2nd S. Thomas and 3rd J. Allcock. The club match will be fished on Saturday July .18th at Barrow Lock, Northwich.
The members of the Broadheath and District A. S. fished a match for gudgeon only on S aturday last at Bollington.—Result : Ist G. Shannon, 2nd W. Piercey and 3rd C. Higginbottom.

The river Bollin is still very low and a freshel is badly wanted. There was not much sport recorded last week end, though a number of anglers were ob- served. Mr. W. Wood recorded a dace of 7oz. 9drs. and Mr. Fred Bonnell creeled three nice trout. Messrs. Kendal, Holt, and Hollingsworth all had decent trout. Mr. Ellis and Mr. Hind have registered sport with the trout by means of the red spinner and black gnat.
Two bream respectively 41b. 14oz. 2drs. and lb. 3 oz. have been recorded in the batch book of the Associa- tion as caught by Mr. C. Weedle from Newbridge (club water.)
A splendid specimen of gudgeon scaling 2ozs. 3drs: was captured by Mr. James Appleton on Wednesday evening last from the Bridgewater Canal at Grappen- hall.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSEUM. Complimentary References in the " Morning Leader."
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSEUM. Complimentary References in the " Morning Leader."
In the "Morning Leader " for Monday there appears the following complimentary paragraph relating to the Warrington Museum,and penned by a regular contribu- tor, F. G. Afialo

div.head: MODEL MUSEUM'.
div.p: A MODEL MUSEUM'.

Warrington is not an ideal Eden for one trainbound,! as I was the other day, but, I had reason to be thankful for the hour's interruption to my journey, if only that it gave mean opportunity of visiting and admiring the excellently-arranged zoological collections in the NVar- rington Museum. I do not know who the Curator is, but I allow myself to congratulate him unreservedly on the method of his arrangements. Those interested in nature study might with advantage pay a visit to his oases, and study themas models. The cases, with speci- mens illustrating every animal group, may be understood by children. For fishes a perch, for batrachians a frog and spotted salamander, for reptiles a horned lizard and tortoise, for birds a wren, a robin, and a parrakeet, for mammals a weasel and a bat. Neighbouring cases display a score or so of invertebrate types, and the whole furnish a capital epitome. Another case show the hard parts of the lobster, disarticulated and mounted to show the crustacean structure. Others deal with insects injurious to fruits or vegetables. Here and there, too, as in a case of kingfishers and another of water ousels, down in the art room, there is evidence of highly tasteful taxidermy. At first I thought that my pet group—fishes —had been strangely neglected, but these also are down in the art room. I do not, perhaps, quite like the Mersey sturgeon in with the sharks and rays, nor am I perfectly happy about the "Thames Turbot," as the occurrance of that fish in the metropolitan river seems to me open to doubt. But the others, mostly casts, are excellent, particularly the flatfishes.
