div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JULY 4th, 1903.
THE Go vern- A GREAT CAMPAIGN FOR ment has not been UNTAXED FOOD able to postpone

the campaign to which the country has been invited. If it did not wish to fight until the autumn it should have muzzled Mr. CHAMBERLAIN until the autumn. But the seriousness of the issues raised by the Colonial Secretary is much too clearly apprehended by the other side to make it possible for him to steal the march that he contemplated. The Liberal party is awake, ad there is a no less alert wake- fulness on the part of the Conservative Free Traders. These latter held a meeting at the House of Commons on Wednesday. They are not, a numerous body, counting about forty-six in all, with one peer, Lord GOSCHEN, among them. How- ever, they are, as we understand, determined to enter the field against Mr. CHAMBERLAIN without delay. Whilst they were coming to this resolution on Wednesday afternoon a meeting which is likely to he recorded as an historic event, was being held at Caxton Hall, Westminster Building, which has an emblazoned window, recording incidents in Sir FRANCIS BURDETT'S struggle for reform. The National Liberal Federation had called an emerg- ency meeting at what, as Mr. ASQUITH said, is a typical moment of national emergency. There were representatives from all parts of England and Wales, men who are again to quote Mr. ASQUITH, "the active forces of tile militant Liberalism of the country." There were no signs of divided opinion. Over eighty members of Parliament were present, including several peers. They were members who have expressed almost exactly opposite views on questions with the late war, but there was no divergence of view on Wednesday. Sir HENRY FOWLER was of the same opinion, and Sir WILFRED LAWSON agreed with and applauded Mr. Isclutra. The meeting illustrated in a most remarkable way the truth of Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH'S declar- ation in the Budget Bill debate, "the right hon. gentleman has united our opponents." If any new divisions should arise in the Liberal party it will certainly not be until the anti-Protectionist campaign has been fought and won. The contest on which we are about to enter is peculiar- ly provocative of military metaphors, "We are in for a big fight," said Mr. CHAMBERLAIN on May 22nd. SIR HENRY FOWLER repeated his words with the supplementary remark that this is the one subject on which he agrees with him. None of the speakers at the Caxton Hall meeting were disposed to underrate the seriousness of the struggle that is about to be entered upon. "It will be the biggest political fight of this genera- tion," said SIR HENRY FOWLER, adding that it must be won by evidence and argument, and not by declamation. The issues to be decided are the taxation of food, retaliation on the foreign pro- ducer, and our future relations to our Colonies. Nothing could be more momentous. Mr. Asourrx's fine speech was one in which he may be said to have stripped; himself for the fray. Endorsing every word which had been said by SIR EDWARD GREY on the previous evening, he attacked the Colonial Secretary by argument by statistics and by keen irony. The Empire can now only be held together by preferential tariffs, says the COLONIAL SECRETARY. "What an admission exclaimed Mr. ASQUITH," "what a condition of things to have produced in eight years ! " There were subsequent sneakers whom this admission had actually astonished. " What has happened to the Empire ? " asked a son of JOHN BRIGHT. "I want to know whether the Colonies have sent us an ultimatum or whether we have sent an ulti- matum to the Colonies ? " Nothing has happened Lof course. The necessity of a new election cry has

presented itself, and if Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had not thrown this apple of discord into the banqueting hall we should shortly have witnessed the complete discomfiture of a Government whose self-complac- ency has even excelled its incompetence,and whose impatience of good advice has been equal to its native incapacity for wise conduct. Mr. CHAMBER"' LAIN understands very thoroughly the mind of the least thoughtful section of his countrymen. COBDEN, as Sir HENRY FowLErt reminded his audience on Wednesday, once said " Every man is a Free Trader except in his own trade." That is one reason why the co:ning conflict will be severe. Then there was something said ten years ago to Sir HENRY by JOHN BRIGHT. ".The young men," said the great orator,who used to be spoken of as the Tribune of the People, "know nothing of 11 the old C,irn Law fight; they may easily be per- snaded." There are fewer now who remember it. It was, therefore, a great education campaign that I was entered upon on Wednesday.
A story gained THE GOVERNMENT AND cur rency on PASSIVE RESISTANCE. Tuesday to the

effect that the Government intends to drop the London Educa- tion Bill. It may have been unfounded, but pos- sibly it was only premature. In the House of Commons Sir A. ACLAND HOOD stated that the Bill is to be proceeded with, and that the notice will shortly be given of the date. This cannoc be accepted as a declaration that the measure will be passed during the present session. Toe time that now remains would b 3 barely sufficient for the pur- pose; but the dropping of the Bill at this stage would have had unique significance. It would have meant the practical triumph of the Non- conformist policy of passive resistance. We should have learned in this way that the Govern- ment shrinks from producing in L indon the situation which, in spite of all warning, it has pro- duced throughout the country. , But this it will be readily understood,lllr. BALFOUR is exceedingly reluctant to acknowledge. If the Education Bill is dropped it will be when we are nearing the end of the session. Meantime the lesson that Free Churchmen "will not submit" to a revived Church rate in a more odious forma than the old, will con- tinue to be driven home by the police court appear. ances, by the seizure of goods and by the sale of household treasures in the yards of police stations. It will have been noticed that in most cases the passive resisters find the bench not merely un- sympathetic but hostile. This is a circumstance of the new persecution which will excite no wonder among those who have taken note of the system, or the two systems, on which additional names are added to the Commission of the Peace. In the counties the nominations are those of the Lords-Lieutenant, and most holders of that office not only belong to the party which has passed the Education Act,but notoriously select new magistrates almost exclu- sively from those who are of the same political faith as themselves. In cities and, boroughs Lord HALSBURY keeps the appointments in his own hands. Some previous Lord Chancellors have con- sulted the local authorities as to new magisterial appointments, but that is much too democratic a proceeding for the present occupant of the wool- sack, who is content to consult the local mem- bers of Parliament if they are of his own parthend the local Conservative organisation if they are not. It thus comes about that practically the whole of the additions to the Bench are made from those who are supporters of the Government, though of late years it has been Lord HALSBURY'S frequent, but not invariable practice, to add one Liberal to each live or six Conservatives—a little leaven which is very far indeed from leavening the whole lump. Such a process, continued with a short interval from 188(3, has produced a bench from which passive resisters must expect nothing but severe disapproval. Their attitude of mind, the motive of their action, the nature of the conscientious objection which they allege, will be no more understood by the bulk of magistrates than they are understood by Mr. BALFOUR, who thinks it is some process of " dull logic" which is inducing thorn to resist the new tyranny that he has established. But magisterial severity, the roughness of the bailiffs, and the hostility of officials generally will merely add to the force and ultimately to the effectiveness •of the protest. Mr. BALFOUR is not to be the only judge in the great contest which he has provoked. The whole nation is looking on in absorbed interest and forming its Opinion of the wisdom of a piece of legislation which is driving large numbers of the most quiet, the most deeply religious, and the most esteemed citizens in all parts of England to make their pro- testation after the manner which was illustrated a few days since at Wirksworth, in Derbyshire. However firmly he may adhere to his own views of what is politic, Mr. BALFOUR is likely to find that no inconsiderable number of his supporters in the House of Commons are unwilling to support him in applying to London those unjust and oppressive principles which have lighted so fierce a flame in the country. If the London Bill is not abandoned at once it will almost inevitably be abandoned before the beginning of August. Even the Angli- can Church is finding. ont that it has applied the principle of ascendancy in a way which is threaten- ing to be vastly mischievous to its own interests. Sir GEORGE KEKEWICH is probably rather above than below the mark when he says that in ben years it will completely have lost its hold over the schools.

Pageantry and festivity held sway in Warring- ton yesterday. Walking day is the day of days in this busy old town of ours, and few townspeople, we imagine, will be disposed to complain of the monopoly of the streets by the children for the Sunday school processions. One wonders if the youngsters could exist through the summer months without their" Walking Day." How long they look forward to the long and even toilsome march through the gaily-bedecked streets before the admiring gaze of their seniors! And, above all, the prospect of a romp in the fields fills the juvenile heart with joy. Yesterday the children iv, re able to enjoy themselves to their hearts' content. True, there were some smart showers, but only oF short duration, and then the sun would shed his g-nial influence on the scenes of festivity. The processions in the morning were much on the usual lines and they were carried through without the slightest mishap. The Roman Catholics once more excelled in the beauty of their pageantry and it is questionable whether a more charming spectacle than theirs has ever been seen in Warrington. All praise is due to the teachers and parents for the spirit with which, year after yectr,they enter into the arrange- meat; for a function which must entail consider- able trouble as well as expense. The Walking Day of 1903 will leave pleasurable recollections in the minds of young and old. May the time be far distant—if it ever comes—whei Warrington shall grudge a day entirely set apart for the enioymea of the Hang generation!

The question of paramount importance at the 'Council meeting on Tuesday will be the motion by Alderman Bolton in regard to the long deferred inquiry "into all trading by past and present i'embers of the Council or officials of the Corpora- lion with the Corporation either direct or indirect." A scheme has been formulated by the Joint Committee representing the Corporation and the Non-Traders, and this is submitted to the Council in Alderman Bolton's motion. Our readers will find the whole of the eleven clauses embodied, in another column. We have no doubt that it Will be a source of satisfaction to the ratepayers of the town to find that there is at last a possibility 'Of an inquiry being held on lines satisfactory to both parties concerned—for we presume that the 'recommendations of the special preliminary coin- Mittee will be accepted by the Council. It is •not to be supposed for a moment, however, that the details of the whole scheme will meet With full approval. Probably it would pass the Wit of man to devise a means of inquiry to which there could be no reasonable objection in any one Particular. The object is to provide some method by which an inquiry can be conducted on lines Which will be just to everybody concerned. This Much,we think,the committee has accomplished.

Whatever objections are raised to details it will be admitted, we believe, that the scheme as pro- Posed will operate fairly and impartially. The inquiry will cover a period of seven years dat,ng backward from the 31st March last, which should be ample time for the Non-traders to throw all the light necessary on the trading transactions of ineinbers of the Council with the Corporation. It Will be some disappointment to the public to learn that whatever disclosures are made they will not of necessity be published broadcast. The sittings 01 the Inquiry Commissioners are to be private, and their findings only are to be reported to the Town Council and the Non-Trading Committee. Though this may baulk certain people of an un- holy joy in witnessing the process of exposure—if there is any—it seems to us perfectly fair. The inquiry will enter into practically the whole of the commercial dealingb of the Corporation and its customers and it would obviously injure both to give the particulars of all trading transactions to the general public.

The weakest point in the scheme appears to us to be contained in clause 4: " that the costs of the inquiry shall be borne by the Corporation and that the Commissioners shall receive no remuneration." In fact the inquiry may be wrecked in its initial stage by this peculiar pr -vision. We can quite imagine that the Non-Traders will have no difficulty io nominating three Commissioners who will, for nothing, undertake the arduous task set them but where are the Corporation going to find three Such self-macrificing individuals P It is incon- ceivable that there are three members of the Town Council, net Non-Traders, who would be prepared to ent&ly desote themselves for weeks to the Pursuit of an inquiry for which they have little liking and for which they will receive no pay. And then again the Corporation will probably not desire to nominate members of its own elected body. They will probably prefer to be represented by disinterested professional men, who most Certainly will not give their time and labour to kich a task. There is the unmistakable prObability of a dead-lock here. Why should Lot clause 4 aierely specify: "That the costs of the inquiry Shall be borne by the Corporation," and nothing ttiore? A me-nber of the Town Council could not, i t°,l3vionsly, receive any payment were he one of ' t'ae Inquiry Commissioners, but the Corporation ;43111d still be free to remunerate the nominees °lll either side who happened to be outsiders. f rankly, we do not see how it is possible for any I.oquiry to be held under the conditions contained :Ilk Clause 4 as drafted, and it is not conceivable '7°t, seeing that they have to pay the" costs" the inquiry, the ratepayers would look upon tltasonable remuneration for those Commissioners itao were entitled to it as an unjust call upon 'lair pockets.

Possibly the borrowers from the library litte cause to thank the critics for the appearance sZ, the catalogue at this juncture—possibly not. 6 do not profess to know whether the pen-pricks ‘lAr the critics have in any way hastened the pro- of the bulky tome issued by Mr. Madeley huls Week. Anyhow it will be welcomed, for its was by no means imaginary. From the Rs. Lice we learn that the first volume of itule catalogue was printed in 1876, since when we tiol°l/ there has been at least one other issue prior the volume under notice. Library catalogues, (low ever,do not blossom forth annually even under iCbest conditions. With complimentary 7ferences to the museum in the "Morning Zetider ", and a brand new library catalogue, the Flleh-abuied committee should just now be in high eitther.

The Hon. Mrs. Bertrand Russell gives her ex- periences as a factory girl in the current Contem- porary. It is not so vivid an account of that kind of life as was presented by Sir Walter Besant in "East London," but it has some touches of human nature and some rough realism. Mrs. Russell had a good deal of trouble to get experimental employ- ment, and this part of the story is amusing.. We I are told how she disguised herself in cheap and shoddy and ill-fitting garments, and dexterously applied the curling-tongs to give her hair the right presentment for an East-End factory girl. She maintained the deception to he end of four days, and preserves her ticket, "No. 28, A. Russell, ss. 40." The conclusions at which sha arrivad are those that have impressed every, foreigner, though they have been strangely neglect- ed by our own people. There is probably no country in the world where women so openly give way to drink, and yet there are women who but for this failing have excellent characters. Pro- portionately to means, you would not find half so much generosity in Park-lane as is manifested by these factory girls Then, again who can wonder at the subsequent squalor and poverty, when the same drinking habits are found among the men from whom they, have to choose their husbands? It must not be forgotten that the drinkers are generally more interesting than the teetotalers. Somehow alcohol seems to inspire liber-dity and humour and so people with the same weakness for liquor perpetuate it in their off- spring.

Coming Events. The annual sermons in connection with Latchford Baptist Church will be preached to-morrow (Sunday), by Mr. R. Cameron, M.P. A young people's service in the morning will be addressed by Mr. C. E. Parker.

The ladies of Warrington and district are invited to meet tho Mayoress at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon for the purpose of forming a ladies' com- mittee to raise funds in aid of the Warrington Life- boat Saturday fund.
It is announced that a Labour Demonstration under tho auspices of the Trades Council and Labour Representation Committee will be held in the Parr Hall on Tuesday, October 6th. Personal.

Mr. A. E. Havle, whose appointment as assistant master at Wycliffe school was recently approved by the Education Committee has successfully passed the Batchelor of Science degree of the Victoria University Mr. Fred Stott (secretary of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council) has been invited to contest Orford Ward as an Independent labour candidate at the next November elections.

Maio GE-STREET.—Achit. Gallant Rescue. A gallant rescue from drowning has been reported. At about half-past seven on Tuesday evening a number of boys were playing near the pottery pit in Winwick-road, when one of them, Harry Wainwright, eight year of age, fell into the water. An alarm was raised and a youth named Henry Bretherton (18), who resides at 337, Winwick-road, jumped into the pit and pluckily rescued the drowning boy. The water was, so deep that Bretherton was completely immersed. "First aid" was rendered by Mr. J. G. Buckley, and the boy was afterwards taken home. It is stated that this is the second rescue Bretherton has effected from this pit. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH•CLASS MINERA. WATERS.—Advt. A Carter's Claim. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K.C., William Ward, carter, 13, Lower Ship-yard, brought an action against Denham and Company, contractors, Warrington, for £1 wages in lieu of notice.—Mr. Steel defended.—Plaintiff stated that when he was engaged it was agreed that a week's notice should terminate the engagement. Mr. H. Denham, however, dismissed him at a moment's notice.—ln cross-examination plaintiff denied that it was a recognized rule among carters that no notice should be given. He admitted that complaints had been made to Mr. Denham about the manner in which he (plaintiff) discharged his duties.—Mr. Denham was called, and said no agree- ment was made with the plaintiff.—His Honour gave judgment. for the defendant. A somewhat serious accident befel Mr. and Mrs. Harold Miller, Bridge street, in North Wales last week. They were driving between Colwyn Bay and Rhyl, when the pony suddenly bolted. The harness became loose and Mr. Miller was thrown out of the trap, and waS trampled on by the pony. Airs. Miller jumped out of the vehicle, and the force of the fall caused a bad fracture of the leg. She was also very severely shaken. Mr. Miller's back was injured, but his injuries are not serious. It will be many weeks before Mrs. Miller can be moved from Rhyl to her home at Sankey.

The Master of the Workhouse. Mr. and Mrs. Frederick Gate completed their duties as master and matron of the Warrington Work- house on Wednesday, and left at noon to undertake a similar appointment under the King's Norton Union, Worcestershire. Mr. and Mrs. .kubery' the new master and matron of the Warrington Workhouse will commence their duties at the end of the month. In the meantime, the assistant master will undertake the duties. shades.--J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 15, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Lancashire and Cheshire Union of Institutes. The complete statistics regarding the spring exami- nations of the Union of Lancashire and Cheshire Institutes have been presented at a Council meeting; in Manchester, and constitute a record in every res- pect. The figures are :—Nurnber of papers applied for, 55.751, against 51,162 in 1902 ; number of actual exercises. 46,100, against 41,576 ; number of exer- cises which satisfied the examiners, 36,223, against 31,532; total percentage of passes 78.57, as compared with 75.81 last year.—The Earl of Crewe wrote promising to become a vice-president of the union. Mr. G-. Hervey Wood was appointed treasurer in the place of the late Mr, T. R . Wilkinson.
FOR CLASS AND CHINA of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Messrs. Cartons' Experimental Grounds.

Messrs. Garton Ltd., the well-known Warrington firm of seed growers and merchants, have just issued an attractively compiled booklet in the shape of "A Souvenir of Messrs. Gartons experimental grounds, Newton-le-Willows." It contains a series of excellent views of the grounds at Newton, together with photo- graphs of deputations of agriculturalists who have visited them. There is also a mass of information con- cerning the methods employed at the grounds and the success which has attended the operations of the firm, mainly extracted from press notices and appreciative letters from leading agriculturalists. The book is worthy of perusal by all who are interested in the particular department of agriculture to which the firm has devoted its attention with such excellent results. The will o; the late Mr. Robert Garnett, J.P., of Hall Nook, Penketh, has been proved. : iThe deceased gentleman left a real and personal estate at the net Isum of £81,606, exclusive of amounts recently distri- buted by the testator of £18,200, making a total of £99,806. _ A cycling accident occurred at Liverpool last week which resulted in the death of a youth named Ernest Lake, eldest son of Mr. William Lake, who formerly resided in Warrington. Deceased was cycling in the neighbourhood of Wavertree and Woolton, when his back wheel skidded, and he was thrown against a passing cart. He was able to pick himself up and went to the house of a friend. After rasting he seemed to recover, and was able to proceed to his home in Fearndale-road. Sefton Park in a cab. In the night he became much worse and died. Deceased was a grandson of the late Mr. and Mrs. Philip Lake, of Knutsford-road, Latchford. He was a clerk in the employ of Messrs. Renton, Gibbs and Co., hot water engineers, Duke-street, Liverpol. His remains were sonveyed to Warrington on Sunday and interred in the Cemetery in the presence of his parents and a large number of relatives and friends. He was borne to the graveside by members of the choir and Bible Class of St. Pancras Church, Sefton Park (of which deceased was a member) and who also escorted the cortege for several miles of the road 'to Warrington in the morning. The funeral service was read by the Rev. J. 0. Coop, of St. Pancras Church. In addition to wreaths sent by his parents and immediate relatives were a large number from friends, including the Sunday school, the Cricket Club, and the choir of St. Pancras Church ;also the offin staff and employees of Messrs. Renton, Gibbs and Co.

Volunteer Manoeuvres. Next Saturday afternoon the Warrington Volunteers will parade at four o'clock and march to a position near St retton where manceuvres will take place. The band and bugle band will attend.

Warrington Royal Cycling Club. A special general meeting of the above was held last Friday at which it was decided to form a hockey club for the benefit of the members during the winter season ; under the name of the Warrington Royal Hockey Club. The Hon. Secretary, Mr. C. E. Hatton, 8, Cliffe-view, Lower Walton, will be pleased to arrange dates with local clubs. The other officers are :—Captain, Mr. H.Davenport ; sub-captain,Mr. D. Knight ;hon. treasurer, Mr. H.J, Powell;hon. auditors, Messrs. H. G-errard and A. Wright.

A Gruesome Discovery. On Wednesday, during dredging operations in the river Mersey, at Arpley, carried on by Samuel Appleton and other men, the remains of a man were brought up. The police were notified and the remains were taken to the police mortuary. The body appeared to have been in the ivater for twelve to eighteen months, and there WaS nothing to lead to identification. Choir Trip. _ . .

The members of Wycliffe choir had their annual trip on Saturday. The affair was a pronounced success, 23 members of the choir, male and female, taking part in it. The party left by train at Bank Quay Station at 1.40, and arriving at Chester made their way to the river, where a boat—facetiously called by one of the visitors "the Cestrain gondola "—was chartered to convey the party to Eccleston Ferry, where an excellent tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed was provided by Mr. Partington. After a pleasant ramble through Eaton Park all assembled later on in the evening at-the Iron Bridge, where they again made use of the boat and were conveyed to the landing stage some walking to the station and others making use of the tram cars. Warrington was reached at 9.30 without mishap —a fact which cannot be recorded of the previous visit of the choir to the city. The whole of the arrangements for the visit were carried out by Mr. NV. H. Payton, This. l3ac. (organist) and Mr. C. H. Hibbert.

Warrington Board of Guardians. An interim meeting of this Thard was held in the Board room at the Workhouse on Wednesday. Mr. A. Brcoks presided. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Dr Murray, Messrs. G. Pilling, S. Davies, T. 11. Ashcroft, A. J, Jolley, William Houghton, G. Mather, with J. C. Sutton (clerk.)—A letter was read from the Town Clerk stating that the Electricity Committee had given permission to Mr. Grimsdale to advise the Board respecting the electric plant belonging to the Guardians. It was understood, however, that Mr. Grimsdale was not to reecive any fee.—Mr. Mather said the matter was urgent, and the sooner the Guar- dians were in possession of the reporti the better.—lt was decided that the matter should be brought before the next meeting of the House Committee

Volunteer Camp. The following appears in this week's Volunteer ordors :—The Battalion will parade in marching order (kersey frocks but not helmets) water bottles (filled), and haversacks at the Drill Hall on Saturday, the 25th July, to proceed to Isle of Man, to be there encamped till Stli August. All members should there- fore now arrange to attend for this period so that the Battalion may be a credit to themselves and Warring- ton. Every assistance will be given regimentally (as last year) to help members to obtain leave where it is difficult for them to do so. The minimum period of attendance is 13 days. The annual inspection will take place this year whilst the battalion is encamped at the Isle of Man. Owing to the distance to be travelled, only those men who can attend for the full period can be present at inspection.

div.head: Church Society.—Lively Meeting.
div.p: The Church Society.—Lively Meeting.

The Rector presided- at the annual meeting of this society which was held in St. Paul's School,Kendrick- street, on Tuesday evening. There was a good attend- ance.—The Rev. H. A. Lester, hon. secretary, pre- sented a report on the work of the eleventh session, which, he stated, had been of a distinctly encouraging nature, and the effort of the society had been attended with a considerable amount of success. The attend- ance at the lectures was a great improvement on the previous year. The society had 210 members, and was doing a useful work and had every prospect of extending its influence.—Mr. C. S. Burgess. hon. treasurer, presented the balance sheet, which showed that the income for the year, including the sum of £6. 10s. Bd. in hand at the commencement, amounted to' £73 4s. 2d. After paying all the expenses there was now a credit balance of £9 7s. Bd.—Mr. H. N. Houghton proposed the adoption of the report and balance sheet.—Mr. H. J. Westbrook seconded, and said many workingmen who attended the Lenten services thought that the fact of these services being held was a sufficient reason why the society should exist.—On the motion of the Rev. Morley Stevenson, seconded by the Rev. C.A. M. Evans, the Rector was re-elected President.—Mr. C. S. Burgess was re-elec- ted hon. treasurer, and the Rev. H. A. Lester, hon. secretary.—At this point a somewhat heated discus- sion arose as to the constitution of the Committee. Mr. C. S. Burgess proposed the election of gentlemen recommended by the old Committee, but the Rev. G. W. Dickenson took exception to the action of the old committee in the matter. The discussion lasted about an hour, the point in dispute being the representa- tive character or otherwise of the Committee. Eventu- ally the names suggested by the old Committee were approved, with the addition of the Rev. A. S. Cameron

div.head: UNSUCCESSFUL CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON BUILDER.
div.p: UNSUCCESSFUL CLAIM AGAINST A WARRINGTON BUILDER.
Machine Guards Provided but not Used.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour, Judge Bowen RovrlandsiK.C., and a special jury, Thomas Henry Burke (son of John Burke) of 13, Miller-street, Latchford, sued -William Twiss, jun., of 114, Wilderspool-road, Warrington, for £250 damages for personal injuries sustained because of the defendant negligently and improperly omitting to fence a dangerous part of machinery, i.e.. a planing machine in his factory at Wilderspool-road, Warrington, on the 25th November' 1902. In consequence of such omission, the first, second and third fingers of the left hand were severely crushed and lacerated by the knives and had to be amputated. The action was commenced in the High Court of Justice and was remitted to the County Court for hearing. Mr. Rigby Swift (instructed by Mr. R. W. H. Thomas of St. Helens) represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Acton (instructed by Messrs. Browne and Crompton) appeared for the respondent. In opening the case, Mr. Swift stated that the plaintiff was apprenticed to Mr. Twiss and had completed about 5 years of his apprenticeship. On the 25th November, Burke was working in the plaintiff's work- shop. sawing stair treads. He worked at a bench with a circular saw at one side and a planing 'machine on the other. Both machines were driven together by a gas engine. Something went wrong with the saw and it was necessary for the plaintiff to put a wedge in. He obtained the wedge produced, but found it was too thick and in order to reduce it he went to the planing machine and met with• the accident. This was obviously a dangerous part of the machinery, and the law said distinctly that every dangerous part of a machine in a factory must be fenced in such a way as to be absolutely safe to the persons using it. At the time of the. accident, the machine was only partially guarded and in order to make it perfectly secure another guard had been pro- vided but it had not been used for some time. Since the accident this additional guard had been used regularly and if it had been on the machine at the time the accid- ent would not have happened. In referring to the ques- tion of damages, Mr. Swift said the plaintiff had spent five of the best years of his life in learninghis trade,but this accident had dimished his earning capacity by 50 per cent. In future he would not be able to earn more than 255. a week.

Thomas Henry Burke, the plaintiff, gave evidence in support of Mr. Swift's statement.—Cross-examined : He had only used the planing machine once previously. He did not know that &he piece of wood he was planing was too small for the machine or that it was liable to "kick-up." On one occasion the respondent warned him against using the machine without the guard. He knew that the guard was put on at the suggestion of the Factory inspector. The men took the guard off because they could not work with it without a great deal of trouble. He did' not put on the guard because it was not the practice of the workmen to use it and because he did not use the machine regularly. It did not suggest itself to him that he should use the guard. He knew that the guard was in a box at the time and that it was dangerous to work the machine without it. The respondent had never put the machine out of gear because witness was not working the machine with the guard on.

Joseph Edge, joiner and builder, said the wages of a joiner were 911. an hour. In summer a joiner's wages. averaged £2 2s a week and in winter 345. a week. 'he accident would reduce the applicant's earning capacity to about 255. a week. He would be excluded from the benefits of the sick and accident fund of the joiner's society.. Mr. Acton submitted there was no breach of the statutory law. The evidence, on the admission of the plaintiff, showed that a guard was supplied to the order of the Factory Inspector, which made the machine safe. The guard was placed on the machine and used for some time. It was the business of the workman who had the job in hand to put the guard on. The plaintiff knew of that but did not put the guard on. On the day of the accident tio guara was in a box at the side of the machine, and although the plaintiff had been warned againstpsing the machine without the guard, he did so. He (Mr. Acton) submitted there was no case to answer. There was no suggestion that the employer did not pro- vide everything he was called upon to provide by the Factory Inspector. Mr. Swift contended that there had been negligence on the part of the respondent inasmuch as he had not seen to it that the machine was guarded. It was ob- vious that a machine could not be fenced if the guard was put away in a box. The respondent ought to have seen that the guard was in its proper place. His Honour said he should ask the jury to say whether di the respondent d not do all he could 'clo under the circumstances.
Mr. Swift: To put a gund in a box is not maintaining a machine in an efficient state.

His Honour thought Mr. Swift's suggestion was carrying the law of protection too fat. An employer could not be supposed to possess power to make the workmen use a guard against their will. Mr. Swift said the employer could dismiss the men if they would not use a guard.. If he took the risk of seeing whether it was put on or not he did no dis- charge his statutory duties. Mr. Acton said with all due respect to his learned friend, that was the greatest nonsense he had heard and the point had been decided the other way. !Hs Honour: That I did not know but T de know that law and commonsense sometimes agree. (Laughter.) The jury returned a verdict for the defendant.

THE DRUNKARDS GALLERY. On Monday at the Earlestown Occasional Court, before Mr. J. W. Emmett, Sarah Hickey, of Golborne, who bears a very black record, was charged with her usual offence of having been drunk and incapable at Newton. P.C. Lynsky stated that on Saturday he found prisoner lying helplessly drunk in High-street, Newton. Inspector Foster said that Uteri were three previous convictions against prisoner for drunkenness, and she had only come out of gaol on Friday last after serving 114 days. A fine of ss. and costs was imposed or 14 days in default. The money was paid.—John Goulden, collier. of Legh-street, Earlestown, was fined ss. and costs for having been intoxicated at Earlestown on Satnr- day.—Thomas McLoughlin. of Earlestown, for hying been inebriated in Queen-street, was ordered to pay 2s. Gd. and costs. He asked P. C. Butler to lock him up and the constable obliged him.—Thomas Waters was similarly fined for having been drunk in Market- street, Earlestown. P.C. Mellor stated that when he was taking prisoner to the station he used very threaten- ing language. Thomas Collins was charged with having been drunk at Earlestown on Saturday night. P.C. Doyle stated that he was called to prisoner's father's house in Vitriol-square, where he resided. Witness went and found him in the house very drunk. His father complained that his son had been threatening him andall the family, and they were frightened of him. On being put outside prisoner became very abusive. He threatened to poison himself, and he had a glass ;in which he pretended he had some poison. Inspector Foster stated that prisoner had not been before the Court before, but he had been a terror to his father and family. He was a worthless fellow and would not work. He had accused his sister of poisoning her mother, andhad even gone so far as to go to the station and ask that the confession should be taken down. A fine of ss. and costs was im- . _ _ _ _ _

William Powell, of Haydock-street, Earlestown.stated that he was a vaninan in the employ of Mr. T. Moly- neux, who was the owner of the horse that knocked deceased down, and on the Bth May his horse and four- wheeled van stood outside the shop in Booth-street. He was taking bread from the van to the back of the shop, and whilsthe was in the shop the horse made a rush and ran down the street. He ran after it and afterwards found that it had knocked a little girl over. He did not see the horse bolt, as he was in the shop, about four or live yards away. There was a lad in front of the van getting some cakes eut, and when the horse started it threw him down. He had had the horse 18 months; it was six years old, and had never run away before. Fred Wrigley, 13 years of age corroborated. Thomas Merick, of 230 Wargra.ve-road, stated that he was working in Mr. Molyneux's shop when he• heard the horse run away. He picked up a piece of rope, which had come off an orange box. He took the rope to the house of deceased,because he thought it was their's. The mother of deceased stated that there were four or live children playing together in the street when the horse started off and knocked her little daughter down. She was not skipping at the time, but had been about a quarter of an hour before the accident happened. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death,' and added that they did not attach any blame whatever to the driver. VICTORIA-ROAD BOARD SCHOOL. RUNCORN. Honours Board Unveiled.

The 29 years of the Runcorn School Board's existence has been terminated by a ceremonial which records permanently the good work done at the above school. On Monday afternoon Mr. James Pritchard, chairman of the Board, unveiled an honours board at the school. On the board are recorded the names of the pupils who have during the last nine years won county and town scholarships. The board is a handsome piece of work. It ,igiseven feet six by five feet six, and is of stained Ce - try wood. It was designed by Mr. James Wilding, cotructed by Messrs.W.Farrell and Sons, and lettered and varnished by Mr. James Green. The body consists of six movable thirteen inch panels. Pour are devoted to the names of county scholarship pupils, and the re- mainder to local scholarship winners. The top is sur- mounted by a pediment mould, bearing the w* s "Victoria-road Board School. Roll of honour sch - ships "in gold letters. There are already 35 name the board. RACES, On Monday and Tuesday next a cheap excursion train will he run by the Great Central Railway Company to Nottingham from St. Helens, Haydock, Ashton-in- Maker&ld, and Golborne, starting from the first-named place at 8-50 a.m. The fare of the day is 4s. 3d. third class and Bs. 6d. first class. Brurr AL SON GETS SIX MONTHS. On Thursday, at the Police Court, Joseph Canavan,l6, years of age, 4, Appleton street, was Charged with assaulting his mother. Mrs. Canavan informed the bench that on Saturday her son thumped and kicked her; on Monday he knocked her down in the street, and on Tuesday threatened her with the rolling pin. The Perk said that the prisoner had been several times con- victed for assaulting his mother. Prisoner who it was said would not work, was sent to prison for six months. THE PUBLIC-HOUSE MUSIC QUESTION. . . . _

The magisterial prohibition of music in Si. Helens public-houses which has since the general annual licensing meeting caused much irritation amongst, the publicans, came up for review before a special adjourned licensingsession. Colonel W. W. Pilkin,gton presided, and was accompanied by twelve other magis- trates.—Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for twenty licensees, who made application for licenses quite apart from any- thing the Licensed Victuallers' Association had done, though, as the bench know, a memorial on the subject had been handed in. He applied for the licenses under the St. Helens Improvement Act, which provided the extreme penalty of conviction for keeping a disorderly house for any lieensee who allowed anyone to sing or play on his premises without a license under the Act. As a matter of law, and in view of a long list of undecided cases, he submitted that it was ultra vires for magistrates to decide a matter like that en bloc by the general resolution, and if any of the applicants went to another court on that ground, the court abovewould decide against the Bench. He detailed the regulations under which singing-rooms had been locally conducted, and said they conduced to orderliness.—Seven of the magistrates returned into court after the private consultation, when Councillor Martin said that the Bench has given the matter full and careful consideration, and decided to adjourn the whole matter until July 20th for further consideration

At this Gaut on Saturday, before Messrs. G. L. Davies and E. Imison, Ann Gorst was charged with begging in Bridge-street on the 13th ult. Sergeant Gill and P. C. Brayford proved the case and she was sent to gaol for seven days.

div.head: WIFi DESERTION AT WIDNES,
div.p: WIFi DESERTION AT WIDNES,

Before the Mayor and Mr. B. Brown, at Widnes, on Monday morning, John Fallon, of no fixed abode, was charged with leaving his wife and four children charge- able to the Whiston Workhouse. From the evidence it appeared that Fallon and his family entered the work- house on March 22, 1902. He was sick at the time, and upon recovering he was released on promising to get work. Nothing was heard of his whereabouts till recently. His wife obtained a month's leave, and he joined her in Stockport, where she persuaded him to come back to Widnes, where he gave himself up to the police. The cost of maintenance had been £49 125., a previous desertion totalling over £3O. Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour.
AN AsclEyr OFFENCE.

Before Messrs. F. J. Norman and S. Taylor at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday Elizabeth Barker Lowe's court, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly on January 17th. P.C. Gre,gory (Altrincham) proved the case. Defendant said she had been away in service but when she heard of the summons she decided to return and have the matter cleared up. Superintend- ent Ennion said there were 59 previous convictions. Defendant promised to return to service and she was bound over for three months.—Martin O'Neil, Heath. road, was summoned for using obscene language on June 20th. P.C. Bratt stated that defendant used bad language in his house and his wife and children had to run out of the place. The Chairman said some people used obscene language and thought there was no wrong in it. A fine of 10s. was imuosed.—Henry Burton (13), and William Johnson (13), Ashbridge-street, were fined in the costs 4s. 6d for throwing stones in Ashridge- street on June 22nd.—James Kaye, Fryer-street, was fined ss. for having been drunk and incapable in Fryer- street, on June 28th. P.C. Preston proved the case.

div.head: SOUTH LANCASHIRE TRAMWAYS. An Agreement with St. Helens.
div.p: THE SOUTH LANCASHIRE TRAMWAYS. An Agreement with St. Helens.

The bill promoted by the South Lancashire Tramways Company, which has passed the House of Lords, was on Tuesday before a Committee of the House of Commons presided over by Mr. Bond. The only opponents were the Corporation of St. Helens. In the end an arrangement was arrived at by which the Companyare to have such running powers over the lines of the Corporation (now leased to a company) as are necessary to conduct a through communication of passengers, passengers'luggage, and small parcels, and the Company are not to enter into agreements with the Company working the St. Helens lines except so far as is necessary to give effect to the running powers. Any dispute on the matter is to be rererred to the Board of Trade.
The billas amended will be reported to the House for third rea.dine.
POLICEMAN HAS A ROUGH TIME.-A HOSTILE CROWD

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday before Mr. F. Monks and other magistrates, John Moran, 26, James-street, was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly in Tilley-street on June 22nd and assaulting P. C. Whalley. .Tames Bennett, 49, Tilley-street, was summoned for assaulting the officer and Bridget Wheeler, 2, Jolley's-court, was charged with obstructing him.— Moran did not appear.—Constable Whalley stated that he was on duty in Tilley-streetand had occasion to take Moran into custody. Whilst he was struggling with his prisoner the defendant Bennett kicked him in the stomach. The woman Wheeler was enticing the crowd to "go for" him (witness). Eventually Moran was rescued by the crowd in conse- quence of the defendant's conduct. Witness was attacked on all sides but he was assisted by Phillip Johnstone and George Gill.—Phillip Johnstone corrobor- ated and stated that he received a black eye during the struggle.—George Gill also gave evidence but said he did not see Bennett commit the assault.—Mr. E. A. Connor, solicitor, represented Bennett and stated that his client denied having assaulted the officer. He was not at any time near enough to kick Whalley. Bennett had previously borne an excellent character.—Defendant gave evidence and called as witnesses William Maxwell, William Willcocks, and William Clare.—The magistrates granted a warrant for the apprehension of Moran who, it was stated, is a notorious pugilist. They found the other defendants guilty of the charges against them and fined Bennett 20s. and costs and Wheeler 10s. and costs. The Chief Constable said the woman had been before the Court 12 times.

div.head: DYING SCHOOL BOARDS.
div.p: THE DYING SCHOOL BOARDS.
RUNCORN.

The Final Meeting. The final meeting of the Runcorn School Board was held at the °dices last Friday evening. There were present :—Mr. J. W. Pritchard (chairman), the Rev. Father Donlevy, and Messrs. F. J. Norman, W. Handley, and J. Littler; J. W. Lightburn (clerk), and A. Light- burn (assistant clerk).

div.head: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.
div.p: FINANCIAL STATEMENT.

The financial statement for the half-year ended March 25th was laid before the Board and approved. The balance brought forward from September 29th was £945 18s. 9d. The receipts Were as follows :—Pee grants from the Education Department,under the Elementary Educa- tion Act, 1891, £277 ; grants under the Agricultural Rates Act. 1896, £8 9s. 6d. ; school fees, £l9 9s. 9d. from sales to children of books and othet school requisities, £8 us. 7d.; from the rating autho- rities, being equivalent to a rate of -lid. in thepound on £56,031 10s., the ratable value of the district, according to the valuation list in force at the beginning of the half-year. £1.000; hire of rooms and fees figinjoupik teachers at Central Class, £57 135.; total, £2,3Trls. id. The expenditure was as follows :—Salaries of officers of the Board, legal and other expenses, £lB7 6s. 9d.; salaries of teachers, books, and stationery, fuel, light and cleaning, (tc., Ste., £1,435 19s. 11d.; principal and interest repaid on loans, £342 12s. 4d.; leaving a credit balance of £351 3s. 7d. The outstanding amount of loans from the Public Works Commissioners at the end of the half-ytar was £8,340 4s. sd.

div.head: LAST PRECEPT.
div.p: LAST PRECEPT.
The Assistant Clerk intimated that a precept of 327 lAs. Bd. would be required to clear off all liabilities to the close of the Board's office.
Mr. Handley asked what would be due to the Board which would have to be turned over to the County Council.

The Clerk : About £1,400 on the ordinary grant for the day schools and £BO for the night schools. The amount will be placed to our credit. Mr. Handley proposed that the precept be issued.—Mr. Norman seconded, and it was carried. The Chairman gave a retrospect of the work of the Board, which wits followed by a discussion, taken part in by Messrs. Handley, Norman, Frank Donlevy, and Littler.

The Clerk pointed out that in view of the amount which would come to their credit the town for at least four or five years would have to meet only the common rate of the onnty. That would be asaving of 3d. or 4d, in the mull& Mr. Little r: That is one of the effects of the new Act.
Mr. Norman said it was due to the sound financial position of the Board. Very few were in such a healthy condition.
THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.
A cordial vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman. Mr. Norman observed that they had thanked him in the best way by making him chairman of the new anthority.

div.head: WHITLEY UNITED DISTRICT.
div.p: WHITLEY UNITED DISTRICT.

The final meeting of the Whitley (United District) School Board was held on Tuesday evening at Whitley, the Ist of July being the day appointed by the Cheshire County Council for the Ethication Act 1902 to come into operation in the Education area of the Council. The members present were Mr. Henry Nield (chairman), Mr. C. E. Ruruney (vice-chairman) Mr. Alfred Barber and Mr. Charles Nfounfield. Mr. J.H. Clarke the remaining member was prevented from attending. Mr. Nield had that day travelled over 100 miles to be present at the meeting, and special efforts to attend had also been made by the other members,Mr.Rumney having journeyed from London and Mr. Barber from Derby. ' The accounts of the Board to the 30th it were sub- mitted by the clerk (gr. C. H. Smith) and signed, and various other business transacted.

Mr. Barber, in proposing a vote of thanks to the Chairman and Vice-Chairman, referred to the long services of the Chairman, and expressed the pleasure it had always given him to attend the meetings. Mr. 141ounfield seconded. _
In responding, Mr. Rumney said he felt thatthe thanks were undeserved as with such an excellent chairman his office bad been almost a sinecure.

Mr. Nield thanked the members for the support they had always given to him and referred to the services of the Clerk and his predecessor. The work of the Board had been performed in a most harmonious manner, and he did not think they could be reproached for any omission of duty. It is interesting to note that Mr. Nield has held the office of Chairman of the Board continuously for over 27 years, having been appointed in June, 1876. During that time he has attended almost every meeting of the Board, the total number of meetings at which beh as been present being 332. Mr. liounfield was a member of the original Board and attended the first meeting after its formation in 1873. He thereforehad the dis- tinction of being present at the first and last meeting of the Board.

div.head: KR. F. STOTT AND THE CANADIAN
div.p: KR. F. STOTT AND THE CANADIAN
POPULATIOR.
Undier the nom-de-plutne "JEAN BAPTISTE," a corres- pondent writes :--

1 Mr. Stott, secretary of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council, in your issue of the 13th June says: "In Canada at the present time not two-fifths of the Population are British settlers, the remainder consist- ing of representatives of almost every nation on the face of the globe."

If used in connection with the United States this .might be somewhat near the truth, but as regards Canada it is altogether erroneous, and as our cousins on the other side are somewhat touchy in this matter, lam sure he will excuse my correction. The population of Canada, at the last census was : 8riti5h,5,233,701 ; foreign 135,834; the latter being composed of 40,850 Americans (U. S.), 19,087 Austro-Hungarian, 6,417 German, 19,837 Russian, 16,375 Chinese, &c., &c. This is something like one in three hundred, a very different position to one hundred and eighty in three hundred as Mr. Slot t says. I had to get these figures officially confirmed or this would have appeared in your last print."

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AS HIS OWN
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN AS HIS OWN
CRITIC.

Interesting extracts have been published, from a speech delivered by the present Colonial Secretary in the House of Commons on the 12th Augu.st, 1881, in reply to a Fair Trade resolution mcive'd on the same occasion by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. History, it is said, repeats itself; Mr. Chamberlain never does. He always contradicts himself. It is interesting, how- ever, to note that he and Mr. Ritchie are still at vari- ance on this question, the only difference being that the two statesmen have changed places,the Protectionist of 1881 having developed into a Cobdenite, while the Free Trader of that year, in growing older, has receded to the position formerly held by his antagonist. Among other things in that speech, he said

England is of all countries the most vulnerable in this matter—that is to say that in spite of, or rather, I am inclined to say, in consequence of the Protectionist policy of foreign countries, we export a great deal more than we import in the way of manufactures. Therefore such a commercial war as the hon. member proposes would do us more harm than the foreigner, who might retaliate on our retaliation by prohibiting or still further in- creasing his duties on our geods, or even by putting a duty on the exports of articles which we do not produce for ourselves. Well, then, does anyone , propose to put a duty on raw materials? Is it conceivable that we should ever be foolish enough to do away with the foundation of a great part of our trade—namely, the freedom with which we receive the raw material ? Then he came to food taxation, and he asked— Is anyone bold enough to propose that we should put duties upon food? Icm conceive it just possible, although it is very improbable, that, under the sting of great suffering and deceived by mis- representations, the working classes might be will- ing to try strange ra:nedies, and might be foolish enough to submit for a time to a proposal to tax the food of the country‘ but one thing I am certain of: If this course is even taken, and if the depres- sion were to continue or to recur, it would be the signal for a state of things more dangerous and more disastrous than anything which has been seen in this country since the repeal of the corn law, With the growth of intelligence on the part of the working classes, and with the knowledge they now possess of their own power, the reaction against such a policy would be attended by consequences so serious that I do not like to contemplate them. A tax on food would • mean a decline in wages. It would certainly involve a.reduction in their productive value—the same amount of money would have a smaller purchasing power. It would mean more than this, for it would raise the price of every article produced in the United Kingdom, and it would indubitably bring about the loss of that gigantic export trade which the, industry and energy of the country working un der conditions of absolute freedom has been able

vi to c Mr. Chamberlain must think the "growth of intel- ligence on the part of the working classes "has- been a backward growth, or he would never come to them and ask them to adopt the course which he so strongly con- demned in 1881. But the most notable sentence in that speech was this—" A tax on food would mean a decline in wages." That remains as true to-day as it was then. And yet, with this speech of his own on record against him, Mr. Chamberlain has the audacity to say a food tax to-day would raise wages as well as, by some sort magic, provide Old-Aga Paaiio.23.

div.head: PADGATE WALKING DAY.
div.p: PADGATE WALKING DAY.

The children attending the Sunday Schools at Padgate had their annual festival on Saturday afternoon. Daring the morning and the early part of the afternoon the weather was very threatening, but prior to the time of assembly it improved, resulting, fortunately,in the Organizing Committee being able to carry out their arrangements completely. At two o'clock the children were placed in order of procession by the marshals, Dr. Bennett and Mr. G. Mather. The Wesleyan scholars, preceded by the Buckley-street band, and accompanied by the Revs. W.C. J. Neville andFG. H. Carnson, Messrs. H. Ward and F. Wright (superintendents), J. Jackson, F. White (secretary), and L. Bennett led the way. They were immediately followed by the band and children of the industrial Schools, in charge of the Superintendent and Matron (Mr. and Mrs. Wright) and other officers,Mr. T. H. Ashcroft (chairman of the industrial Schools Committee) was also present. The Church schools brought up the year, and were attended by the Revs. W. H. Pollock-Hill (vicar). Vale Owen (curate), Lieu- tenant Colonel Buckton, Messrs. F. Royston, C. Turner J. Critchley, H. Houghton, H. Holt and J. Whittaker- Harrison. The procession traversed Padgate-lane to the corner of Orford-road, and thence to Fearnhead Cross. Here the scholars were massed, and before separating all joined in singing the, National Anthem. The Wesleyan and Indus- trial . Schools children then returned to their respective schools for tea. Through the kindness of Mr. G. 11,iather,accommodation for this purpose in close proximity to the sports field (also lent by Mr. Mather for the occasion) was placed at the disposal of the church schools. Tea over, the Wesleyan scholars ad- journed, to a field provided for their use by Mr. W. Bennett; and the Church and Industrial Schools children to Mr. Mather's at Cinnamon-brow, Fearnhead. div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

THE CRICKET Crxn.—The Ist eleven had as visitors the Knott Mill Hall combination, who arrived late and in very threatening, though almost tropically hot weather. The home players elected to field, and the wicket, rather soft to begin with, was not improved as rain came on shortly after starting. This favoured the bowlers, who quickly disposed of the batsmen, the innings closins for 19. Carter and Warburton gave a good account of themselves the first named taking three wickets for two runs,and the latterfive for 15. Grappen- hall replied with 58, but the individual scores were poor, Hallows being the only decent attempt among them. His 18 was a meritorious and useful innings. Johnes for the visitors bowled throughout the game and took the greatest part of the wickets. The 2nd. eleven at Crompton, made a draw much in favour of Cromplon. GRAPPENHALL HEYES.—The Mayor of Warrington, Mr. J. Charlton Parr, IP., C.C., has kindly thrown open the gardens and grounds to the public to-day at Grappen- hall Heyes, from 2to 6 p.m. Given fine weather, a pleasant and interesting afternoon may be spent them.

A HIDEOUS REVOLUTION IN WARFARE. There is a terrible report that the people of Macedonia intend to use plague bacillus against their enemies, the Turks. If this awful project is true (and we have the authority of the "Daily News") the result, not to the Turks alone,but to the whole of Europe, will be serious. Many say that fortunes have been spent by the Mace- donians in obtaining supplies of the culture of Asiatic plague. The people intend to poison all the water supply of the Turks, and this would bring almost a universal and terrible epidemic.. If. this Macedonian method of revenge is carried out it will indeed show the superiority of scientific methods over every other way , of warfare !

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THE WARRINGTON SHOPBREAKING CASE.

At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Aldermen Sutton and Hutchinson,Dr. Fox and Mr. J. R. Young, George Wilson, a native of Dublin, was charged on remand with stealin from the shop of James Hall- wood, grocer and provision dealer, Wilderspool-road, between 9.20 and 11.55 on the night of June 22nd, 4) pounds of tobacco and other goods, of the value of He pleaded guilty.—The Chief Constable stated thk Police Constable Bennett was in Wilson Patten-street at about midnight on the date in question, when he noticed the prisoner coming along. He waited until the man approached and then stopped him. On examining a bundle he was carrying he found the tobacco, and a further search resulted in other goods being found in prisoner's possession. The constable thee took him to the Police Station, where prisoner admitted having stolen the articles, and .said he got into the shop through the back window by climbing up a pole. Mr. Hallwood was afterwards aroused, and on going over the shop found it had been entered by the window, against whichan 18 foot pole had been reared. In order to get to the front part of the shop a sheet of zinc, covering a window,had been removed by the prisoner. Prisoner was a native of Dublin, and had come from Cardiff. He said he was a seaman and judging from the way he climbed the pole to ehter the shop that was ikely to be true.—Wilson was committed to gaol for a month.

div.head: Minor Cases. -- Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Minor Cases. -- Warrington Borough Police Court.

THURSDAY.—Before Mr. Hepherd (in the chair), and Mr. J. Rymer Young. WINDOW Slli ASHlNG.—Patrick Carey, Back Dallam- lane, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Winvvick-street at 9.5 the previous night, and with wilfully breaking a window at the "Brewer's Arms" Inn.—Frank Ritchies, the landlord, stated that his wife informed him that a window had been broken, and on going into t.:.e street he saw prisouer, who was drunk, standing near the window with his hand cut and bleed- ing. He admitted breaking the window.—P.C. Cooper having given evidence, prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, including the amount of the damage. A CANNIBALISTIC THREAT.—Harry Llewellyn, 363 Liverpool-road was summoned for making use of threats towards John William Jennings, Liverpool-road, and Thomas Henry Welsh, 132, Evelyn-street on June 23rd.— Mr. Steel appeared for complainants.—The evidence was to the effect that defendant threatened to kill complain- ants and "eat them with a pinch of salt."—Defendant denied the offence but the magistrates bound him over to keep the peace. ASSAULT.—Kate Kelly, 10, Dial Court, was fined 10s. for assaulting Ellen Chadwick, 3, Dial Court.

Education at Stockton Heath. At a caucus meeting of Stockton Heath Parish Council held on Wednesday evening under the presid- .eney of Mr. Clarke, Mr. W. J. Bouchier was unani- mously nominated as a co-optative member of the Board of managers of St. Thomas's school.

A Carter's Claim. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, 8.0., William Ward, carter, 13, Lower Ship-yard, brought an action against Denham and Company, contractors, Warrington, for £1 wages in Het of notice.—Mr. Steel defended.—Plaintiff stated that when he was engaged it was agreed that a week's notice should terminate the engagement. Mr. H. Denham, however, dismissed him at a moment's notice.—ln cross-examination plaintiff denied that it was a recognized rule among carters that no notice should be given. He admitted that consplaints had been made to Mr. Denham about the manner in which he (plaintiff) discharged his duties.—Mr. Denham was called, and said no agree- ment was made with the plaintiff.—His Honour gave judgment for the defendant.

div.head: WALKING DAY.
div.p: WALKING DAY.
STATISTICS FOR THE VARIOUS SCHOOLS.
How the Day was Spent.
We have obtained the following information regarding most of the schools which took part in yesterday's festival :--

div.head: Church of England.
div.p: Church of England.

BLUE COAT SCHOOL :—Number of scholars on books, 40 boys, 30 girls; number of teachers, 4; Master, Mr. Edward Rose. The children took part in the general procession headed by the school band and the beautiful banner bearing the words "Fear God, honour the King, love the Brotherhood." Afterwards they attended service at the Parish Church, and in the afternoon spent a pleasant time at the schools, many relatives and friends being present. A special tea was served and in the evening games were indulged in, in the grounds.

PADGATE INDUSTRIAL :—Number of scholars on books, 114 boys, 93 girls ; number of teachers, 4; chaplain, the Rev. W. Pollock Hill; superintendent and , officials, Mr. and Mrs. A. Wright, Misses Ivey, French, ; Roberts, Dyke, Mr. and Mrs. I. Jones, Mr. and Mrs. Woodhouse, Messrs. Jones and Antrobus. The children took part in the procession at Warrington, headedby the school band. On returning from town, dinner was served in the Homes. Afterwards the children pro- ,* ceeded to a field kindly lent by Mr. J. W. Houghton, , where sports and games were indulged in until bed-time. i Tea was served in picnic fashion on the field. NATIONAL (Boys) :—Number of scholars on books, 320; average attendance, 240; number of teachers, 30; Clergy, Rev. G. W. Dickenson; Superintendent, Mr. F. • Taylor. The scholars took part in the procession in I the morning headed byCresfield's band and in the after- noon proceeded to St. Elphin's park where the usual sports were engaged in. Tea was provided at the school.

FAIRFIELD (GIRLS) :—Number of scholars on books, 440; average attendance, 350; number of teachers, 26; Clergy, Rev. Canon Willis • Superintendent, Miss E. i White. The arrangements Willis; the day were exactly the same as for the National school. ST. GEORGE'S MISSION :—Number of scholars on books, 300 boys, 450 girls; average attendance, 680; number of teachers, 35; Curate-in-charge and Superin- tendent. Rev. A. F. White. The children marched in procession with the other Parish Church schools, Lymm subscription band supplying the music. The afternoon and evening were spent in St. Elphin's park and tea was served at the mission.

ST. CLEMENT'S MISSION :—Number of scholars on books, 275 boys, 400 girls ; average attendance, ”0; number of teachers, 35; Curate-in-charge and Superintendent, Rev. A. S. Cameron. The programme arranged for all the Parish Church schools was carried out, the children partaking of tea in the missicsii; 1, - - -

HOLY TRINITY :—Number of scholars Ow. books' 130 boys, 135 girls ; Average attendance, 235; number of teachers, 19 ; clergy, Revs. E. C. E. Carleton, and E. A. Inglis; superintendent, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton; secretary, Mr. Jos. J. Hesketh. The children took part in the procession as usual, and in the afternoon the elder scholars proceeded to Frodsham. Sports Bcc. were indulged in at Mersey View. The infants went to a field at Arpley,by kind permission of Mr. James Bowcock and spent a pleasant time.

FACTORY YARD :—Number of scholars on books 120 boys, 125 girls; average attendance, 220; number of teachers, 12; Superintendent, Mrs. Carleton; Secretary, Mr. J. H. Halton. The arrangements were exactly the same as for Holy Trinity. S. BARNABAS :—Number of scholars on books, 260 boys, 240 girls ; number of teachers, 21 ; clergy, Revs. J. H. G. Hollingworth and P. M. Forrest; superin- tendents, Mrs. J. H. G. Hollingworth (girls), Mr. W. P. James (boys and infants). The children assembled at the Church at 8.45 a.m.' and formed into procession. Headed by the band of Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co., Ltd., they marched to the Park and took part in the general procession round the town. At 1 p.m. the scholars proceeded to a field opposite the church in Lovely-lane, where the usual games and sports were indulged in. Tea was provided in the schoolroom at 4.30 for the children and at 5.30 for the adults. The distribution of prizes at 8.30 brought the day's enjoy- ment to a close. ST. ANN'S: —Number of scholars on books, 500;, average attendance, 350; number of teachers, 26; Clergy, Revs. James Davies, and Daniel Kerrin ; Superintendents, Miss Davies and Miss Bunch; ' Treasurer, Miss M. Rigbey; Secretaries, Rev. D. Ktrrin and Mr. S. Houghton. The scholars assembled at the schools at 8.45 and marched to the Town Hall 'via Winwick-road, Winwick-street, Horsemarket-street and Sankey-street, the music being supplied by Walker's Brewery band. The handsome large school banner was borne at the head of the procession and some of the children carried bannerettes bearing scripture texts worked in various colours on scrolls. On leaving the Town Hall the scholars walked in the general procession as far as Market-gate. On reaching this point they proceeded 'along Horsemarket-street to the Parish Church in Winwick-road, where service was held. At 3 o'clock tea was partaken of in the schools in Dannett- street. Afterwards the children adjourned to a field (kindly lent by Mr. Robinson, Orford-lane), at the end of Orford-avenue, where games and various competitions were provided for the various classes. The prizes were distributed at 7 o'clock, each child also received a bun and the children dispersed about 8 o'clock. ST. LUKE'S :—Number of scholars on books, 500; number of teachers 30; Curate-in-charge and Superin- tendent of Sunday School, Rev. H. R. Wild; Secretaries, Messrs. T. Sutcliffe and R. Gtaham. The scholars took part in the procession in the morning and spent the afternoon and evening in a field off Liverpool-road. The usual games were indulged in. Nonconformist.

WYCLIFFE (CONGREGATIONAL) :- Number Of scholars on books, boys 247, girls 238 ; average attendance, 270: number of teachers, 38 ; minister, Rev. John Yonge ; officials, Mr. George Wallington, superintendent : Mr. W. Beswick, deputy superinten- dent ; Messrs. L. Brown and E. Pickavance, hon. secre- taries; Mr. D. Owen hon. treasurer.—The scholars assembled at 9.30 a.m., and headed by Wycliffe Band paraded the principal streets to Bank Quay Station, where they entrained for Dunham Hill. Sports of various kinds were indulged in during the day, and special prizes were given. Dinner and tea were provi- ded on the field in true picnic fashion. In the evening the scholars marched through the village to the station, and Warrington was reached by about 9.30.

COCKHEDGE MISSION :—Number of scholars on books, 154 boys 154 girls ; (We are informed that each Sunday the attendance of boys and girls is invariably equal); average attendance, morning, 150; afternoon, 200; number of teachers, 18; Superintendent, Mr. Andrew Scriven; Treasurer, Mr. William Lister; Secre- tary, Mr. Caleb Riley. The procession left the mission at 8.45 a.m. and headed by Wycliffe band proceeded via Lythgoes-lane, Haydock-street, and Tanners-lane to Bewsey-street. Here the Wycliffe scholars had assembled and the combined procession marched to the station. Cockhedge scholars then proceeded via Wilson- Patten-street, Arpley Station, Mersey-street, Fennel- street, Battersby-lane, and Orford Avenue to a field in Orford-road. The infants rode in prettily decorated lurries. Dinner and tea were provided at the field and games *ere indulged in. There were about fourteen races for the different classes and useful prizes were awarded. Votes of thanks were accorded to Mr. Bennett, for the use of the field, Mr. Isherwood and Mr. Bailey for the use of horses and lorries, and to the ladies and gentlemen who had taken charge of the various stalls.

- ST. JOHN'S, (PRESBYTERIAN) :—Number of scholars on books 50 boys, 56 girls ; average attendance, 82; number of teachers, 7; Pastor, Rev. J. L. Milne, M.A., 8.D.; Superintendent, Mr. D. Cowan; Treasurer, Miss Spend°low • Secretary, Mr. Barlow, 23, Folly-lane. The scholars did take part in the procession, but assembled at the schoolroom in John-street at 9.30 a.m., proceeded to Bank Quay station and entrained for Frodsham by the 10.25 a.m. train. On arrival at the picturesque village games &c., were indulged in and after a pleasant day the return journey was made by the 6.55 p.m. train. GOSPEL HALL, (FORSTER-STREET) :—Number of scholars on books, 210 boys 240, girls ' • average attendance, 335 ; number of teachers 26 • Superinten- dent, Mr. J. Green;Treasuter,Mr.J. Reynolds ;Secretary Mr.J. Myles. The children leftthe school at 9 a.m. and proceeded to a field at Padgate via Orford,Marshhouse and Padgate-lanes, the infantsbeing conveyed on lurries. Dinner, consisting of buns, meat pies &c., was served at one o'clock and afterwards the usual games were in- dulged in. At 4.30 the children sat down toan excellent tea and at five o'clock the adults partook of a hearty repast. Scholars parents and teachers alike spent a very happy day. PARTICULAR BAPTIST,(LEGH-sTREET):—Number of scholors on books 30 boys, 42 girls; average attendance, 54 ;'number of teachers, 7; Superintendent, Mr. W. Turton; Other officers, Messrs. William John Bate, Joseph B. Groom, and John L. Bate. The scholars assembled in the school at one o'clock and proceeded to a field at Walton, kindly lent by Mr. Dodd. Refresh- ments and tea were served in the field and there were various games for the amusement of the children.

CAIRO-STREET, (UNITARIAN) : --Number of scholars on baoks, 130 boys 129 girls ; number of teachers, 18; superintendents, Messrs. J. S. Hill and Chas. A. Pember- ton. The scholars left Cairo-street in 'buses at 9.30 a.m., and proceeded to the beautiful grounds at Walton Old Hall, by kind permission of Mr. Monks. Lunch and tea were provided and the usual sports and games were indulged in. The children returned about 8 p.m. after a very pleasant day. GOLBORNE-STREET (BAPTIsT): Number of scholars on books. 213; number of teachers, 22; minister, Rev.
