div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, july 4, 1903.
than that of Mr. Chamberlain of taxing food and raw goods. But I would submit that the proposals of the latter must for the preseat hold the field an d not the competitive ones of your correspondent.

Mr. Bindloss will excuse me therefore, if I do not deal with his plan at any length on this occasion. But I will promise him that I will return to it when space ' allows. It would assist me however when we come to . , proposals if he would state more clearly what he means by" manufactured goods"? Is pig iron and are steel billets "manufactured goods"? Or would he enly protect the manufactures of iron that are made in War- rington? He further speaks of taxing goods that "could be equally well made here." boes he mean equally well in quality, or does he also include the question of cost of production and the selling prices? I trust that Mr. Bindloss will be courteous enough to reply •to these legitimate questions and not evade them as he does my former questions on the plea that he has not Ezekiel's vision, &c. I notice that our friend says that he is a Free Trader . in principlea would be unnecessary for him to add,after stating his proposals,that he is a Protectionist in practice. .1 suppose however, that if pressed he would say as many are doing that he is not a "one-sided Free Trader. This I saying is almost as common as the assertion that "Free ITraders make a Fetish of Free Trade." We generally find that such phrases are used by those who have nat I, mastered the basic principles of Free Trade, but have ' gone with the multitude in a blind faith which was not • founded upon reason.and when a taking propossl is put before the country, at once abandon their foundation- less faith and think that everyone should do the same.
It reminds us of the proverbial fox who having lost his own tail tried to induce all his comrades to part with theirs, on the ground that it was far more becoming to be without.

There are many who have fallen into the same error as Mr. Bindloss in regard to Cobden and Bright. They make various attempts, by implication and assertion, to prove that if the great pioneers of Free Trade had been now alive and had seen that other countries had not, as they hoped,followed the lead of Briton they would now be against what is called "one-sided Free Trade." The following quotation from a letter written by Mr. Bright in 1887 will effectually dispel this misconception. "1 never held the opinion that the reform in the tariff would be at once followed by a like change of policy in other countries. If Mr. Cobden expressed such an opinion, of which I have no recollection, I can only say that he had more faith in the common sense of other nations than I had. As to the change of circumstances since the year 1846, it is in every way in oar favour, for we have had forty years of Free Trade, and all the facts are wonderfully-on our side. Further I would assert without fear of error that our adherence to our Free Trade policy is the more necessary and advantageous to us seeing that other countries have not yet followed our example. Surely if other nations injure us by their high duties it would be no compensation to us to put difficulties in the way of our buyng what we want. It would be better if we were free to buy and to sell, but to make it difficult to buy by high duties in our tariff because foreign nations make it difficult to sell seems to me an idea which can only be entertained by men who are totally unable to reason."

But Mr. Bright was in part wrong because in a speedit in the House of Commons in 1846 Mr. Cobden did ex- press the belief that universal Free Trade would follow our adoption of it. But neither Cobden, Bright, Peel nor Gladstone, ever allowed that it was a mistake for Britain to adopt Free Trade, even if no other n ttion followed our example. These men had too firm a grip of the economic advantages of free imports and of their effects on exports to take such a stand. Sir Robert Peel said in a speech on the Corn Laws of 1846: "I fairly avow to you that in making this great reduction upon the import of articles—the produce and manufacture of other countries—l have no guarantee to give you that other countries will immediately follow our example. I give you that advantage in the argument. It is a fact that other countries have not followed our example and have levied higher duties in some cases upon our goods, but what has been the sesult upon our exports? You have defied the regulations of these countries. Your exports have greatly increased."
It is the effect of free imports upon exports that Arr. Bindloss and many more ignore. I very much doubt if your correspondent has ever mastered the A B C of this aspect of the question.
I now come to the uestions which Mr. Bindloss de- clines to answer. They are as follows, and have refer- ence more to the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain than those of Mr. Bindloss.

1. If we put ona duty with the object of exclud- ing American corn of which they have excess, is i not probable that they will retaliate by putting an export duty on cotton with the object of keeping and manufacturing it in the States? And would not this be disastrous to the staple trade of Lanca- shire? 2. The cost of manufacture in the cotton trade (and other trades also) would be increased if the workers, directly and indirectly engaged, were to get higher wages to compensate them for the in- creased price of food. How would such increased cost effect the sale of these cotton manufactures, four-fifths of which are exported, when brought into competition with the like manufactures from other countries? 3. If to meet this difficulty of increased cost, a bounty is given on exported.cotton and other goods,

div.head: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
div.p: MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S TARIFF PROPOSALS.
THE ARGUMENT BETWEEN MESSRS. PETER RYLANDS AND A. H. CROSFIELD.

div.head: Mn. W. P. RYLANDS writes :
div.p: Mn. W. P. RYLANDS writes :
I must congratulate Mr. Crosfteld on having dis- covered some system whereby it is more easy to make money on the Turf, than by the ordinary process of hard work.

On reflection, however, he must agree that the value of a sovereign to a man who can obtain as much money as he desires by a simple process of backing certainties must be entirely different from its value to a man who is earning 20s. per week by hard work. The purchasing power of a sovereign in each case may be the same, but the cost of living must obviously be of more considera- tion to a man earning money with ease, than to a man who with difficulty makes tongue and buckle meet. Double a man's earnings, and he can clearly afford to pay 50 per cent. more for the necessities of life, and till be very much better off. It only re- quired Mr. Crosfield to bring this point into prominence to oonfirm the proposition I put forward in my former letter, namely,that the purchasing power of a sovereign must not be regarded by itself without consideration to surrounding circumstances, fazuiliar instance of this is found in the case of the gold diggings, or in the old days of the Kimberley diamond field, when a man might be earning £2OO per week. At such a time the value of a sovereign was re- flected in the enormous prices which had to be paid for commodities. These prices it will be remembered had little to do with cost, as the largest fortunes in those days were undoubtedly made by the men who supplied the miners with their requiremants. The small pur- chasing power of a sovereign was the result of the ease with which it was secured. The high price of every- thing was not a sign of distress, on the contrary, it was the indication and result of unbounded prosperity. Mr. Crosfield has put the cart before the horse in this matter. It is not the cost of necessaries of life which settles the value of a sovereign. It would be more correct to say, the value of a sovereign settles the cost of necessaries of life. In very poor countries prices of necessities are always low, while the more prosperous a country is, the higher, as a general rule, will be the cost of living. The mere fact, therefore, that the cost of necessaries of life might be slightly increased by the adoption of preferential duties within the empire is not in itself an argument against their adoption, if it can be shown that the result of. such a policy would be more than a corresponding increase in the earning power of the people. With regard to the export trade of the United States, Mr. Crosfield appears to have fallen into a very serious error. Instead of being one-fourth of the export trade of this country, the export trade of the United States actually exceeds that of this country by about 30 millions sterling. In 1893 the value of exports from the United States amounted to 150 millions sterling. This increased every year up to 1901 when the value of her exports was 300 millions sterling. The exports of Great Britain, on the other hand, have practically remained stationary during the last 30 years. In 1872 our exports were 256 millions, while in 1902 the total was 280 millions. It is seen therefore that even taking into account the whole of our export trade, the volume falls short of the exports of the United States, instead of being four times as great as suggested by Mr. Crosfield. t must, however, be borne in mind that of that 280 millions, 100 millions are exports from this country to our Colonies, which, under the suggested policy would become internal trade, and the comparison must be made between the exports of America to countries out- side the United States, with exports from Great Britain and her Colonies to countries outside Great Britain and her Colonies. The exports from Great Britain to foreign countries have remained at about 175 millions from 1899 to 1902. In view of the fact that the great bulk of the Colonial productions are sent to this country, the total exports of the British Empire will be but little in excess of 200 millions sterling per annum. do not know' upon what information Mr. Crosfield

oundshis opinion that the McKinley Tariff will soon be,out down. I have clear recollection of the same opinion being expressed any time during the last 10 years. The only outward indication of it is that each Tariff Act puts on higher duties than its pre- decessors, and the American trade papers con- tinually dwell upon the benefits which have been derived from the protective policy. There is, however no suggestion that we should imitate the United States in this respect. My object is merely to lay stress upon the fact that the case of the British Empire in territory and population is analogous to the United States, and that the United States has proved that the adoption in such a case of a heavy system of protection, will not prevent the people enjoying unbounded prosperity while at the same time the country may command an export trade, which, as I have shown, is almost 50 per cent. greater than the export trade of the British Empire. I call the United States to witness that under conditions analogous to the British Empire, Protection need not be incompatible with prosperity, and I hay shown that the mere fact that the purchasing power of a sovereign might possibly be reduced, is not in itself an argument against an alteration in our fiscal policy, provided that the earning power of the people is more than proportionately increased. With your per- mission, sir, I will defer to a later letter some of the considerations which seem to me to point strongly to the belief that a modification in our fiscal policy in the direction of preferential trade within our empire will add to the earning power of this country, and will add to it to a degree far in excess of the trifling cost at which it will be bought. In the meantime, my endeavour has been to remove what I may call some of the prejudice which surrounds this question. The purchasing power of a sovereign and the dear loaf are bogies to frighten the ignorant. I only ask your readers to reserve an open mind to consider this question upon its merits, and to believe that fiscal policy is a matter of expediency, and not of Divine Law, and that the price of a loaf is nothing like so important as a full purse. Before closing, I extract the following from a leading article in the " Iron Age", the leading trade paper in the United States.

"For years the patient attitude of Great Britain in keeping her ports open to products of other coun- tries has been the subject of increasing wonder to the other nations of the world. The prestige of Great Britain as a manufacturing nation has been so seriously weakened, of course, not wholly by her fiscal policy, but partly as a result thereof that it has seemed to all careful observers that the time would surely come when there would be an awaken ing among her people, and they would refuse longer to permit their country to be a dumping ground for all the world."

div.head: MR. C. E. PARKER'S REPLY TO MR. E. W.
div.p: MR. C. E. PARKER'S REPLY TO MR. E. W.
BINDLOSS.
MR. PARKICR says :

Anyone in reading the last letter of Mr. Bindloss will be struck with the fact that he has wandered far from the object of this correspondence. The Editor of this paper asked several Manufacturers their opinion on the fiscal proposals of Mr. Chamberlain ad headed these letters accordingly. The main feature of these proposals was the consolidation of the Empire, which it was proposed should as far as possible approach to a fiscal unity. With this object in view it was proposed to tax food and possibly raw material from abroad, letting in the Colonial products free and further that as a return, the Colonies were to grant a preferential tariff to our manufactured goods. The central feature in the proposal of Mr. Bindloss is to "tax all manufac- tured goods coming into this country—that could be equally well made here—equivalent in amount to the tax other nations put upon our goods. It is not ttro- tection we ask for but only self-protection." Now in our opinion the alternative method of Mr. Bindloss of taxing manufactured goods, is only a little less foolish

div.head: out of whOse pockets. is this bounty to come.?
div.p: out of whOse pockets. is this bounty to come.?

Now Iclaim that the difficulties suggested by these questions arise directly out of the proposals of Mr. Chamberlain and are therefore pertinent to the main issue. These questions will have to he answered and answered satisfactorily before the country will adopt this scheme for taxing food and raw materials, or the alternative,—and more dangerous be- cause more attractive—scheme of Mr. Bindloss. Our friend evades these dißc ulties on the lame plea that he has not Ezekiel's gift and that he knows more aboutiron than cotton. It is a pity he did not recognize his limited gifts and his avowed ignorance before he ventured to challenge my argument relating to the ottori itti ritry out of which these questions spring.

In my last I refer at some length to the efforts trAders, buyers, and sellers have been making for long ye trs to facilitate the flow of trada. Mr. Bindloss says this is not true. lam not in the habit of making statements that are inaccurate, and in the future of this correspond- deuce I would recommend Mr. Bindloss to be a little more careful in his perusal of what I write, before he ventures to contradict a statement which is correct in every detail.

Mr. Bindloss asks: "Why should anyone o')ject to a calm, dispassionate ooasideration of the different circumstances now existing, proposed by Mr. Chamber- lain or anyone else?" Mr. Chamberlain's words in regard to this proposal are: "Were in for a big fight." When the proposer of this inquiry shouts his battle cries and puts on his war paint, he does not help to create an atmosphere in which the subject can ba dis- cussed in a "calm and dispassionate manner." Mr. Bindloss ends his letter by stating that we have carried the gospel of "offering the other cheek" alto- gether too far. I think it was Mr. Gladstone who said in reference to this subject: "If foreign countries try to strike you on the right cheek, are you going to be so foolish as to strike, yourself on the left?" And yet this is what Messrs. Chamberlain and Bindloss would have u s do. •

div.head: CORRECTION.
div.p: A CORRECTION.

In Mr. E. W. Bindloss's letter of last week we made an error of one word which confused the sense of his remarks. The word " removal " in the following extract from the letter should, of course, have been " renewal " :—" But to give Mr. Parker a chance of coming down from the clouds and standing on solid ground I should be inclined to advocate a re-noval of the corn tax which has been lately so much debated, with a remission in the case of our own Colonies . . .

div.head: MOSELY COMMISSION. WORK AND WAGES IN AMERICA.
div.p: THE MOSELY COMMISSION. WORK AND WAGES IN AMERICA.
A Chatty Letter from Mr. Whitham.

1 stated in my last paper that I was not satisfied with the Mosley report as reported in the "Examiner." I must now make an effort to show why I was dis- satisfied with what I must feel was as much, if not more, as could be fairly expected from visitors who would be rushed about the country, and who would to a certainty be made to see and feel all that could and must impress them. To begin with, their time was limited, and as a con- sequence they could not get behind the scenes. It is close on sixteen years since I left Warrington for San Flancisco and I am free to say that lam only now—and surely it is too late now to profit by the knowledge— beginning, to feel the immensity of the country. How could our friends be expected to see more than they did? The American feels he has a great country, and he has wide relations in his patriotism. He loves things that are great, and this goes a long way in the making of a people's character. When a man must fix his affecti ins on the small it tends to belittle him. The American is never afraid of exaggeration, and so he boasts of his country, and never lies. American patriotism comes near to hinnanitarism, for he wel- comes all nations. At least he says he does. Just now he is making a wry face because the British3r and his near relations are at the foot of the immigration lists, and the least desirable of Europe's South Eastern populations are at the top. In other respects the American feels he has lots of room to turn round in, and would continue to rejoice therein. It is necessary one sh mid get into this spirit thoroughly, so that when Washington's birthday comes r fund, he shall feel the blood tingle in h s veins when he hangs out the Stars and Stripes. He should feel th tt no amount of discomfort, and no limit can be placed on the risk he will run on the 4th of July when he feels that it was Britisher to Britisher, with the Hessian thrown in that over a hundred years ago made the Dutchman's throne totter,and laid the foundation of the mightiest nation the world has ever seen.

W:3 talking to an English-born friend who had been over to the old country just recently. He told me of the strange feeling that came over him on seeing the Stars and Stripes floating out to the breeze of London's Strand. I questioned him closely, and he did emphatically assert he "was proud to be an American citizen." Think of it. Well, my friend came to the United States a young man, I, if not an old man was certainly no spring chicken, and there- fore I must be esicused if I skip to the main question, and talk about it.

If our English friends had remained in the States months instead of days they would have learned to know the inner life of the Industrial Frankenstein. Now, I in no sense wish to depreciate the work of the commission. What it saw and has reported goes a long way in confirming what hr. Stephen Jeans and the "London Times" has been asserting "that not all the blame must be laid on the shoulders of the Trade Unions doctrine of Ca-Canny,"and "that the employers must shoulder their portion." I have found that to a very large extent the management and control of large developing industrial concerns is in the hands of men British-born, and the steadiest workers, the most re- liable and law abiding managers of the mills, mines, factories, and ship building yards are to a large ex- tent either British-born, or, are the sons of such. Dollars are at the bottom of the question. Does any- one think for a moment that my son Charlie would in Warrington have been to-day a very fair Spanish scholar receiving £3 lOs a week, and knowing when he moves he will get 1,5 a week, or that my daughter Ruby would be earning £3 15s. a week as stenographer and typewriter? Qf course the expense of living is high. Only a very moderate house can be had for 255. a week. Clothing is cheap and shoes are fairly so. Food has risen very much. The real expenses of an Atnerican family are in a direction that are not given in the market quotations. Of course what I have to say now on my personality must be left out. A man nearing 61 cuts no figure only in the sense of living )n others, if he has no savings of his own.

It costs in riding to and fro to business and other purposes for my family of six about 14s. a week, and the motor man and conductor are now asking for a shorter day with a minimum wage of 12s. for same. If I want a new hat, which I (1,3 by the way, I must give 10s. for it, and it will not be a tall shiner. I have just had my hair cut, and that cost me just a shilling. If I had not been an exception to the rule, which said rule is to carry around a bare face, I should have had to pay 7.1 d. extra. I save that! When I came out of the barber's shop,l might have stepped into the shoe-black's chair, and have had a shine cheap at sd. lam in a great hurry and money is pleLtiful when Ido the likes of that. My good dame is getting along in years, like her" boss," so she is hardly equal to the washing day. To get out of this trouble she pays her washer woman 6s. a day and does her best to make things nice while the suds are around. A laundry man then turns up, and where there is a crowd of young ladies and only one gentleman I can assure you that skirts, shirt waists, cuffs, collars,and starched shirts make quite an item in the total. If I have my shoes soled and heeled I pay 6s. for that little job, because I must have them done by a Union.

lam putting the Union man off for a while, he must be treated tenderly. I was a Union man at one time, but my way 4 looking at things didn't suit, so I was expelled. By the sway I should like the " Examiner 'to reprint the report of my trial. It would throw a little light on this question. I am going to the theatre this evening, at a cost of 2s sd. including cab fare. If I feel supperish when I come out that would cost another is., but that may be saved as something towards a new Latin school book for my youngest daughter Marion, who, although turned eighteen is still a school girl. If I were to approach the very interesting question of the young " ladies " gear, from the head down, or from the feet up, I should want them all around me to give me a few pinters. By the way did the reader notice I said "ladies." I wish him or her to understand that we have no" women" in America. Those whom others know as women, we only know as" ladies." I must say just here that lam writing on the 30th day of May, 1903. It is known as Decoration Day." The people all load themselves with flowers, and in crowds they flock to the cemeteries, and there theyl decorate the graves of the honoured dead who fell in the Civil War. It is a holiday and ' my folks have left me to cultivate the sad spirit all alone, but I refuse. Once upon a time there was a very eminent American statesman, and by the way all American Statesmen, are either eminent Judges or Colonels, who, in the midst of a very interesting speech came to a full stop and put this frank ques- tion to his spell-bound audience, "Let me see, where was I at, can you tell me ?" Now I know my readers are not spell-bound, but I must find out the answer to "where was I at." In all seriousness then I think the matter of dollars is at the bottom of the question we are probing. The commissioners say the worker is better off with lower wages in the United Kingdom than he would be in the United States. This is a hard thing to say. For eating and drinking, good clothes and good homes I think England cannotkompare with America. I thought different a dozen years ago, but there is no comparison between the America of fifteen years ago and the America of to-day. All that enters into the gaiety of life, even slum life is altogether different here. Where there is plenty of money coming into the home, there is plenty to spend, and life takes on its brightest colours. I have read scores of articles on this subject, and find no two agree. You may read in English papers and reviews the opinions of writers about it and still be no wiser. And yet there is a test. You seldom see an English workingman who has lived a few years in the United States return to his old home and setde down. On the other hand you never see an American workingman taking his family to England in the hope of bettering himself. Of course there is no comparison with any other country. I don't want anyone to run away with the idea that it is all just as it should be here in America. Take San Francisco for instance. The railroad is bringing into the State every week-end thousands of poor fellows. I am now in a position to know of what I speak. Every morning scores question me of the foreman, they are seeking work. Advertisements liberally spread through the eastern and middle States speak of low fares and the riches of California. I question these newcomers, they have all one tale. They • were told there was plenty of work and high wages. They were deceived, and there are thousands in this city to-day who wish they were elsewhere. And now to finish up this talk that has never approached the subject in view, I must say that I fear a terrible day of reckoning is near at hand, and as it deserves a fresh start we will do as Trestram Shandy did and take it into c new chapter. H. WHITHAM. San Francisco.

In the peaceful graveyard at Hill Cliffe the remains of I the late Councillor John Baird were laid to rest on 1 Saturday amid striking manifestations of respect. A ! large concourse of townspeople witnessed the last rites and the scene afforded a tribute to the esteem with which the deceased gentleman was regarded. The breweries of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son' Limited, where Councillor Baird had for so many years been employed, were closed at breakfast time and the work- men headed the funeral cortbge. Many of the deceased's colleagues in the Town Council together with officials of the Corporation attended the obs.equies. They left the Town Hall in cabs at 11-15. and joined the funeral procession at the late residence of the d N 3 ease d, Ha wth o rn• Lodge, Knutsford-road. Amongst those present were:— Aldermen Fairclough (deputy mayor), Francomb, Smethurst, Hutchinson, and Bennett; Councillors Davies, Duncan, W. Roberts, James Evans, Wilkinson, Tinnion, F. R. Roberts, Ellison, Lord, Sampson, Barton, and John Roberts; the Town Clerk,Deputy Town Clerk, Borough Treasurer. Borough Surveyor. and Mr. W Flood (chief inspector of nuisances.) The Mayor sent his carriage. A detachment of police under the direction of Sergeant Hollingworth walked first and behind them came the workmen from the breweries and representatives of the Ancient Order of Foresters. The chief mourners were :—First carriage, Messrs. Alec. Baird (son), Geo. Baird (brother), R. Wil- son, and W. Boyle; second carriage, Messrs. A. Baird (nephew), A. Baird (nephew), W. Lowe and T. Lowe; third carriage, Messrs. R. Lowe G. Moon J. Boyle, and T. Armstrong • fourth carriage, C. H. Unsworth (solicitor), Jolla Glover (representing as headmaster St. Ann's School), Griffiths, and Dr. Leadbetter (deceased's medical attendant) •, fifth carriage, Messrs. A. Eddowes, Charles Holland, and James Waldron (representing the firm of Messrs. Eddowes and Co., mineral water manu- facturers, of which the deceased was a director) IMessrs. Peter Walker and Son Ltd., were represented by Sir Peter Carlaw Walker (chairman of the direc- tors); Colonel John Reid Walker (managing director). Mr. James Monro (head brewer), Mr. Ernest Elli- secretary of the firm, Liverpool), Mr. J. Fulton Smith manager), Messrs. E. Parry, J. Y. Dunn, F. Parsonage, S. Parsonage, W. Parsonage, C. J. Smith, J. Ivan Smith, and J. Booth (brewers) ; Messrs. A. F. G. Potter (cashier), P. Wells, George Johnson, and J. Brunt (office staff) ; Messrs. T. H. Cox, S. Ross, J. Tilling, W• Hall, and T. H. Pretty (foremen of departments). The Con- ! servative Association and Club were represented by Messrs. George Jolley and William Holbrook I (registratign agent), and the Junior Conserva- tive Club by Mr. W. L. Williams; St. Ann's school (of which Mr. Baird was one of the foundation managers), by the Rev. James Davies and Mr. Wm. Richardson; and the Ancient Order of Foresters by about 60 members(all employees of Messrs Peter Walker and Sons,) chief among them being Bro. John Chrimes, P.D.C.R. •, Bro. Joseph Jenns, S.W. ; and Bro. James Marsh, P.C.R. The Gilbert Greenall Lodge ' of Freemasons (No. 1250) of which deceased had been a member for a considerable number of years. was repre- sented by Bros. E. Rose, P.M., P.P.D.G.D.C., secretary: W. H. J4Jenkins, P.M. P.P.G.R. ;R. Lunt, P.M. ;J. R. Griffiths, P. M.;A. F. G. Potter, P.M.; C, Holland, P.M. J. H. Lee, M.E.Z., 1250 Chapter; T. Showan, S.N. 1250 Chapter; T. Laws, 1250 Chapter; Rev. B. Percival, chaplain, 1250 ,• Rev. W. Bracecamp, dep. chap. 1250; C. G. McDowell, S.W., 1250 ; John Roberts, Wm. Rogers, John Hedgecock, W. J. Shaw, G. D. Southerden, A. Jolley, W. Roberts. Other brethren present were Messrs H. F. Greenough, P.M., 148, and Chas. Leigh, S.D., 148 Bros. J. S. Patten, P. Z. J. W.IG. Craddock, W.M., and C. B. Aylward wrote regrettingtheirlinability to attend. Amongst others present were Mr. F. Monks, Mr. V. E. Heathcote-Hacker,of Sale (representing the Manbte Saccharine Co., London) ; the Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mr. E. R. Parry (Liverpool), and Mr. Bonehill. The burial service was conducted by the Rev. B. Percival, vicar of St. Peter's, and the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's. The whole of the funeral arrangements had been carried out by Mr. H. F. greenough, of Heathside. Floral tributes were forwarded by the following : Mrs. A. Baird, Warrington; Mr. and Mrs. W. The only way of overcoming this is to serve them with sauces, made with a good thickening of Brown & Poison's" Patent" Corn Flour. In this way a wonderful variety can be obtained For instance, you can have Cauliflower au Gratin Tomato Sauce, Gratin Sauce, Dutch Sauce, Mushroom Sauce. div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
LIVERPOOL AND DISTRICT LEAGUE. FIRST-DIVISION.

WARRINGTON V. ST. HELEN. s.—Up to the present the Warrington team has had a very unsuccessful season, defeats being the order of the day. It has now been decided to abandon further efforts in the senior league and devote all attention to the junior competition. Only a poor team did duty for Warrington in the en- counterwith St.Helens at the Corporation baths on Tues- day evening and the visitors had matters all their own way. During the first half five goals were registered and after the interval four more were added. The War- rington men were totally unableto pierce the visitors defence and the result was.:—St. Helens, nine goals; Warrington, nil.

div.head: SECOND DIVISION.
div.p: SECOND DIVISION.

WARRINGTON RESERVE V. BIRKENHEAD RESERVE.— This match proved considerably more interesting than the senior encounter, both teams displaying capital form. Birkenhead ledat the interval by three goals to two, whilst early on the Cestrians added a fourth. War- rington, however, pluckily pulled themselves together, and added three goals in the last few minutes, andwon an exciting contest by five goals to four.

div.head: DEATH OF EX-JUDGE FFOULKES. Twenty-four Years on the Bench.
div.p: DEATH OF EX-JUDGE FFOULKES. Twenty-four Years on the Bench.

We regret to annouce that ex-Judge Wynne-Ffoulkes passed away at five o'clock on Saturday morning, at his residence, Northgate House, Chester. Born on the 14th July, 1821, Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes was the fourth and youngest son of the late Lieut.-Col. John Powell Ffoulkes, of Eriviat, Denbighshire, his mothen being the daughter and co-heiress of Captain Robert Jocelyn, R.N.—Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes was educated at Shrewsbury School, from which ha went to Jesus College, Oxford. He entered Lincoln's Int and was called to the Bar in 1847. He was nominated Revising Barrister for the North Wales circuit in 1868, and a Commissioner of Escheat for Chester and North Wales, the duties of which office he performed from 1872 to 1874. In the following year he was appointed County Court Judge of circuit No. 7, which includes Birkenhead, Warrington, Runcorn, Leigh, Northwich and WinSford, and formerly Wigan also. After twenty-four years on the Bench he retired. The late judge was twice married. His two wives had pre- deoeased him, and four sons and a daughter survive him. Early in his career he was agent to the Marquis of Westminster, father of the late Duke of Westminster. In his day he was an athlete. A good oarsrnan, he rowed in at least one race every year from the ages 0f,15 to 23
BOY MURDERER SENT TO AN ASYhUM.

An intimation was received at Stockton on Wednes- day that the Home Secretary had ordered the removal of the eight-year-old boy, Patrick Knowles, to Broad- moor Criminal Lunatic Asylum, instead of placing him upon his trial for the murder Of Frederick Hughes, a fifteen months' old child, by burying the infant alive at stockton, on May 30.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
St. Peter's Church.

There was a good attendance at an "open" meeting in connection with the Men's Service 'which was held on Sunday afternoon. The Rev. D. R. James presided. The vocalists were Miss Longdin and Mr. Edward Pownall, who rendered several solos in a very creditable manner. An inspiring address was delivered by the Rev. A. S. Cameron, M.A., on the "Last Judgment." Mr. F. Webster prenided at the organ. The offertory was devoted to the church repair fund.

div.head: Christ Church, Latchford.
div.p: Christ Church, Latchford.

At this Church on Sunday afternoon, the Bishop of Chester preached to a good congregation from the words " And your feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of Peace" (Ephes. vi. 15). The offectory, mwhich in aid of the endowment fund e ounted to 49 17s.

div.head: St. Paul's Church.
div.p: St. Paul's Church.

At this Church, on Sunday, the annual sermons in aid of the Assistant Curates' Society were preached in the morning by 4he Rev. Morley Stevenson, and in the evening by the Rev. W. Braceoamp. The collections realized £lO, being an advance of £2 on last year. The Rev. T. W. Barber, formerly ef St. John's, Longsight, Manchester, and Holy Trinity, Warrington, will, to-morrow (Sunday) enter upon his duties as sezlior curate of St. Paul's.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golborne-street.

On Sunday last at the above church the Pastor took as the subject of his evening disoourse Dr. Haeckel's well-known book, entitled "The Riddle of the Universe." The writer's views on such subjects as monism, immor- tality, human freewill and liberty were discussed, and it was pointed out that Haeckel, although one of the greatest scientists of the day, could not be considered anauthority in the religious sphere. In conclusion the preacher stated that the arguments of scientists and philosophers could not affect Christianity, that when these men had done their work the Christian Ch urch which Christ came to found would still remain firm and secure. Mr. Dunnico will continue the discourse next Sunday, when many of the views advocated by Dr. Haeokel will be dealt with.

div.head: Open-Air Services at Hill Cliffe.
div.p: Open-Air Services at Hill Cliffe.

The first of these open-air services, which have proved so successful in past years, was held at Hill Cliffe on Sunday evening last. The evening was an ideal one for the purpose. The day had been hot and oppressive, and there was a slight, pleasant breeze blowing, so that an open-air service was much to be preferred to a service within doors. Although the service had not been publicly announced, there was a good attendance, andas the fact of their being held on each favourable Sunday evening will become better known, they will doubtless be as popular as ever. The pastor (Rev. J. S. Hughes) conducted the service. The chapel hymn book was used, and the choir gave as a chorus one of Sankey's newest pieces. The Nineteenth Psalm was given as the lesson, and the preacher took as his theme "Jesus Christ and Him Crucified." The service was only a short one, being kept well within the hour specified, and everyoneseemed to enjoy the season of public worship in the temple of nature.

div.head: Emmanuel Reformed Chtirch.
div.p: Emmanuel Reformed Chtirch.

IThe Rev. E. R. Venables Greene, MA. from the Pun- jab, Inditt, preached the Sunday School sermons at this church on Sunday. In the evening, speaking from the words " Prees forward," the speaker gave an interesting resume of his work, and dwelt at length on the necessity for pressing forward the spread of the Gospel message amongst the natives of our great Indian Empire. Mr. Greene alluded to the preparation of Mr. Joseph Callan— a former member of the church—for work in the mission field, he having been accepted by the Reformed Church as i missionary. It is interesting to note, as showing Mr. Greene's love for the work, that he has for the last three and a half years borne the eat ire cost of main- taining the Punjab Mission. Special hymns were sung by the choir, and the solo "Jesus,lover of my Soul" was I exceedingly well rendered by Miss Beatrice Carriage I Mrs. A. Landon presided at the organ.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The usual meeting of Wycliffe P.S.A. was held on Sunday last. Mr. George Wallington presided, and spoke upon " Press Forward." After drawing lessons from the walking contest, which are just now so com- mon, he alluded to the great Christian race, and exhorted all to cast off everything that prevented their good running. Rev. A. Kirk, of Peasley Cross, was the speaker, and took as his subject "Temptations." He said all were tempted, therefore it was the experience of all. The great Patriarchs were tempted,the man in the pulpit as well as the man in the pew; the man in the church as well as the man in the street. Then our great exemplar was tempted, even Christ, the perfect man was Son of God,therefore Christ was the great healer and soother in the darkest and most severe temptations. The tempter came in various ways, sometimes with his glaring temptations at other times with all his deceptive and cunning ways. Temptations to all had theiepeculiar side, to trap men in their weakest parts, and unguarded moments. To overcome was beyond the human help, Christ alone, who understood theminutest parts of our moral and spiritual being could help, succour, and deliver as His presence could at all times le felt. Mr. R. H. Pearson rendered two violin solos. Mr. Greenleaves and Mr. B. Farrar took part in the meeting. Consider- ing the very hot day, there was a fair attendance.

div.head: Old Brunswick (Runcorn) Anniversary.
div.p: Old Brunswick (Runcorn) Anniversary.

Runcorn Methodists have been pleasantly employed in celebrating the 103rd anniversary of Old Brunswick which was observed on Sunday and Monday. Services were held at the Drill Hall on Sunday morning and evening. The preacher was the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones. On Monday evening Mr. Jones delivered a lecture on John Wesley and the meaning of Me tho- dism." The Drill Hall was crowded. Mr. David Wet, kins, of Upton, Chester, presided, and was supported on the platform by the ministers of the circuit and several other gentlemen. The Rev. E. Lloyd Jones traced Wesley's career. He said that Churchpeople made much of the fact that he was a Churchman. He was a Churchman who did not believe in a State Church. He said that more corrup- tion was brought into the Church through alliance with the State than all the persecutions which the Church had ever experienced from enemies outside. He was a Churchman who did not believe in the parochial system. He asked how could they have Godly discipline with the parochial system? He was a Churchman who did not believe that a bishop was any better than any other parson. He believed that men who had not been ordained were called to preach the gospel. He believed a man could be saved though he was not baptized. There were two periods in John Wesley's life. There was the period previous to 1836 when he was a miser- able, narrow High Churchman. That was John Wesley, curate and unconverted. He said himself that he was at that time an unmixed Pharisee. The Church did nothing to bring John Wesley to see salvation faith. After detailing the events which caused Wesley severance from the Established Church, the lecturer went on to say that his message through Methodism was to the poor. He had a profound reverence for the poor. If he wanted the doctrine of realtentleness and the highest of Christian religion he always went to the poor. Methodism supremely was a message to the poor There was no higher mission for any Church than minis- tering to the poor. Methodism stood for the re- discovery of the doctrine of the Holy Ghost. The greatest discovery, however, was the pardon of sin. John Wesley was the first to point out that Christian experience was an unanswerable argument for the truth of the Christian religion. Was this Church to continue asked the lecturer in conclusion? Yes, he replied, if she always began where John Wesley began, and his Christianity began where Churchism ended. ' There was special singing by the scholars and choir at the services and lectures. The accompaniment was provided by the Runcorn Orchestral Society. Collec- tions were taken in aid of the school funds.

div.head: LONDON'S BEST.
div.p: LONDON'S BEST.
" The British Weekly," June 20th, 1903, says:

Alike among journalists, the general public, and Free Churchmen, there is much said on the growing interest. and excellence of "The Daily News." It seems to improve day by day, and in all its splendid history, was never more vigorous and vital than it is now. Every department of the paper is being brought up to a high level. We are very glad to know that the result has been a largely increasedcirculation alike in London and in the provinces. "The Daily News" deserved support, were it only for its noble renunciation in the abandonment of betting news. But after all, no paper will succeed for negative merits, and "The Daily News" can stand safely ea its quality as a great newspaper. We hope that Free Churchmen everywhere will give it their heartiest support. They may begin this support for the sake of thepaper, but we promise they will continue it for their own salres. Select " The Daily News " as your morning paper,and read it in the Train, Tram and 'Bus, as a silent protest against the Betting and Gambling Evil.

div.head: COLNE ALDERMAN RESIGNS.
div.p: COLNE ALDERMAN RESIGNS.

- - -- At Colne Town Council on Wednesday night a letter was read from Alderman Brooker Carey resigning his positionyon the Council and on the Education Com- mittee. Mr. Brooker Carey is secretary of the Colne Beneiltßuilding Society, in connection with which there have recently been heavy defalcations. In the letter to the Council he asked not to be judged too Iharshly. The resignation was accepted.

div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must mall cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended for publication must be written on one side Only of the paper and sent in, if possible,not later than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short letter has a much greater chance of insertion than a long one.
We cannot under ordinary circumstancesundertake return themanuscripts which are not used.

div.head: Music in the Park.
div.p: Music in the Park.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to reply to Mr. Armstrong's letter, which appeared in your last issue. This gentleman has somewhat misread my letter, for I distinctly referred to brass banal, not military, for both bands that he refers to viz—Volunteers and Fletcher's, are not brass, but military. T beg to differ with him in reference to the" Messiah" being played threadbare. The Volunteer programme of Sunday lasti apparentivihears out the opinion expressed in my first letter, for I noticed with pleasure that five items from leading oratorios were inserted. He also mentions the "Pastoral Symphony" being unsuitable to brass bands. Did I not refer to choruses, not instru- mental items ? I contend that any chorus when cor- rectly played by a good brass band, is quite as effective, if not more so, than any other combination of in- struments.

I should be pleased to have Mr. Armstrong's definition of secular/ music. Surely he will not class Sullivan's operas, waltzes, Sze., as sacred music, for he states that, all music is sacred when properly played. I am sorry if I have written one word that will in any way discourage bands,—and I am surprised Mr. Arm-. strong can see anything in my letter bearing on same- My letter was not written with that intention, rather the other way, for I follow with deep interest every local band's success,or otherwise,and m 3 sole object in writing was to endeavour to raise the standard of brass bands in this town. Further, I did not draw attention to the bands of 20 years ago, but to bands of the present, for lit is possible for bands to degenerate; I am quite certain the majority have not improved. I have always had the deepest regard for the Volunteer Band,and would not like to say one word to its depreci- ation. Also I greatly respect and admire its late veteran conductor, and I am sorry if I have given him the slightest offence.—With every good wish for the pros- perity of local bands, Yours,
ONWARD.

div.head: Trades Unionists and the Price of Shaving.
div.p: Trades Unionists and the Price of Shaving.

Sir,—Thanking you for this and other insertions T must again encroach upon your valuable space and reply to the letter which appeared in your columns last, Saturday signed "The Committee Warrington Hair- dressers' Society." Although the author tries to hide his identity he has utterly failed to disguise himself. If the letter had been written in a more gentlemanly spirit and free from sarcasm its origin would be more difficult to trace. Sarcasm is one of the author's well-known characteristics. He is quite an adept in that particular art. That the letter was not an official one is proved by the absence of the Secretary's signature and my letter which appeared in your issue of the 20th is styled a free ad- vertisement. This is very true indeed, its it was free' from expense thanks to the editor's generosity. The author then assumes to be a school master and tries to enlighten your readers upon matters they have known for years, respecting the way in which strikes and lock- outs are conducted, but even in this he displays his ignorance, for I never knew a strike where men were asked to help without conforming to the rules. lam then accusedlof boasting of my secretarial duties and also wanting to "boss the show." Such statements are puerile and purely false. I have always had my suspicions that any advance in the price of shaving would not be an all-round success, without giving the public something extra for the increase. I could not obtain the advance and still work on the old- fashioned methods, so I am determined to offer each of my customers pot, brush and fresh water. This has been quite a success, but without the innovation my business would have been greatly reduced. Mr. Editor excuse me if I have taken up too much of your valuable space, but I am quite willing to let the public arbitrate and no one else.—Yours respectfully, E. SMITH.

div.head: Warrington Summer Camp for Poor Children.
div.p: Warrington Summer Camp for Poor Children.

the company of Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins awl Inspector Hackett, -f paid a visit on Thursday afternoon to the Camp already formed at Moreton in the Wirral ' District and which camp can be utilised this year as a Warrington Seaside Summer Camp for poor children. On making a general, survey of the camp, one could not help being- struck by the suitability of the place for such a purpose. There is an excellent supply of water obtainable; there ,are capital facilities for bathing; the arrangements for cooking and storing food are all that could be desired; the sanitary arrangements appear to be satisfactory; there is plenty of open and free ground for playing purposes, for drill, or for walks; and the air is of a,very bracing nature. Now, sir, seeing that it is desired by the committee who have the work in hand, that the first squad of boys be sent on Saturday, July 18th, it is hoped that the necessary funds will be forthcoming, and thatthose who are in sympathy with the movement may accord their most generous support, so that a permanent Warrington Camp may be organised and maintained.—Yours (tc.. FRED J. EMSON.

div.head: TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: THE TOWN COUNCIL.
Forthcoming Business.
The monthly meeting of the Council will be held on Tuesday at 6 p.m. when the following among other business, will be transacted :
SPECIAL MOTIONS.

By Councillor Dodds: That the case of tram,con- ductor Spencer be investigated by the Tramway and Electricity Committee, and that in harmony with the resolution of the Council of the Ist July, 1902, he be allowed to be represented by such persons as he may appoint. By Councillor Pemberton: (1.) That the resolution passed at the last meeting of the Council to pull down the Old Armoury and build an inspector's house be rescinded. (2.) That a committee be appointed•to ;in- vestigate the last three slack contracts for Wiawick and Delph-lane waterworks.

div.head: QUEnIONS.
div.p: QUEnIONS.

By __Councillor Pemberton.—To ask the Chairman of the Watch Committee :1. What was the amount allowed by the Contractor for the police buildings for the old materials under the contract? 2. As the Contractor did not take all the materials was not an allowance .made,,and if so,what was the amount allowed? 3. Has the whole account been adjusted, and if so, what are the figures now? By Councillor Lord.—To ask the Chairman of the Water Committee: 1. Has the Water Committee corn- pleted its investigation regarding the Slack Contract? 2. When will a complete report thereon be presented to this Council? 3. What firm is at present sending in supplies.?
VICTORIA PARK AND THE SITE OF THE OLD POLICE
STATION.

The Street Improvement Committee recommends that the Borough surveyor be instructed to prepare plansand estimates for the widening of tinutsford-road near Victoria Park by the construction of a permanent river wall; that the site of the old police premises, after the widening and improvement of the several streets in Howard-place, be paved with flags.

div.head: PURCHASE OF SETTS.
div.p: PURCHASE OF SETTS.

The Paving and Sewerage Committee has resolved that the Chairman, Deputy-Chairman, Mr. Alderman Hutchinson, and Mr. Councillor Pemberton be appo in t,ed a sub-committee to inspect and report from time to time upon the delivery and quality of setts purchased by the Committee.

div.head: OPEN' SPACES.-IMPORTANT RECOM MEND AT lONS.
div.p: OPEN' SPACES.-IMPORTANT RECOM MEND AT lONS.
The General Purposes Committee submit the follow- ing report of the Open Spaces Sub-Committee : The Open Spaces Sub-Committee beg to recom- mend :

1. That a row of trees be planted in St. James' Old Burial Ground along the river side,and that the same be protected byan unclimbable fence. 2. That the ground near theentranee to Victoria Park be suitably laid out. 3. That Messrs. John White, Maclver and Co. be ap- proached with a view of obtaining an open space for the Fairfield Ward. 4. That application be made to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £5OO, being the estimated cost of fencing and laying out the Recreation Ground off Liverpool-road vecently purchased from Lord Lilford. 5. That the members of this committee be authorized to inspect the open spaces in the Wallasey District with a view of laying out the open space in Orford-lane in a similar manner.
