div.p: The Examiner, Saturday July ,4 1903.

the same idea of uniformity being observed. Several THE MECCA OF METHODISM voting men carried a statue of the Madonna and Child very prettily decorated with lilies and trailing greenery. St. Benedicts' school made a brave show. There were some exquisite floral devices including a lovely harp of ferns and greenery set off by roses with vane-coloured streamers. Several young ladies carried a floral arch and there was also across of artistic design. The infants carried gilt crosses decked with roses and some little boys were tastefully clad in Court suits of blue. St. Mary's, Buttermarket-street, was headed by the League of the Cross band, and the banners formed the most striking feature of the display. The in- fant boys in one class all wore white sailor hats whilst on the heads of manylof the little girls were dainty wreaths ofiroses. St. Mary's School, Latchford, was headed by St. Edmund's Band, Runcorn. A pretty floral device bearing the word" Mary" excited general admiration: The children were very pleasingly dressed, and presen- ted a charming picture. The Sacred Heart School brought up the rear of the procession, the music being supplied by the Pioneer Band. A statue of the Sacred Heart decorated with artificial flowers was borne by young men, and a number of the banners also depicted the Sacred Heart. There was a beautiful cross com- posed of lilies Scc., and an arch from which baskets of flowers were suspended heightened the effect. The pro- cession occupied about half an hour to pass a given point,and all who witnessed it appeared to agree that it excelled . all previous efforts. After traversing the arranged route the scholars proceeded to their respective churches, where there was the Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament.

div.head: WARRINGTON WALKING DAY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WALKING DAY.
THE PROCESSIONS.

Warrington gave itself up yesterday to the celebration of the annual ,children's festival known for so many years as Walking Day. It was again an unqualified success and proved to be as popular as ever. There have been sinister rumours recently as to the abandonment of the festival, bet the mere thought of such an undesir- able procedure is a pure invention, and has no founda- tion in fact. To blot out Walking Day from the children's calendar would be a dire calamity, for the festival has for raany years been looked upon as the happiest in the year by Sunday School children and no other attraction •could compensate for its removal. One had but to look at the expressions of happiness so apparent on the faces of the children yesterday to be convinced of the real enjoyment which the festival affords.

The town wore its annual festive appearance, and the bright sunshine which shone so radiantly added to the joyousness ef the occasion. Flags and banners floated lazily in the gentle breeze and the whole length of the route of the procession was gay with bunting. Here and there lines of flags were stretched across the street, whilst numerous banners were to be seen protruding from windows, , and others suspending from flag-staffs. People assembled along the line of the processiondand others took up positions at the windows of upper storeys and other coigns of vantage to witness the pro- cession. The scholars commenced to arrive on the lawn in front of the Town Hall shortly after nine o'clock. The Mayor and Mayoress and partya.ssembled on the Town Hall steps and • from this elevated position a good view was obtained of the schools as they entered and left the park. Detailed decorative effects were less easily attained in so vast a throng but the eye was attracted by the living wealth of colour and beauty. In the mass the display was imposing and quite up to the reputation of previous years. When the children filed through the central gate and walked along the streets the effect was even more pleasing. The scholars passed along in what seemed an almost endless chain to the strains of lively music, and their pretty dresses and smiling faces,with banners and•floral designs borne aloft helped to make up a pleasing picture. The Nonconformists did not, as was the case last year on the occasion of the Coronation celebrations, proceed to the Town Hall. There were, however, pro- cessions of numerous Nonconformist schools early in the morning, and they made an excellent display. A few proceeded to the Town Hall, but most of them paraded the principal streets and then entrained at the railway, stations for pleasant spots in the immediate neighbour- hood or proceeded direct to fields just outside the town. The Wycliffe scholars again journeyed to Dunham Hill. Bold-street Wesleyans paid a visit to Lymm whilst their friends at Silver-street spent the Clay at Helsby. The Golborne-street Baptists had an enjoy- able tune at Acton Bridge and St. John's Presbyterian scholars went to Frodsharn. The Cairo-street school and congregation accepted the invitation of Mr. F.Monks to spend the davat Walton Old Hall. Walton Lea being no longer available as the rendezvous of the Workingmen's Mission, the scholars disported them- selves in it field in Rose-lane, Sankey. Shortly after ten o'clock the signal was given for the first school to lead off the procession from the Town Hall. One or two schools had still to arrive but it was ' thought advisable as several threatening clouds were gathering, to start the general procession without delay. Fortunately the rain kept off and the warm sun continued to shower down its welcome rays until the evening. One or two slight showers were experienced during the day but these did not interfere with the children's en- joyment. The Blue Coat school occupied the place of honour and headed by their own band, the children in their neat dresses of blue serge and white collars and collarettes, filed through the central arch. They were followed by the children 1 from the Padgate Industrial Schools, in charge of Mr. 1 and Mrs. Wright (the superintendent and matron), and were accompanied by several Guardians. The boys wore the usual uniform of corduroy, with white collars, and the girls wore neat yet simple grey dresses, with white straw hats and blue bands. The industrial band was in the forefront, and the lads looked very smart in their corduroy suits and peaked caps. The usual route was taken, and the arrangements were on a similar scale to .those of last year. The proces- sion was much the same as in previous years, very few special features having been introduced. Some of the banners were tasteful and expressive; others " redeemed crudity of design by an excellent moral I purpose. Held high above a bevy of little girls attired in white was a banner bearing the inscription, I "Consider the lilies, how•they grew," whilst on another I banner in the midst of some pretty girls were thewords 1 "Harmless as doves!" Floral designs were displayed I on the top of poles and suspended from them were coloured ribbons in Maypole fashion, held by charming little fairies dressed in white. Others carried baskets I filled with choice flowers. Decorated mail carts were I again much to the fore, and pretty children were to be seen cosily ensconced under canopies of bright material. Flowers and ferns were also used in the decoration of several mail carts.

A feature of the Emmanuel Reformed *Church pro- cession waggle carrying of small triumphal arches of roses, clematis and daffodils. Church Lads' Brigades figured in the processions of the St. Clement's and St. James's schools. Thelast named school also introduced a model yacht on wheels which was jealously guarded by boys in naval costume. In the forefront of St. Peter's school there walked a number of pretty little dames in Old English costumes. Their long white dresses were relieved with orange-coloured sashes and their poke bonnets gave them an old-worldappearance. Lurries rejoined the procession in Arpley-street. These heavy and substantial vehicles drawn by horses, decor- ated with ribbons and bells, waited with their human freight of smiling youngsters in Hanover-street, and joined their respective schools as they passed along. The following was the order in which the schools left the park:- 1 Blue Coat School and Band. 2 Padgate Industrial School and Band 3 Parish Church and St. Helen's Church, Hollinfare andCrosfield's band.

4 St. Gnome's Missionand Lymin Band. 5 St. Clement's Mission and Church Lads Brigade Bugle Band. 6 St. Paul's and Ardwick Green Industrial Band. 7 All Saint's Mission. 8 Holy Trinity and Preston Brook Band. 9 Factory-yard Mission. 10 St. Luke's School. 11 St. James' and the Volunteer Brass Band. 12 St. Ann's and Walker's Band., 13 St. Barnabas' and Fletcher's Band.l 14 St. Peter's and" Guardian" Band. 15 Emmanuel Reformed Church. 16 Legh-street Primitive Methodist and own Band. 17 Latchford Primitive Methodist. 18 Sharpe-street Primitive Methodist. 19 Buckley-street Independent Methodist and own Band.

20 Salvation Army. The procession was a little shorter than usual owing to the children walking four deep instead of two. The Ragged School and Sankey Bridges Wesleyan did not i join n the general procession this year. The schools were marshalled into position by Mr. R. T. Fairclough and Mr. Councillor Craik, who have filled the onerous position of maishals for a number of years. Perfect order was kept by the Chief Constable and his excellent staff, and they are to becongratulated upon the efficient manner in which they carried out their duties. After proceeding along the appointed route, many of the scholars attended services at their respective churches. In the afternoon they adjourned to fields in the dis- trict where they disported themselves to their hearts' content.

div.head: ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION. A Beautiful Spectacle.
div.p: THE ROMAN CATHOLIC PROCESSION. A Beautiful Spectacle.

A prettier spectacle than the Roman Catholic pro- cession has seldom, if ever, been seen in Warrington. Everyone will be willing to concede that in point of spectacular display the Roman Catholics always carry off the palm, but yesterday they enhanced their repu- tation. Teachers and parents alike must have been to infinite pains to prepare the children for the beautiful pageant in !which they figured so proudly. In the art of marching the Roman Catholic children are very much to the fore. Whenever there was a momentary halt one could hear the little feet marking time in quite military style, and it was fully evident that this proficiency alone was the outcome of careful training. Bridge-street was the only thoroughfare in which one could view the proces- sion in its entirety, and as was to be expected, a great crowd assembled. The spectators did not show very much consideration for the comfort of the procession. jets. Even in the widest parts of the street the foot- paths were' practically unoccupied. The people pressed as near to the centre of the road as possible, and the spacalleft for the children to pass iiionewas very limited indeed. As a consequence the effect of the marching in Indian file was not as pleasing as it other- wise would have been. At one time it seemed as if the procession would be spoiled by rain. The sky was over- cast and in fact there was a sharp shower. Soon, however, the sun burst through the clouds and the fears of children and anxious parents were allayed. The pageant from beginning to end presented a very beauti- ful sight. There were banners of rich texture and workmanship depicting the Seven Sacraments of the Church, the Blessed Virgin, and the Saints, and here and there a glittering precessional cross, followed by a group of acolytes in eassocks and surplices. arrested the attention of the spectator. The grouping of the children was perfect and as they marched along in all the glory of fine raiment the public could not refrain front applauding. St. Alban's scholars had the honour of heading the procession and they marched to the strains of the Borough band. The infants were very charmingly attired in white with sashes of various colours, but the uniformity in each group was a note- worthy feature. Each little child carried a bouquet or basket of flowers, Tbe elder scholars also wore sashes,

div.head: GREAT SANKEY AND PENKETH.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY AND PENKETH.

Walking Day was celebrated in the usual way at Great Sankey and Peniketh yesterday afternoon, and was as successful as any of its predecessors. The weather was showery at times, but this did not inter- fere with the afternoon's programme, or damp the enthusiasm of the participants. The scholars attending Sankey Sunday School (St. Mary's Church) assembled shortly after one o'clock, and headed by Walker's Brewery Band they proceeded along the high road and Stocks-lane to Penketh, where they were joined by the scholars attending the Penketh Mission. The proces- sion was then continued as far as the "Black Horse,"and the processiOnist retraced their steps to a field near the Vicarage,kindly leht by the Vicar. Amongst those who took part in the procession were the Rev. J. R. Jones, M.A., (vicar), Mr. W. Hodgkinson (superintendent) and Mr. Hill. The band played a number of lively tunes, and games were indulged in until tea-time, when the scholars proceeded to the schoolroom and partbok of tea. On returning to the field games were played until dusk. —The scholars attending the Wesleyan *Schools turned out in large numbers and those too young to undertake the walk were accommodated in lurries. There was a plentiful supply of banners and Penkeih Tannery Band headed the procession. A start was made from . the schools about 1.30. The route lay along Heath-road back through the village and round by the park to the recreation ground. Amongst those who joined the pro- cession were the Rev. John Gunnell (resident minister), Mr. C. E. Parker, Mr. Ambler and Mr. Watson. Tea was served in the schoolroom and full justice done to the good things provided.Sportsand games of various kinds were afterwards held on the recreation ground where an enjoyable time was spent.

div.head: MUNICIPAL TRADING INOUIRY.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL TRADING INOUIRY.

Details of the Scheme. At the meetina of the Town Council on Tuesday even- ing the result of the deliberations of the special joint committee appointed to formulate an inquiry scheme will be submitted. Alderman BOLTON will move:—

(1.) That an inquiry be held into all trading by past and present members of the Council or officials of the Corporation with the Corporation, either direct or indirect, through limited companies or officials of such companies, or as contractors or sub-contractors, or any dealings or transactions of any kind whatever between members of the Town Council or officials of the Corporation and the Corporation. (2.) That the inquiry shall be made bysix persons to be called Commissioners, three of whom shall be selected by the rown Council and three by the members of the Non-Trading Committee. That each side shall agree to the person selected with- out demur, and that neither side shall appoint a lawyer. (3.) That the period of inquiry shall be from the Ist of April, 1896, to the 31st March, 1903. (4.) That the costs of the inquiry shall be borne by the Corporation, and that the Commissioners shall receive no remuneration. (5.) That the Commissioners shall have power to call anybody and everybody, member of the Council, official or servant, contractor, sub-con- tractor, or other person to give evidence or information touching the inquiry.. (6.) That the Commissioners shall have power to call for every minute book, paper, and document of the Council and of any and every Committee to be at the service of the Commissioners, or of such clerks or assistants as are acting for the Commissioners. (7.) That any person who desires to give evidence (one way or the other) shall be allowed to do so provided that such evidence has, in the opinion of the Commissioners a direct bearing upon the matter to be inqui;ect into. (8.) That the Mayor shall give a written indemnity to ally witness, being an employee of the Corpora- tion, and requiring it, in respect of any truthful evidence he may give. (9.) That neither the public nor the press be ad- mitted to the sittings of the Commissioners. (10.) That a shorthand report of the proceedings shall be taken by such persons as the Commissio- ners may appoint. (11.) That the Commissioners shall report their findings to the Town Council and to the Non- Trading Committee.

div.head: PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY. The Question of Audit.
div.p: THE PARLIAMENTARY INQUIRY. The Question of Audit.
The Joint Parliamentary Committee which is inquir- ing into the question of Municipal Trading met again on Monday at the House of Lords, the Earl of Crewe presiding.

Mr. Cliarles Henry Wilson, President of the Society of Accountants and Auditors, and chairman of the Parliamentary Committee of the Leeds City Council, was the first witness called. Questioned by the Chair- man, he said he thought the system of keeping munici- pal accounts was a good one, but he was in favour of a change in the system of electing auditors. The Chairman : How should they be appointed.—By the Corporation themselves, subject, if necessary, to the criticism of the Local Government Board. Asked if he would retain the elective auditors, wit- ness said he would not for several reasons. First. of all very few voters could be induced to take part in the election. In Leeds there were 80,000 and not more than 800 went to the poll when an auditor had to be elected. Then there was no guarantee that the elective auditors would be men trained to acoounts. His Society had endeavoured to get accountants to stand for stuch positions, but the men had declined to do so befauie they found the matters committed to them were not confined to accounts. Socialism and many other things were in- cluded in the matter submitted to them. Corporations had in some cases appointed and paid professional auditors, but witness did not know whether their action was legal. He suggested that the auditor should be appointed for a term of not less than three years and should not be removed without the approval of the Local Government Board.

Mr. Jeeves, Town Clerk of Leeds also gave evidence. He said the accounts of municipal undertak- ings were carefully kept. Usually each under- taking was in charge of a separate com- mittee, who jealously guarded the interests of the undertaking and who in turn were carefully watched and criticised by other committees and the Council, In his opinion the most critical audit would 1 not affect much change in the relative position of the , various undertakings. He objected to the Local Government Board audit, and pointed out that Mr. Long had definitely stated that the Educa- tion Act audit was not to be taken as a, precedent for further change in that direc- tion. On the question of allowances for de- peciation witness said he would point out that a sinking fund was to the Corporation what the depreciation fund was to a company. It might be desirable to have a reserve fund in addition, but the need for this was obviously less by reason of the sinking fund. Corporation undertakings were at least as well and as economically managed as those of companies,and the accounts were certainly as accurately kept. Other, witnesses having been called, the Committee adjourned.

Garden Party. A garden party was held at the Rectory on Saturday afternoon in aid of the funds of the Society for the Promotion of Christian Knowledge. The society was represented by the Rev. VT. Robinson, organizing secretary of the Northern Province, and amongst the other clergy present were—The Revs. Canon Penrhyn (Winwick), Canon Willis, E. C. E. Carleton, A. S. Cameron, E. Chadwick, and C. A. M. Edwards (curate of St. Thomas's, Stockton Heath). Garden games had been provided and tea prepared, the tables , having been beautifully decorated with flowers under the superintendence of Mrs. Willis. It was pro- posed to listen to an address in the open air from Mr. Robinson on the claims of the society, but as he was about to commence his address rain fell heavily, and it was decided to adjourn to the side chapel of the Parish Church. Here prayer was offered and two appropriate hymns sung. The organizing secretary delivered an interesting address on the work of the society in all parts of the world. The rev, gentleman was heartily thanked for his address, on the motion of the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, seconded by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. The service was then brought to a con- clusion,.and tea -was served in the rectory gardens,

div.head: PILGRIMAGE TO WESLEY'S BIRTHPLACE.
div.p: A PILGRIMAGE TO WESLEY'S BIRTHPLACE.
[By Arthur Bennett.]

It has been a cherished wish of mine for many years to visit Wesley's birthplace. But the little town in Linc.)lnshire had always seemed remote and inac- cessible, and this illusion had been sedulously fostered by my friends in the same county, and I had been con- tent, as yet, to take them at their word. But; when I suddenly awoke t: the the fact that we were on the eve of the two hundredth anniversary of Wesley's birth, and recollected all I owed to him and to the church he founded, and what England owed to both, I made a sudden vow to pay the long-anticipated pilgrimage forthwith, and found at once that, to anyb xly who possessed a spark of enterprize, Epworila was not really inaccessible at all, and that, if it were diffi- cult to visit it from Lincolnshire, at any rate, it was easy enough to visit it from Warrington. It is quite true that it meant getting lip at five o'clock, an under- taking not too easy to "St John's" degenerate dis- ciples in this lazy age; but one recollected that he rose himself habitually at four, and pilgrims worthy of the name could surely not object to rise, for once, an hour later.

And so on Wednesday morning, 'June the 17th, accompanied by two enthusiastic pilgrims of the other sex, I found myself comfortably seated in the train for Doncaster at nine minutes to six. Another lady and two ogler gentlemen got in at Godley, and something seemed to tell us quite instinctively that these were fellow-pilgrims. We parted at Penistone, but the surmise proved corrept, as will appear a I:ttle later. At Barnsley three men joined us whom .ve also mentally set down as pilgrims. This surmise likewise proved correct in part, f ,r two of. them were local preachers, one a rustic-looking blacksmith, and one a thriving grocer from the town ; whilst the other was a Wesleyan, but, alas ! instead of going to Epworth, was pulling himself up by the roots, so to speak, and leaving all his old associates to find a lonely home in Yarmouth.

The ride through the great colliery district which lies between Barnsley and Doncaster was new ground to me, and it was with a thrill of interest that I looked and listened as my comrades pointed out the dwellings of the Denaby miners; detailed to me the real history of the evictions, and proudly said that those gray ruins on the hill beyond were the remains of Conisborough Castle. It was altogether a delightful journey. At Doncaster, a buxom, but hard-headed, Yorkshire widow—who kept an inn, as we had rightly guessed,—and a particularly rubicund and cheery butcher joined us, both of whom were bound, they told us, for Thorne Show, concerning which they waxed so eulogistic that it made us long tef accompany' them, the widow mak- ing many a shrewd and sensible remark in a rich Yorkshire brogue; the butcher pleasantly discoursing with our pious friend, the blacksmith, not, alas! of Wesley and of Methodism, but upon the virtues of "the undercut" and the "possibilities of obtaining it, and the blacksmith making our mouths water with his appetizing details of a certain country tea. The widow and the butcher left us as we came in sight of a green field beset with canvas, and strolled off amid a crowd of similar enthusiasts towards the show; and, as we dived still deeper into the cool c auntry side, and reached,at last,the sleepy Isle of Axholme, Methodism once again was obviously in the ascendant, and at Crowle—a curious old leafy village flanked by a broad, cpol canal—where several brakes awaited us, the whole surroundings seemed to take a Methodist hue. I could almost, have sworn to every occupant of our own brake,for you can tell a really good Methodistic as certainly as you can tell a barrister, a curate, or a country squire. The Methodist face is essentially 3,1 kindly face, with a touch of almost womanly tender- i ness in it. Sometimes it is narrow, and sometimes it ' is ignorant, but it is nearly always lovable, and Methodism is the truest and the best freemasonry I know.

The Mecca of Methodism is five miles from any station, and to that extent it justified the legends Of our Lincolnshire friends as to its inaccessibility; but the drive was through a flat, fertile, leafy country, with a peep at the fine church and rectory of Belton, and a glimpse of Temple Belton—a picturesque old home of the Knights Templars—on the way. We also got a view of the new line from Goole to Elaxey, which will ultimately link "the capital of Axholme " with the outer world; and our companions (most of whom were local preachers) all discoursed so pleasantly as we pro- ceeded that the drive seemed strangely short. One assured me that Axholme, once, had really been an island. One took particular pains to impress upon me that he was thoroughly acquainted with agriculture, and spoke with much authority upon the crops, and on the unfenced fields which lined the road, and are, it seems, a char tcteristie feature of" the Island." Another spun "ghostly yarn as we rode up a long and lonely country lane which wis the scene of it. /VIA yet another, fat and flourishing, a builder from the town of Wombwell (whom, ray neighbour said, had greatly prospered in his trade), with business pride, de3larad that he had drawn a thousand p3unds for various rep tirs to Belton or to Epworth Church. I.greatly wished to ascertain if he w6re the misguided Individual who hadsold the Epvvorth pulpit and a quantity of the old oak in it (they were now somewhere in America, I understood), but he occupied the end of the long brake remote from me, and so my curiosity was unappeased. And perhaps it was just as well, for I might have boiled over! rhe black- smith and the grocer were among the party, and were busily comparing notes concerning sermons preached in various country places • and the lady and two gentlemen who had joined us in the train at Godley sat just'opposite, the lady verifling our surmise by declaring that she was not only a Wesleyan,but an actual native of John Wesley's native village. - -

But presently the land began td rise a little, and soon we saw, amid the trees, a low, square tower from which a flag was floating, and we thrilled to learn that we were actually gazing on the tower of Epworth Church. And then we passed along a straight and dismal road, saw two immense marquees in an adjacent field, and turned abruptly into the old place itself. A strip of canvas hung across the longandpicturesque main street, and on it were inscribed brief words of welcome; whilst, immediately in front of us, we saw the beautiful Memorial Church, which stands, with its graceful spire, and schools, and ministerial residence amid a spacious garden, and is in every way a worthy tribute to a great man's name. Almost directly opposite, we saw the Memorial Church erected to the memory of Alexander Kilham, founder of the Methodist New Con- nexion, who, like Wesley, was an Epworth man. The narrow, winding thoroughfare was gay with flags, and over it there also stretched, suspended high in air, the words of Epworth's most distinguished son—" The world is my parisll," "The best of all is God is with us," and "One Heart, One Way." On one of the sus- pended flags a portrait of "St. John" confronted us,and, on the other side of it, a portrait which we vainly tried to make into his brother Charles, but which, we found, was a presentment of old Mr. Barnes, the much res- pected founder of "The Epworth Bells," a little local newspaper with a melodious name which issues weekly from the tiny office where the street diverges into two, to form a tiny isle of shops and houses near the Market Place. And here we called to purchase from a , pretty damsel a pictorial Guide to"Epworth and its sur- roundings," some picture post cards, and an illustrated programme for the day. In many of the old-fashioned windows we could see old copies of the various engravings so well-known to all good Metho- dists—the fire at the Rectory, The Holy Club" at Oxford, John Wesley preaching from hi 5 father's grave, and the triumphant death-bed scene among the rest. The doors of nearly all the houses framed good-natured groups of smiling natives, mani- festly proud of their small town and big with the importance of the day. The path; and roads were occupied with eager visitors, the major part of them sincere and simple old-world Methodists frotn the surrounding villages, with many who had come from places more remote. Black coats, white ties, and soft round hats were frequent; at the office of "The Epworth Bells," we brushed against the Rev. Nehemiah Curnock, editor of" The Methodist Recorder " ; and on tbe ancient Cross in the Old Market Place (disfigured by an iron canopy erected at the Coronation) we perceived the sturdy figure of the Rev. C. H. Kelly, an Ex-President of the Conference, and the leading ministerial lion of the day. From this rude monument John Wesley preached to his fellow-townsfolk, and it naturally attracted crowds of pilgrims all the day. The open space a little to the left of it, in front of the Red Lion—the chief local inn—was occupied with booths, and shooting galleries, and the like ; and the woman in charge of one of them, produced a venerable tea caddy, which, she said, had been presented to her by a former mistress into whose appreciative hands it had descended from an ancestor who actually saved it from the Rectory Fire. Its pedigree appeared to be authentic, but, as she asked six pounds for it, I closed my heart and purse, and turned instead into the Red Lion, to try to obtain accommodation for the night. The inn was full, the genial hostess said, and she appeared to doubt if we should manage to find room elsewhere. And certainly it was not easy. Every bed in Epworth seemed to be bespoken; and we had serious thoughts of going on to Temple Belton (now a sort of leafy Guest House) for the night; but, I bethought me of the lady- pilgrims, and remembered that it was quite three miles away; and, after many interviews and several disappointments, the ladies were provided with accommodation by the kindly wife of the local photo- grapher; whilst I went on to the King's Head andinter. viewed the landlady, who, after anxious consultation

with her buxom daughters, presently relieved my mind by stating that they would manage to find me a room. The King's Head faced a narrow street which ran up from the Market Place. Between its gable end and the approaches to the village school, a noble avenue of limes conducted us directly to the Church. A man with a collecting plate stood at the gate, and a printed notice told us that our offerings would be applied towards the restoration of the bells. We paid our tribute, and passed on into the venerable building. It was "old, bat of uncertain date," the Guide Book said, "and of plain Gothic architecture." It could boast some tablets and some coloured glass in memory of later rectors; but these were of little interest, and the Rector who had made the church's fame appeared to be entirely uncornmernorated, nor was • there any monument to any of his nineteen children; but a distinguished-looking old gentleman with a long white beard was good enough to show us two fine oak chairs, on one of which he pointed out the date, " 1560." This, I understand, is known as "Wesley's Chair." The com- munion plate, I subsequently learnt from Mr. Kelly, was contemporaneous with the Wesley's but, for some unearthly reason, the white-bearded gentleman said nothing about it, and did not show us either this or the stone coffin which is said to be among the treasures of the church, and seemed, indeed, to think considerably more of his stained glass windows. It was only by actual enquiry from two owlish-looking vergers near the door that we discovered that the font was used in Wesley's time (both John and Charles were said to have been baptized in it), and, when I talked of climb- ing the tower, they dissuaded me by tales of birds and other difficulties, and said that visitors were not per- mitted to ascend. The communion table had (through someone's kindness) been presented to the beautiful Memorial Church.

Outside, however, we were frail, at any rate, of Samuel Wesley's graveaandets we gathered round it in the greenand leafy yard,we each recalled how Mr. Romley— a poor, narrow-minded curate—had declined to let John occupy his father's pulpit, and had actually refused the sacred bread and wine to him, exclaiming, "Pray tell Mr. Wesley I shall not give him thesacrament, for he is not fit." It was also fit, in the highest degree," John writes,in his incisive style,"that he who repelled me from that very table where I had myself so often distributed the bread of life, should be one who owed his all in this world to the tender love which my father had shown to his, as well as personally to himself." Refused admit- tance to his father's pulpit, John preached bravely from his father's tomb, to "such a congregation," he says, "as I believe Epworth never saw before." Two curious indentations marked with lead are said to in- dicate the spot where Wesley stood on this occasion, and where afterwards, each evening fora week, he "cried aloud to the earnestly-attentivecongregation." We were amused to find that some of the assembled crowd appeared to think that these were actually Wesley's feet- marks, but even those less credulous were fain to stand upon the sacred spot, and conjure up the memorable scene. "I've come all the way from Scarborough to stand here 1" said one old men, with quivering voiceand dewy eyes. There were many who. had come much farther who were glad to stand there too ! We had imagined that the Rectory adjoined the church but found that it was SOlll9 distance away,ahough just a glimpse of its red roof was visible above the trees. But thither we resorted, now, to find four stately damsels—daughters of the Rector—at the door of the walled erden,taking toll of Weoley's followers to repair the ancient building we had lately left; and a singularly genial youth who intimated that he was the Rector's san took oharge of us,andjled us over velvet lawns and through the pleasant shado.v of gigantic trees, into the house, a picturesque, two-storied, creeper-covered, red-roofed, comfortable place which, after all, was the chief object of our pilgrimage. With charming courtesy, the Rector's son conducted us to his own room—which occupied the same position as the room from which that earlier Rector's son had been so providentially saved from the great fire when only six years old; smiled pleasantly when somebody suggested that he must find inspiration from such sancti- fled surroundings, and declared that Wesley's fame at any rate, had been the means of introducing him to us; and liatened with surprizing patience to a pompous fellow who appeared to think it was his duty to talk patronizingly of England's Church, arid thrust the claims of its evangelistic off-skaOt almost rudely down the young man's throat; expressed his cordial sympathy with my belief in ultimate Re-union; asked interesting questions of a minister who had come all the way from America to attend these celebrations ; and fenced with our contention that the Wesleyans outnumbered, now, the Mother Church itself, by leaving the American Methodists outside his calcula- tions altogether on the curious ground that they had Bishops! We met his reverend father coming up a narrow flight of stairs, and pioneering cheerfully another pilgrim-party. He pointed out to us the ancientschool- room of the nineteen budding scions of the Wesley family (a bathroom now), and corroborated the report that Ann and Martha Wesley, two of Samuel and Susanna's children, had scratched their names upon the plaster of the neighbouring corridor, though these were hidden, now, by the new wall-paper. I But possibly the place which interested us most, was the long, quaint attic known as "Jeffrey's Room "(in memory of a local suicide), for here all sorts of strange disturbances were heard in Wesley's time, so singular and unaccountable as to suggest a supernatural origin, and so alarming as to scare the maids away. And, even yet, the Rector's son informed us, the old tradition served to complicate the servant problem, hard enough to solve without the fear of ghosts ! The little com- pany who heard him were distinctly sceptical, for the most part, and philosophically talked of rats and birds, but the Rector's son was probably wiser, and seemed to half believe the ancient tale.

Returning to the garden, we were show the very spot the window occupied from which the lad of six escaped (some said the old timbers had been used in building the new Rectory), and it did not need the help of any engravings to make us conjure up the vision of that stormy winter night when all the house was wrapped in fiery con- flagration, and the famous boy was "plucked like a brand from the burning" by the stalwart man who stood upon acomrade's shoulders,and restored to his distracted parents just before the roof crashed in, at which his father, kneeling in the snow, thanked God for his miraculous escape, and said that house and home might gladly go. Returnity, by the Cross, we saw two somewhat windy evangelists declaiming to the assembled crowd exactly as in Wesley's time; passed on to join a crowded com- pany at a most ample lunch provided in the beautiful Memorial School; and afterwards strolled back towards the Cross, diverging, on the way, to peep on tip-toe through the broken windows of the old, and now dis- mantled ohapel(erected on the'site of a still earlier ahapel and opened by the famous Dr. Adam Clark in 1821), but decorated now, with some belated placards left as relios of a pArliarnentary election; and then strolled slowly down the street, now thick with visitors, towards the grounds of the Memorial Chapel, from whence we hoped to view the Procession (timed to start at 2-15 from the Cross), and, after watching it, if possible, attend the Official Service. It was the intention of the promoters that the visitors should join in this Procession, but the fact was not explicitly stated, and we somewhat stupidly assumed that it would be a purely local Procession,got up as a sort of spectacle, and that our only chance of seeing it, and also of attending the service, was to make in good time for the pleasant grounds of the Memorial Church. And thither we accordingly resorted, to dis- cover thatialready the steps and a considerable portion of the path were occupied, and that continually the numbers grew. And, long before the time announced for the commencement of the service, theapproaches to the church were thronged, but still there were not any signs of the Procession, and so, to while away the time, some ardent soul burst forth:

1 "0 for a thousand tongues to sing My great Redeemer's praise, The glories of my God and King, The triumphs of His grace." And there, amid the rain which had begun to fall, the multitude struck up this grand old hymn to a grand old unforgotten tune; and, when, at last, the music eied away, we heard, above the murmur of the multitude, the music of a band, and, looking out across the sea of faces, caught a glimpse of unaccustomed movement in the densely crowded street, and tried in vain to make it into the Procession. There was a momentary tumult in the throng of pilgrims gathered round the entrance to the Churchl and then the doors were opened and the crowd began to filter slowly through. But the steps were kept by several big policemen, and my friends and I got separated in the crowd, and it had dawned on me, by this, that it was practically hopeless to attempt to get inside, and that we ought to have joined in the Procession, and so passed in with them. At this, not realizing that it had already passed, I struggled back towards the gates, intending to fall in as it approached, and move with it up the broad way which would, I did not doubt, be made for it; but found, to my intense chargin, that the Procession, such as it was, had followed in the wake of the band, and simply swelled the struggling crowd who still beseiged the doors. And, hurrying back to thern,'l heard that even tke aisles were packed by now, and that no more would be admitted. At this, the bulk of those still left outside dispersed to seek admission at the other Chapel just across the way, or saunter back towards the Cross ; but I resolved' to wait, and try a little later, foaling that the large crowd within would gradually locate itself, and that there would be almost certainly- some space to spare. And, just as the great congre- gation joined with heart and voice in the grand opening hymm, I was rewarded by a place in one of the aisles, which was not yet quite full, and, ere the hymn was over, was accommodated with a seat in an adjacent pew. It was an inspiring sight to see this beautiful memorial building filled with eager faces, pouring out with heart and voice the strains of a familiar hymm; to gaze to- wards the chancel, packed with eager faces too ; and to ' reflect that, there, the actual Communion Table used in Wesley's time now stood, whilst,to the various emo.tions of the hour, a thrill of local pride was added as I recol- lected that the beautiful 'oak reredos was executed by a firm of fellow-townsmen—Messrs. Robert Garnett and Sons, of Warrington. The selected preacher was the Rev. C. H. Kelly.and it was an ideal choice, for he is one of the manliest man who ever occupied a pulpit. His tall, commanding presence, his strong but genial face, his sturdy voice, and his vigorous, incisive style were admirably suited to the place and time, and I listened to his noble tribute to John Wesley's memory with rapt attention, and a pride and thankfulness I found it quite impossible

to repress. On the day that Wesley was born, he said;. a tree was planted in the Epworth church-yard. The tree had long since died,but God had also planted there. a tree which had not died, but lived and grown, sent mighty roots beneath the sea, and reared new trunks in every continent, whose leaves were for the healing of the nations; and we might well rejoice in our great founder, and in all he signified, and all he had achieved. There were some boor creatures who, on getting rich, abandoned their ancestral faith, because, forsooth, they wished" to get into better society."lt is impossible! the grand old fellow said, "There is not any better society." A great Guild Rally at the Cross had been announced for six o'clock, but the skies had altogether ceased to, smile on us ere this; and so, to everyone's intense regret, the evening meeting in the open air, which vcraB to have been 'a specially appropriate feature of the cele- brations had to be reluctantly abandoned, and a service held in the Memorial Church instead. _ _ _

It rained so heavily that, like some half the congre- gation, I was fain to linger there, examining the old chancel table,which somebody had given to the trustees; the interesting memorial tablets, the numerous founda- tion stones, which bore the names of various generous donors to the Building Fund; and, in particular, the fine oak font which had been given by Mr. Thomas EL Walker, of Bolton, in memory of Susannah Wesley, and like the reredos, was the work of Messrs. Robert Garnett and Sons, of Warrington. The rain abating, I set out in search of my lost lady friends, and found that one of them, like me, had heard the Rev. C. H. Kelly, and the other the Rev. Nehemiah' Curnock in the Kilham Memorial Church across the way. There was some time to spare before the evening service, and so we went to one of the immense marquees erected for the accommodation of the multitude of pilgrims in the neighbouring field, and, there, defied the weatherand secured a welcome and substantial tea. , The great • Guild Meeting in the Memorial Church commenced at six, and was in every way most worthy of the Guild and the occasion, the chairman a Leeds lawyer (and a son of the Rev. W. 0. Simpson) making one of the best speeches I have ever heard, and setting forth most lucidly the leading traits in Wesley's life and character. Immediately upon the heels of this another mighty meeting started, with a genial North- umbrian in the chair, Sir W. H. Stephenson, who was,' he said, a Methodist of the fifth generation, his great-great grandfather having sold to Wesley the site of the third preaching place in England. He, too, alluded to the spurious pride of the poor fools who, getting rich, begin to be ashamed of the old faith, and said, like Peter Mackenzie, he "would not give two-• pence a dozen for them." I left when he had finished, and was fortunate enough' to hear Mr. Walker and the Rev. Nehemiah Curnock in. the Kilham Churchlacross the way ; and, as Sir William Stephenson arrived with the same speech went on to, oqe of the marquees to hear an oration from the Rev. J. Pickup, of Widaes, and, later, yetanother stirring speech from the Rev. C. H. Kelly. Returning; at a quarter past eight, I ventured to look in again at the Memorial Church, at which my lady friends had both elected to remain, and found • a local preacher holding forth at idiotic length to the attenuated remnants of an audi- ence, some of whom had actually been sitting there for quite four hours!

a Afterwards with my companions, I sauntered through' the dear old town and past the Rectory again, and leav-- ing them amid a company of belated pilgrims drinking a most dismal fluid misnamed coffee at our friend the photographer's,l rambled to the still awl silent church, and triedj amid the dusk to picture through the trees r the flames which burst, that memorable night, from the old Rectory windows. The streets by this were practically empty, though a few enthusiasts-- not very good Methodists perhaps—still lingered by the booths and shooting galleries in the Market Place; andr as it was nearly closing time, I turned at last into the King's Head: and presently retired to rest upon an' ancient bed in an old room which looked across a far= yard and a small but beautiful green croft to Wesley's. Church ; and, as I lay in dreamy reverie, could hear the bells, which had been chiming pleasantly at intervals all day, toll out the midnight hour, and almost see 01d Samuel Wesley sauntering beneath the sombre shadov? of the churchyard trees. As I was sinking into sleep, I heard a hideous noise in the farm yard below, and was aroused. next moment by the hoarse voice of mine host exclaiming," What's the matter ?" I rose and peered into the yard, and for some time longer I could see him pacing to and fro around the buildings with a lantern apparently accompanied by one of his men. Dogs barked and a stalliod in an adjoining stable loudly neighed,. and curiosity had almost prompted me to join them 111 their midnight quest when presently I saw the glimmer of the returning lantern, watched it disappear within the house below, and then (for eyes and brain and feet were weary)hea,rd the chimes grow gradually fainter,and sank speedily into a sound and restful sleep. Soon after dawn I woke, and, long before the village was astir, was strolling round the church yard once! again, and gathering flowers in it. I asked the landlord what the noises of the night had signified, but he had not been able to unfold the mystery. I rivaa-, der if his midnight visitor could possibly f t been "Old Jeffrey's" ghost? But a homely break as was awaiting me; my friends had promised to join Mil on the brake which left for Haxey Station at a little) ' after eight ; and soon we were descending the sweet slopes of Epworth hill, through smiling country lane bedecked with briar roses, and watching wistfully gradual disappearance of the winding street. the win".„ mill; and the old equarn tower in whose gray shade there had dawned an influence which had saved a churril from ruin and a realm from revolution, flowed out le healing streams into all lands, and made the little "capital of Axholme," at the close of these two hundred years, a shrine for ever sacred to the thirty millior! children of the greatest and most numerous Protest'i' Church in the world.

div.head: MOTOR-CAR SUNK IN THE CLYDE.
div.p: MOTOR-CAR SUNK IN THE CLYDE.

An exciting motor-car accident occurred on Thursdal afternoon at the ferry by which the Clyde is crossed. at Renfrew. A car containing two gentlemen and chauffeur was proceeding down the incline leading t° the ferry, when the brake failed to act. The car ran oa to the ferry boat, and dashing through its back gates, fell into the river. The car Immediately sank, leaving the occupants struggling in the water, whence all three were rapidly rescued.

div.head: Soldier Stabs a Woman.
div.p: Soldier Stabs a Woman.

William Smith, a private in the South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Warrington, was sent to gaol for three months at Manchester on Saturday. He had accosted an old woman in Deansgate and stabbed her in the neck.

If the facts alleged are correct, a bigamous marriage by a Lancashire husband is paralleled by a similaraction on the part of his wife. James Shaw, a Tyldesley miner, who has spent several years in the army, is said to have married his first wife—she was called Emma Leather—at Monton, in 1872,and to have gone through the form of marriage a second time. in November, 1901, at Nottingham, with one Jane Walton, a widow. He told the Manchester County Stipendiary, however, that the second " wife " knew quite well that he was a married man. The magistrates sent him for trial to ' the assizes.
